title: Political Contributions by Certain Investment Advisers

ai_data.summary_of_main_idea: The Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) proposes to rescind Rule 206(4)-5 (the "political contribution rule") under the Investment Advisers Act of 1940, along with related recordkeeping provisions under Rule 204-2(a)(18). Currently, the rule imposes a two-year ban on receiving compensation from a government client if an investment adviser or its covered associates make political contributions to state or local officials who can influence adviser selection. The SEC aims to replace this prescriptive regime with a principles-based compliance framework that relies on existing anti-fraud provisions, general fiduciary duties, compliance procedures under Rule 206(4)-7, and codes of ethics under Rule 204A-1.
ai_data.challenges:
1. Administrative Procedure Act (APA) Flaws: Rescinding a 15-year-old prophylactic rule without empirical evidence demonstrating a reduction in pay-to-play corruption risks is arbitrary and capricious under 5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A). The SEC relies on circular reasoning by arguing that general anti-fraud provisions are sufficient, ignoring its own 2010 factual findings that broad anti-fraud rules failed to prevent pay-to-play practices.
2. Regulatory Enforcement Gap: Exempt Reporting Advisers (ERAs) and Foreign Private Advisers (FPAs) manage trillions in assets (including public pension allocations) but are explicitly exempt from the Compliance Rule (Rule 206(4)-7) and Code of Ethics Rule (Rule 204A-1). Rescinding Rule 206(4)-5 leaves ERAs and FPAs completely unmonitored by internal pay-to-play policies, creating a major regulatory loophole.
3. Defective Economic and Empirical Analysis: The SEC heavily relies on voluntary survey data from regulated industry groups while ignoring academic consensus showing that political connections and campaign contributions systematically distort public pension investment decisions, reduce net returns, and increase advisory fees borne by public retirees and taxpayers.
4. First Amendment Misapplication: The SEC assumes that compliance costs chilling employee political speech justify total rescission, overlooking binding precedent (e.g., Blount v. SEC; N.Y. Republican State Comm. v. SEC) holding that pay-to-play rules narrowly serve a compelling government interest in preventing corruption.

references.title: Blount v. SEC, 61 F.3d 938 (D.C. Cir. 1995) (Upholding pay-to-play regulations against First Amendment challenges under strict/intermediate scrutiny)
N.Y. Republican State Comm. v. SEC, 927 F.3d 499 (D.C. Cir. 2019) (Reaffirming the constitutionality and rational basis of SEC Rule 206(4)-5)

ai_data.proposed_comment:
PUBLIC COMMENT SUBMISSION

Date: November 1, 2026
To: Vanessa A. Countryman, Secretary, Securities and Exchange Commission
From: Civic Policy & Administrative Law Advocacy Coalition
Re: Comments on Proposed Rescission of Political Contributions by Certain Investment Advisers (Release No. IA-6994; File No. S7-2026-31; RIN 3235-AN65)

I. INTRODUCTION
We respectfully submit this comment in opposition to the Securities and Exchange Commission's ('Commission' or 'SEC') proposed rescission of Rule 206(4)-5 under the Investment Advisers Act of 1940 ('Advisers Act'). While we acknowledge the compliance friction and operational complexities cited on Pages 57701–57703 of the Proposing Release, total rescission represents an arbitrary and dangerous reversal of federal oversight that exposes public pension funds, retirees, and taxpayers to renewed quid pro quo corruption.

II. LEGAL DEFECTS UNDER THE ADMINISTRATIVE PROCEDURE ACT
1. Rescission is Arbitrary and Capricious (5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A))
On Page 57705, the Commission attempts to justify rescission by claiming that existing rules—namely Rule 206(4)-7 (Compliance Rule) and Rule 204A-1 (Code of Ethics Rule)—provide a 'sufficient principles-based framework.' This reasoning directly contradicts the Commission’s factual findings in the 2010 Adopting Release (75 FR 41018), where the SEC explicitly concluded that general compliance programs and anti-fraud rules alone are insufficient to deter lucrative pay-to-play schemes. Under Motor Vehicle Mfrs. Ass'n v. State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co., 463 U.S. 29 (1983), an agency changing course must provide a reasoned explanation for disregarding its prior factual findings. The SEC has provided no empirical evidence that underlying corruption risks have abated since 2010.

2. The Regulatory Blindspot for Exempt Reporting Advisers
On Page 57706, the Commission acknowledges that Rule 206(4)-7 and Rule 204A-1 apply *only* to registered investment advisers. Exempt Reporting Advisers (ERAs) and Foreign Private Advisers (FPAs)—which collectively manage over $7.5 trillion in private fund assets—are exempt from both rules. Rescinding Rule 206(4)-5 removes the *only* rule holding ERAs accountable for pay-to-play practices, creating an unjustified enforcement loophole.

III. PROPOSED ALTERNATIVE REGULATORY TEXT
Rather than total rescission, the Commission should adopt targeted amendments to modernize Rule 206(4)-5, eliminating operational burdens while preserving core prophylactic protections.

Proposed Rule Modifications to 17 CFR § 275.206(4)-5:

1. Modernize De Minimis Contribution Thresholds (17 CFR § 275.206(4)-5(b)(1)):
Amend section (b)(1) as follows:
'(1) De minimis contributions. The prohibition in paragraph (a)(1) of this section does not apply to contributions made by a natural person who is a covered associate to officials of a government entity if: (i) The covered associate was entitled to vote at the time of the contribution and the contributions do not exceed $1,000 in the aggregate to any one official per election; or (ii) The covered associate was not entitled to vote at the time of the contribution and the contributions do not exceed $500 in the aggregate to any one official per election, with both thresholds indexed annually for inflation.'

2. Clarify and Restrict 'Covered Associate' Definition (17 CFR § 275.206(4)-5(f)(2)):
Amend section (f)(2) to explicitly exclude non-executive vice presidents and administrative staff whose roles do not involve soliciting government business or direct policy decision-making regarding public pension capital.

3. Streamline Curing of Inadvertent Violations (17 CFR § 275.206(4)-5(b)(3)):
Extend the return timeline from 60 calendar days to 120 calendar days from discovery, and allow a firm-level administrative fine or escrow cure in lieu of a strict two-year compensation ban for inadvertent contributions under $2,500.

CONCLUSION
We urge the Commission to reject total rescission and instead adopt the balanced, modernized amendments proposed above.

COMMENTS OF CIVIC ADVOCATES AND MAILER COMMUNITY

Re: Proposed Rule on Labels 888, 889, 891, and 892 Discontinued (91 FR 57301, Sept. 9, 2026; Docket No. 2026-18371; 39 CFR Part 111)

I. INTRODUCTION
These comments are submitted in response to the Postal Service’s proposed rule published on September 9, 2026 (91 FR 57301–57302) to amend the Mailing Standards of the United States Postal Service, Domestic Mail Manual (DMM), to discontinue Labels 888 (Tracking), 889 (Signature Confirmation), 891 (Insurance up to $500), and 892 (Insurance over $500).

While we support the Postal Service's efforts to enhance visibility, tracking, and operational efficiency through Intelligent Mail package barcode (IMpb) technology, the complete phaseout of manual peel-and-stick extra service labels introduces substantial operational burdens on small businesses, metered mailers, and rural post office patrons.

1. Lack of Readiness Assessment for Non-RSS Post Offices (91 FR 57301-57302)

Proposed Rule: Air Plan Approval; Reconsideration and Repeal of Air Plan Partial Approval and Partial Disapproval of North Dakota's Regional Haze State Implementation Plan for the Second Implementation Period (91 FR 57302, Sept. 9, 2026).

I. INTRODUCTION AND STATEMENT OF INTEREST
The undersigned submit these comments urging the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) to withdraw its proposed approval of North Dakota's 2022 Regional Haze State Implementation Plan (SIP) revision. The EPA’s proposed reversal of its prior 2024 partial disapproval is arbitrary, capricious, and contrary to Clean Air Act (CAA) Section 169A.

II. SPECIFIC CITATIONS AND LEGAL DEFECTS

1. Unlawful Reliance on an Uncodified 'URP Safe Harbor' Policy (91 FR 57308–57310, Section IV.A.1.b)
On pages 57309–57310, EPA asserts that 'so long as the Class I areas impacted by a State are below the URP and the State considers the four statutory factors, the State will have presumptively demonstrated it has made reasonable progress.' This presumption violates the governing 2017 Regional Haze Rule (RHR) regulations. When EPA promulgated the 2017 RHR Revisions (82 FR 3078, 3099), it explicitly rejected establishing a 'safe harbor' for states whose visibility metrics are on or below the URP glidepath. EPA explicitly ruled that '[t]reating the URP as a safe harbor would be inconsistent with the statutory requirement that States assess the potential to make further reasonable progress towards natural visibility goal in every implementation period.' EPA cannot alter codified regulatory requirements via preamble policy shifts in individual state actions.

2. Arbitrary and Capricious Failure to Justify Reversal Under State Farm (91 FR 57309, Section IV.A.1.b)
Under Motor Vehicle Mfrs. Ass'n v. State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co., 463 U.S. 29 (1983) and FCC v. Fox Television Stations, Inc., 556 U.S. 502 (2009), an agency reversing prior factual determinations must provide a reasoned explanation for disregarding its previous record findings. In 2024 (89 FR 95126), EPA documented that North Dakota improperly rejected feasible, cost-effective emission control measures at Coyote Station, Antelope Valley, Coal Creek, and Leland Olds. In the current proposed rule, EPA fails to offer any new technical or economic analysis demonstrating that these controls are no longer cost-effective or necessary under the four statutory factors of CAA § 169A(g)(1). Instead, EPA simply relies on the URP position to excuse the State from requiring controls, rendering the four-factor analysis a meaningless paperwork exercise.

III. PROPOSED ALTERNATIVE Wording
To comply with CAA Section 169A and 40 CFR 51.308(f)(2), EPA must issue a final rule that retains its 2024 partial disapproval of North Dakota's Long-Term Strategy and Reasonable Progress Goals, formatted as follows:

'40 CFR Part 52 [Amended]
Section 52.1820 is amended by disapproving North Dakota's long-term strategy for the second implementation period under 40 CFR 51.308(f)(2) due to the State's failure to conduct lawful four-factor analyses and mandate reasonable, cost-effective NOx and SO2 emission reduction measures for Coyote Station, Antelope Valley Station, Coal Creek Station, and Leland Olds Station. EPA shall promulgate a Federal Implementation Plan (FIP) establishing source-specific emission limitations based on modern control technologies within two years of final disapproval.'

IV. CONCLUSION
EPA should re-affirm its 2024 partial disapproval and ensure meaningful visibility improvements in Theodore Roosevelt National Park and Lostwood Wilderness Area.

RE: Docket No. FAA-2026-8797; Project Identifier MCAI-2025-01338-T; RIN 2120-AA64 – Notice of Proposed Rulemaking: Airworthiness Directives; Bombardier, Inc. Airplanes.

I. INTRODUCTION & SUMMARY
We appreciate the opportunity to submit comments on the Federal Aviation Administration's (FAA) Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) concerning Bombardier, Inc., Model BD-700-2A12 airplanes, published at 91 FR 57278 (September 9, 2026). While supporting the overarching goal of maintaining structural integrity and addressing fatigue risk in wing shear-ties, we urge the FAA to modify the proposed rule to ensure regulatory clarity, procedural fairness under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), and realistic economic accounting.

II. SPECIFIC DEFICIENCIES & RATIONALE

1. Retroactive Compliance Calculation (91 FR 57280)
The NPRM states that compliance must occur within 1,400 flight cycles measured from October 26, 2022 (the issuance date of Bombardier SB 700-57-7525). Measuring regulatory compliance retroactively from a non-binding manufacturer bulletin date creates severe compliance tracking hurdles, particularly for aircraft transferred between operators after October 2022. The FAA must set compliance relative to the effective date of the Final Rule or provide a reasonable grace period (e.g., 100 flight cycles or 90 days after the effective date) for aircraft nearing or exceeding the 1,400 cycle threshold.

2. Unrealistic Economic Impact Assessment (91 FR 57280)
The FAA estimates labor costs at $85 per hour, yielding an inspection cost of $850 per aircraft. Current specialized maintenance repair and overhaul (MRO) labor rates for business jets operating under 14 CFR Part 145 range from $175 to $250 per hour. Furthermore, the FAA fails to evaluate indirect economic costs, such as out-of-service downtime during structural disassembly at rib 6. The agency should update its Regulatory Flexibility Act certification and cost estimates using actual market labor benchmarks.

3. Rigid 'Before Further Flight' Mandatory Action Standard (91 FR 57281, Paragraph (h)(2))
Paragraph (h)(2) mandates that if any discrepancy (such as minor gap under a nut or initial oversizing) is detected, repair must occur 'before further flight.' This standard does not differentiate between urgent structural fatigue cracking and minor, non-critical dimensional anomalies. It creates severe operational disruptions without safety benefit where ferry flights or temporary safe flight limits could be authorized under engineering supervision.

III. PROPOSED ALTERNATIVE REGULATORY TEXT

1. Modify Paragraph (f) Compliance / Paragraph (g) Requirements:
"Comply with all required actions within 1,400 flight cycles accumulated since October 26, 2022, or within 100 flight cycles after the effective date of this AD, whichever occurs later."

2. Modify Paragraph (h)(2) Exception to Read:
"Inspect in accordance with Section 2.B of the Accomplishment Instructions of Bombardier Service Bulletin (SB) 700-57-7525 Revision 01, dated 13 January 2025. If any cracking, structural elongation, or fastener loosening exceeding manufacturer limits is detected, repair the discrepancy before further flight using a method approved by the Manager, International Validation Branch, FAA; Transport Canada; or Bombardier's Design Approval Organization (DAO). For minor non-structural dimensional anomalies, temporary ferry flights or deferred maintenance windows may be permitted in accordance with DAO-approved instructions."

I. INTRODUCTION & SUMMARY

The undersigned submit these comments in response to the Federal Communications Commission's (Commission) Further Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (FNPRM) published at 91 FR 57454 (Sept. 9, 2026). While we support the Commission's objective to curb illegal robocalling, key provisions in the proposed rules regarding database removal procedures and financial guarantees present critical constitutional, statutory, and economic flaws.

II. SPECIFIC COMMENTS AND LEGAL DEFECTS

1. Shortened 5-Day Cure Period for Database Removal Violates Procedural Due Process (Page 57471; Proposed 47 CFR § 64.6305(k)(2)).
The Commission proposes to compress the notice and cure period under the Two-Step Removal Process from 10 days to 5 days. Under 47 CFR § 64.6305(g), removal from the RMD obligates all downstream providers to immediately cease accepting traffic from the removed entity. This effectuates an immediate complete shutdown of the provider's telecommunications business. Reducing the response period to 5 calendar days fails the constitutional due process balancing test set forth in Mathews v. Eldridge, 424 U.S. 319 (1976). Five days is grossly insufficient for a provider to conduct forensic network analysis, consult legal counsel, obtain third-party audit verification, and submit a formal response. 

2. Financial Assurance / Standby Letter of Credit Requirements are Arbitrary and Capricious under the APA (Page 57467).
The FNPRM invites comment on requiring RMD filers to furnish Standby Letters of Credit (LOC) backed by strict banking capitalization standards. Imposing LOC mandates on competitive VoIP providers and small carriers violates the Administrative Procedure Act (5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A)) and the Regulatory Flexibility Act. The Commission offers no empirical economic analysis connecting financial liquidity guarantees to a reduction in illicit robocall generation. Requiring LOCs unfairly penalizes small business carriers that lack capital credit facilities, entrenching incumbent market dominance.

3. Overreach of Section 4(i) Ancillary Authority Regarding Cloud PBX and SaaS Services (Page 57456, 57480).
The Commission seeks to capture over-the-top (OTT) cloud communications, PBXs, and enterprise software platforms within the core definition of 'voice service provider.' Exercising ancillary jurisdiction under Section 4(i) over non-common-carrier software platforms exceeds the statutory boundaries articulated in Comcast Corp. v. FCC, 600 F.3d 642 (D.C. Cir. 2010), as the Commission cannot show that regulating internal enterprise software is strictly ancillary to fulfilling statutory duties under Section 251(e) or Title II.

Amend 47 CFR § 64.6305(k)(2)(i) [Page 57488]:
'(i) the Enforcement Bureau will issue an order finding that the voice service provider's filing qualifies for removal due to a violation under paragraph (j) of this section based on clear and convincing evidence and directing the voice service provider to, within fourteen (14) business days, cure the violation and notify the Enforcement Bureau that the violation has been cured or explain why its filing should not be removed; and'

Amend 47 CFR § 64.6305(a) [Page 57486]:
'(a) Robocall mitigation program requirement. Each voice service provider shall implement a robocall mitigation program that includes reasonable and effective steps to prevent its network or services from being used to transmit illegal calls.'

title: Updated Definition of “Waters of the United States”

ai_data.summary_of_main_idea: This Supplemental Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (SNPRM) issued by the EPA and U.S. Army Corps of Engineers proposes narrow regulatory definitions for 'relatively permanent' waters and 'continuous surface connection' under the Clean Water Act in response to Supreme Court precedent in Sackett v. EPA. Under the proposed supplemental options, Clean Water Act jurisdiction over non-tidal waters would be restricted strictly to perennial bodies of water that flow 365 days per year under ordinary conditions, excluding almost all intermittent streams and non-perennially flooded wetlands. The rule establishes strict bright-line exceptions, allowing jurisdictional status to remain only during droughts or brief non-anomalous dry spells/low tides lasting no more than a single period of 30 consecutive days per year.
ai_data.challenges:
1. APA & Procedural Defects: The agencies arbitrarily established a 30-consecutive-day limit for non-anomalous flow interruptions without supplying empirical or hydrological data justifying why 30 days—as opposed to 60 or 90 days—rationally delineates 'relatively permanent' waters. Furthermore, the 30-day public comment window provided for this complex re-definition is overly restrictive given the vast geographic impact.
2. Legal Overreach & Misinterpretation of Case Law: The proposed rule misinterprets Sackett v. EPA and Rapanos v. United States. Justice Scalia’s plurality opinion in Rapanos explicitly acknowledged that seasonal rivers (e.g., flowing continuously for 3-4 months) can qualify as 'relatively permanent.' By restricting 'relatively permanent' solely to 'perennial' waters (flowing 365 days a year), the agencies exceed Sackett's holdings and misapply the statutory term 'waters.' Additionally, requiring wetlands to possess continuous surface WATER rather than a physical surface connection impermissibly creates a higher threshold than required by Sackett.
3. Scientific Defects: The rule ignores established hydrologic science regarding headwater connectivity and intermittent stream ecology. In the Arid West, up to 80-90% of stream networks are intermittent or ephemeral yet perform critical nutrient cycling, sediment transport, and flood mitigation for downstream traditional navigable waters.
4. Economic Deficiencies: The agencies failed to quantify forgone ecosystem benefits, flood risk increases, and water treatment costs incurred by municipal systems resulting from the deregulation of intermittent streams and headwater wetlands.

COMMENTS OF CIVIC ADVOCATES AND PUBLIC POLICY ANALYSTS

Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OW-2025-0322; FRL 11132.1-04-OW
RIN 2040-AG44: Updated Definition of 'Waters of the United States'

I. INTRODUCTION & SUMMARY
We respectfully submit these comments in response to the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) and U.S. Army Corps of Engineers' ('agencies') Supplemental Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (SNPRM) regarding the definition of 'Waters of the United States' (WOTUS), published at 91 FR 57284 (Sept. 9, 2026). While we appreciate the agencies' intent to provide regulatory certainty following Sackett v. EPA, 598 U.S. 651 (2023), the proposed supplemental definitions of 'relatively permanent' (33 CFR § 328.3(c)(7) / 40 CFR § 120.2(c)(7)) and 'continuous surface connection' (33 CFR § 328.3(c)(3) / 40 CFR § 120.2(c)(3)) are legally defective, scientifically arbitrary, and contrary to the objectives of Section 101(a) of the Clean Water Act (33 U.S.C. § 1251(a)).

II. LEGAL & SCIENTIFIC DEFECTS

1. Misinterpretation of Sackett and Rapanos Precedent:
The agencies propose to define 'relatively permanent' to mean exclusively 'perennial bodies of water' flowing every day of the year under ordinary conditions. This standard conflicts directly with the precedent the agencies purport to implement. In Rapanos v. United States, 547 U.S. 715, 732 n.5 (2006), Justice Scalia explicitly clarified that 'relatively permanent' does not exclude seasonal rivers that flow continuously for extended periods (e.g., typically 3 months or more). Sackett repeatedly endorsed the Rapanos plurality framework without narrowing 'relatively permanent' to strictly 'perennial' flow. By equating 'relatively permanent' with 365-day perennial flow, the agencies adopt an impermissibly restrictive standard unsupported by judicial precedent.

2. Arbitrary Line-Drawing Under the APA (5 U.S.C. § 706):
The agencies propose that non-anomalous flow interruptions exceeding 'a single period of up to 30 consecutive days in any given year' automatically sever Clean Water Act jurisdiction. The preamble fails to provide a rational connection between a 30-day cutoff and hydrological science. Establishing a bright line of 30 days—as opposed to 60 or 90 days—without empirical support is the hallmark of arbitrary and capricious rulemaking under Motor Vehicle Mfrs. Ass'n v. State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co., 463 U.S. 29 (1983).

3. Unsupported Surface WATER Requirement for Wetlands:
The supplemental option for 'continuous surface connection' requires 'perennial surface water in a wetland.' Sackett required a 'continuous surface connection,' making it difficult to tell where the water ends and the wetland begins; it did not mandate that the wetland itself be inundated with surface water continuously throughout the entire year.

III. PROPOSED REGULATORY ALTERNATIVES

To ensure compliance with Sackett while preserving the integrity of downstream waters, the agencies should amend the regulatory text at 33 CFR § 328.3(c) and 40 CFR § 120.2(c) as follows:

Proposed Revision to Section 328.3(c)(7) & 120.2(c)(7):
'(7) Relatively permanent means standing or continuously flowing bodies of surface water that contain standing or continuously flowing water year-round or seasonally (typically for a continuous period of at least 3 months during normal climatic conditions). A body of water does not lose its relatively permanent status due to temporary interruptions resulting from anomalous events such as drought, or non-anomalous seasonal dry periods characteristic of the region.'

Proposed Revision to Section 328.3(c)(3) & 120.2(c)(3):
'(3) Continuous surface connection means a continuous physical surface connection between a wetland and a jurisdictional water such that the wetland directly abuts or touches the jurisdictional water, making it difficult to determine where the water ends and the wetland begins. Temporary interruptions in surface water presence during dry seasons or ordinary climatic fluctuations shall not sever a continuous surface connection.'

IV. CONCLUSION
We urge the agencies to withdraw the supplemental options and adopt a seasonally grounded definition of 'relatively permanent' that aligns with both judicial precedent and hydrological reality.

title: Unleashing Unlicensed Spectrum for Direct-to-Device

ai_data.summary_of_main_idea: The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) proposes expanding Direct-to-Device (D2D) satellite connectivity by allowing unlicensed Part 15 radio frequency devices (such as Wi-Fi and Bluetooth equipment) to communicate directly with FCC-authorized satellites on a non-interference basis. The Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) proposes adding footnote NG36 to the U.S. Table of Frequency Allocations to enable Earth-to-space Mobile-Satellite Service (MSS) in the 2400–2483.5 MHz and 5725–5850 MHz bands, while exploring light-touch Part 25 licensing frameworks such as 'license-by-rule.' Additionally, the rule clarifies that Part 15 equipment may be operated inside spacecraft and seeks comment on space-to-Earth downlinks and in-space operations.
ai_data.challenges:
1. Administrative Procedure Act (APA) Procedural Defects: The Commission proposes a sweeping 'license-by-rule' regime and secondary allocation without providing comprehensive empirical studies or baseline noise-floor modeling demonstrating how aggregate transmissions from millions of Part 15 devices interacting with dense LEO satellite constellations will avoid degrading incumbent Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, and industrial operations, violating reasoned decision-making standards under 5 U.S.C. § 706.
2. Technical & Coexistence Weaknesses: Uplinks in 2.4 GHz and 5.8 GHz bands risk creating widespread aggregate interference for terrestrial unlicensed access points. Furthermore, proposed space-to-Earth downlinks in U-NII-3 (5725–5850 MHz) lack mandatory Listen-Before-Talk (LBT) protocols or well-defined Power Flux Density (PFD) limits, exposing co-channel ground systems to elevated noise levels.
3. International Regulatory Compliance: Authorizing satellite communications in 2.4 GHz and 5.8 GHz without international allocations relies on ITU Radio Regulation No. 4.4 (non-interference basis), creating substantial risk of cross-border interference and jurisdictional ambiguity between Part 15 device certifications and Part 25 satellite operations.

While expanding Direct-to-Device (D2D) connectivity to underserved areas is a commendable goal, the Commission's proposed framework lacks critical safeguards necessary to protect the integrity of the terrestrial Part 15 unlicensed ecosystem, which powers modern Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, and IoT infrastructure.

However, the NPRM fails to include rigorous aggregate RF noise modeling. Millions of terrestrial devices operating at up to 4 Watts EIRP transmitting upward to LEO constellations will inevitably raise the noise floor for terrestrial Wi-Fi access points. Under Motor Vehicle Mfrs. Ass'n v. State Farm, 463 U.S. 29 (1983), promulgating rules without analyzing key environmental impact data renders the action arbitrary and capricious under the APA.

  2. Indefinite Licensing and National Security Risks (Pages 57115–57117, Section III.B.2)
  The proposed 'license-by-rule' mechanism for Part 15 user equipment communicating with satellite systems under Part 25 bypasses essential oversight.   Permitting downlinks in U-NII-3 (5725–5850 MHz) without mandatory Listen-Before-Talk (LBT) or strict Power Flux Density (PFD) limits introduces high risk to incumbent operations. Satellites illuminating large geographic areas will disrupt low-power local mesh networks and industrial IoT sensors.

Covered entities designated under Section 2 of the Secure and Trusted Communications Networks Act are prohibited from utilizing this allocation."

  The Commission should revise its NPRM to incorporate technical empirical testing and strict aggregate noise safeguards prior to finalizing NG36.

ai_data.challenges: The rule suffers from critical legal, procedural, and environmental defects. First, under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA) and NEPA, publishing only Draft Chapters 1 and 2 of the supporting EIS during the public comment period—while withholding Chapters 3 and 4 regarding Affected Environment and Environmental Consequences—violates procedural notice-and-comment requirements by withholding the essential factual baseline and impact analysis. Second, eliminating site-specific NEPA review for production pads up to 25 miles away based on a generic 'analyzed design envelope' violates NEPA's mandate for a site-specific 'hard look' at localized ecological impacts, permafrost degradation, and caribou migration disruption. Third, the 25-mile criterion creates an unintended 'leapfrogging' expansion mechanism, allowing every newly permitted pad to serve as a new anchor for further expansion into sensitive Arctic areas without landscape-scale evaluation. Finally, the rigid 60-day review window dangerously compresses mandatory consultations under ANILCA Section 810 (subsistence), NHPA Section 106, and the Endangered Species Act.

COMMENTS OF CIVIC ADVOCATES AND ENVIRONMENTAL RESEARCHERS ON THE BUREAU OF LAND MANAGEMENT'S PROPOSED RULE REGARDING NATIONAL PETROLEUM RESERVE IN ALASKA PRODUCTION SITE DEVELOPMENT
Docket No. BLM-2026-0133; RIN 1004-AF57; 91 FR 57091–57110

I. INTRODUCTION & SUMMARY
We submit these comments regarding the Bureau of Land Management's (BLM) proposed rule to establish 43 CFR Part 3130, Subpart 3139 ('Streamlined Permitting Procedures for Production Sites in the National Petroleum Reserve in Alaska'). While BLM characterizes this rule as a procedural efficiency measure under the Naval Petroleum Reserves Production Act (NPRPA), the rule creates severe legal vulnerabilities under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), 5 U.S.C. 553, the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), 42 U.S.C. 4321 et seq., and Section 810 of the Alaska National Interest Lands Conservation Act (ANILCA), 16 U.S.C. 3120.

II. PROCEDURAL AND LEGAL DEFECTS

1. Violation of APA Notice-and-Comment Requirements by Withholding EIS Chapters 3 and 4 (91 FR 57095–57096, 57106)
BLM states that it is publishing only Draft Chapters 1 and 2 of the accompanying EIS alongside the NPRM, deferring the publication of Chapters 3 (Affected Environment) and 4 (Environmental Consequences) to the Final EIS stage. This deprives the public of any opportunity to review and comment on the scientific methodology, empirical data, baseline environmental conditions, and projected cumulative impacts supporting the rule. Under APA § 553, an agency must disclose the empirical data and factual studies on which a proposed rule relies in time for meaningful public comment. Withholding the primary environmental consequences analysis makes informed public input impossible and renders any subsequent final rule arbitrary and capricious.

2. Improper Elimination of Site-Specific NEPA Review and Overextension of Programmatic Tiering (§ 3139.7(c), 91 FR 57109)
Section 3139.7(c) provides that a qualification determination 'confirms that the environmental effects... fall within the scope of impacts analyzed in the EIS' and that '[n]o additional project-level NEPA analysis or documentation is required.' This blanket preemption violates NEPA. Programmatic tiering cannot substitute for site-specific evaluations when localized surface disturbance, hydrological cross-drainage, and critical habitat destruction vary drastically across 25-mile radial expanses. A generic 'analyzed design envelope' fails to take the requisite 'hard look' at site-specific impacts mandated by 40 CFR 1501.11.

3. Arbitrary 25-Mile Proximity Criterion and Unchecked 'Leapfrogging' Infrastructure (§ 3139.4(b), 91 FR 57108)
Section 3139.4(b) establishes eligibility for any site within 25 miles of 'existing permanent oil and gas infrastructure.' Because § 3139.3 defines permanent infrastructure to include newly permitted production pads, each streamlined approval creates a new 25-mile radius anchor. This structural defect allows continuous westward 'leapfrogging' across the NPR-A without landscape-level NEPA analysis, directly contradicting BLM's claim that development will remain tightly bounded near existing facilities.

4. Undue Compression of Statutory Consultations within a 60-Day Window (§ 3139.5(e), 91 FR 57108)
Section 3139.5(e) mandates that BLM issue an approval or approval with conditions within 60 days of receiving a complete application. This rigid timeline arbitrarily constrains required statutory reviews under ANILCA § 810, Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act (NHPA), and Section 7 of the Endangered Species Act (ESA), undermining the trust responsibility owed to Alaska Native Tribes.

III. PROPOSED AMENDMENTS AND ALTERNATIVE REGULATORY TEXT

To remedy these legal and environmental defects, BLM must revise the regulatory text of Subpart 3139 as follows:

1. Revise § 3139.4(b) to eliminate leapfrogging infrastructure:
'§ 3139.4(b) The entire location of the proposed production site must be located within 10 miles of permanent oil and gas infrastructure that was constructed and operational prior to September 8, 2026. Infrastructure approved or constructed pursuant to this subpart shall not serve as anchor infrastructure for subsequent qualified production sites.'

2. Amend § 3139.7(c) to restore site-specific NEPA review:
'§ 3139.7(c) Upon receipt of a qualified application under this subpart, the BLM shall prepare a site-specific Environmental Assessment (EA) tiered to the rulemaking EIS to determine whether unique site-specific impacts, localized subsistence disruptions, or extraordinary circumstances require a supplemental EIS or site-specific mitigation measures.'

3. Amend § 3139.5(e) to permit sufficient review time:
'§ 3139.5(e) The BLM shall issue a decision on an application within 120 days of receiving a complete application, provided all required consultations under Section 810 of ANILCA, Section 106 of the NHPA, and Section 7 of the ESA are fully completed.'

IV. CONCLUSION
BLM must halt finalization of Subpart 3139 until the full Draft EIS (including Chapters 3 and 4) is published for a 90-day public comment period, and the regulatory text is amended to ensure rigorous site-specific environmental review and protection of Alaska Native subsistence rights.

title: Modernizing Medical Standards for Non-Insulin Dependent Diabetes Mellitus Cases

ai_data.summary_of_main_idea: The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) proposes to amend 14 CFR Part 67 (specifically §§ 67.113(a), 67.213(a), and 67.313(a)) to eliminate the mandatory Special Issuance (SI) process for applicants with non-insulin dependent diabetes mellitus (NIDDM). By removing the phrase 'or any other hypoglycemic drug' from disqualifying general medical standards, the proposed rule allows Aviation Medical Examiners (AMEs) to directly issue unrestricted first-, second-, and third-class medical certificates to qualified applicants whose diabetes is controlled through non-insulin medications. This update aims to align medical certification with modern therapeutic advancements, significantly reduce administrative delays, and alleviate processing backlogs for both airmen and the FAA.
ai_data.challenges:
1. Administrative Procedure Act (APA) Procedural Defect: The FAA relies heavily on internal, non-public accident and toxicology data (FAA ToxDB / MANTRA / ToxFlo) to justify its safety determinations under Section IV.B. Failing to disclose the raw data or methodologies in the public docket deprives stakeholders of a meaningful opportunity to comment under 5 U.S.C. 553.
2. Scientific and Pharmacological Flaws: The rule treats all 'non-insulin hypoglycemic drugs' uniformly, failing to distinguish high-risk secretagogues (such as sulfonylureas and meglitinides, which carry significant risks of sudden, unpredictable hypoglycemia) from low-risk modern therapies (such as GLP-1 receptor agonists, SGLT2 inhibitors, and metformin). Furthermore, the regulatory text fails to mandate objective clinical baselines (e.g., explicit HbA1c caps or continuous glucose monitoring requirements) within Part 67 itself, improperly delegating binding standard-setting to non-binding sub-regulatory AME guidance manuals.
3. Economic and Cost-Benefit Shortcomings: The Regulatory Impact Analysis completely omits quantitative benefit and cost-savings assessments for Third-Class medical certificate holders (private and student pilots), despite them representing 60% of initial certifications. Additionally, the analysis ignores the administrative burden and liability shifted onto AMEs and treating physicians who must review complex clinical histories without clear codification in the regulation.

PUBLIC COMMENT ON NOTICE OF PROPOSED RULEMAKING
Department of Transportation — Federal Aviation Administration
14 CFR Part 67 [Docket No. FAA-2026-10990; Notice No. 26-15; RIN 2120-AM25]
Modernizing Medical Standards for Non-Insulin Dependent Diabetes Mellitus Cases

I. INTRODUCTION AND STATEMENT OF INTEREST
The undersigned submits these comments in response to the Federal Aviation Administration's (FAA) Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) regarding medical certification standards for Non-Insulin Dependent Diabetes Mellitus (NIDDM). While we strongly support the FAA's initiative to streamline airman medical certification and eliminate redundant administrative burdens associated with Special Issuance (SI) reviews, the rule as proposed contains procedural APA flaws, critical scientific oversights, and inadequate regulatory definitions.

II. PROCEDURAL DEFECT UNDER THE ADMINISTRATIVE PROCEDURE ACT
In Section IV.B of the preamble (91 FR 56800), the FAA cites an internal safety analysis of 51 fatal aviation accidents from 2008–2025 using the FAA ToxDB databases (MANTRA and ToxFlo). The FAA explicitly acknowledges in footnote 14 that these databases 'are internal data sources... and are not available to the public.' Under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), 5 U.S.C. § 553, an agency must disclose the empirical data, methodology, and technical studies upon which it relies to afford the public a meaningful opportunity to comment. See Owner-Operator Indep. Drivers Ass'n v. FMCSA, 494 F.3d 188, 199 (D.C. Cir. 2007). The FAA must release anonymized dataset records for these 51 accident reviews into Docket No. FAA-2026-10990 or extend the public comment period following public disclosure.

III. SCIENTIFIC AND PHARMACOLOGICAL DEFICIENCIES
1. Indiscriminate Classification of Hypoglycemic Agents: The proposed amendment indiscriminately removes 'or any other hypoglycemic drug' without differentiating between pharmacological classes. First-generation and second-generation sulfonylureas (e.g., glipizide, glyburide) directly stimulate insulin secretion and carry an established clinical risk of severe, acute hypoglycemia. In contrast, modern antihyperglycemic therapies—such as GLP-1 receptor agonists (e.g., semaglutide), SGLT2 inhibitors (e.g., empagliflozin), and biguanides (metformin)—work via insulin-independent mechanisms with negligible hypoglycemia risks. The FAA must explicitly distinguish between glucose-lowering drugs with high risk of hypoglycemia versus low-risk euglycemic agents in regulatory definitions.

2. Lack of Explicit Standards in Regulatory Text: Relying entirely on sub-regulatory guidance (such as the FAA Guide for Aviation Medical Examiners) to establish clinical eligibility thresholds (e.g., HbA1c < 8.0%, absence of end-organ disease) creates regulatory instability and deprives airmen of due process. Clear baseline clinical criteria for AME issuance should be codified in the regulatory text of Part 67.

IV. PROPOSED AMENDMENTS TO REGULATORY TEXT
To resolve these defects, the FAA should revise §§ 67.113(a), 67.213(a), and 67.313(a) as follows (proposed additions in **bold**):

14 CFR § 67.113 General medical condition.
(a) No established medical history or clinical diagnosis of diabetes mellitus that requires:
  (1) Insulin for control; or
  (2) Non-insulin hypoglycemic medications with a high risk of induced clinical hypoglycemia (including sulfonylureas and meglitinides), unless evaluated and specifically authorized under § 67.401.
(b) An applicant with non-insulin dependent diabetes mellitus controlled solely through diet, exercise, or low-risk antihyperglycemic agents (including GLP-1 receptor agonists, SGLT2 inhibitors, DPP-4 inhibitors, or biguanides) may be issued a medical certificate by an Aviation Medical Examiner provided the applicant presents clinical documentation establishing an HbA1c level equal to or less than 8.0 percent and no evidence of severe hypoglycemic events or advancing end-organ disease within the preceding 12 months.

V. CONCLUSION
By incorporating clear pharmacological distinctions into the rule text and placing the underlying toxicology safety data in the public docket, the FAA can achieve its policy goals of administrative efficiency while maintaining the highest standard of safety in the National Airspace System.

COMMENTS OF CIVIC AND INDUSTRY ADVOCATES REGARDING SEC PROPOSED RULE: TRANSFER AGENT RULES
File No. S7-2026-30 | RIN 3235-AL55 | Release No. 34-106246

I. INTRODUCTION
We appreciate the opportunity to comment on the Securities and Exchange Commission's (the "Commission" or "SEC") Proposed Rule on Transfer Agent Rules (Release No. 34-106246). While we support regulatory updates that enhance market infrastructure, several core components of the proposal suffer from critical legal, economic, and technical flaws under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), 5 U.S.C. § 706, and Section 17A of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (the "Exchange Act").

II. SPECIFIC LEGAL AND POLICY OBJECTIONS

1. Arbitrary Rescission of Rule 17ad-4 Exemptions for Small Transfer Agents
The proposal to rescind Rule 17ad-4 violates the APA because the Commission fails to provide adequate empirical justification or consider less burdensome alternatives for small, non-bank transfer agents servicing thinly traded equity or mutual fund issues. Imposing full annual audit requirements under Rule 17ad-13 ($40,000+ per year) and rigid turnaround policies on entities processing fewer than 500 items per six months will drive small agents out of business, concentrating the market further into the hands of mega-agents.

2. Excessive Statutory Authority in Rule 17ad-7(i) (15-Day Record Delivery Mandate)
Proposed Rule 17ad-7(i) mandates that a terminated transfer agent deliver all issuer records within 15 calendar days, regardless of pending fee disputes or common-law possessory liens recognized under state commercial law. Section 17A of the Exchange Act authorizes the SEC to regulate national clearance and settlement, not to rewrite private contract remedies or state commercial lien laws. Overriding state-law contractual protections without explicit Congressional authorization exceeds statutory authority under Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, 144 S. Ct. 2244 (2024).

3. Rule 17ad-9(h) Impairs Blockchain and Tokenized Securities Innovation
Proposed Rule 17ad-9(h) specifies that '[t]here can be only one recordkeeping transfer agent for a given issue of securities.' This rigid requirement fails to accommodate multi-node, smart-contract-driven, distributed ledger technology (DLT) where multi-entity validation and co-recordkeeping models enhance clearance resiliency. This restriction is arbitrary and capricious under 5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A).

4. Unrealistic T+1 Turnaround Timelines under Rule 17ad-2(a)
Requiring a strict 1-day turnaround for all routine items, combined with mandatory 1-day written rejection notices under 17ad-2(e)(2), imposes an unworkable standard for physical certificates or complex estate/trust transfers, exposing small agents to severe liability.

III. PROPOSED AMENDATORY TEXT

To cure these defects, we urge the Commission to modify the proposed regulatory text as follows:

1. Rule 17ad-4 (Retain Small Agent Exemption):

By removing the qualifying phrase 'which is being used as a means of transportation,' the rule excludes unattached vessels and floating craft (such as mobile seafood processing trawlers) operating in the contiguous zone (3-12 miles) and ocean (>12 miles) from requiring NPDES permits. Raimondo (2024) to assert that removing the transportation qualifier reflects the 'best reading' of CWA § 502(12)(B). Economic & Environmental Flaws: The economic analysis focuses on $1.8 million in private compliance and federal administrative cost savings while dismissing environmental degradation as 'potential foregone benefits.' The EPA fails to quantify localized environmental harms, such as benthic hypoxia, pathogen loading, and marine toxicity caused by high-volume seafood processing discharges in ocean waters.

Misinterpretation of Statutory Context: Under CWA § 502(12)(B) (33 U.S.C. § 1362(12)(B)), Congress intended to prevent double regulation of traditional navigation vessels, not to create a blanket regulatory haven for industrial processing facilities operating off-shore. 2. Arbitrary Creation of Regulatory Gaps: At 91 FR 56822, EPA acknowledges that activities such as ocean dumping are regulated under MPRSA, OPA, and VIDA. 3. Arbitrary Cost-Benefit Analysis: The draft Economic Analysis (91 FR 56820) highlights $1.8 million in private industry cost savings while failing to monetize or adequately evaluate environmental degradation, localized hypoxia, and loss of public water quality data resulting from zero reporting requirements (91 FR 56824).

The agency fails to define key statutory and regulatory terms, including 'qualified mental health professional' and 'unavailability.' Leaving these terms undefined creates arbitrary implementation across different ports of entry and state jurisdictions.

'(e) Due process safeguards and voluntary consent. All temporary care, treatment, and hospitalization provided under this section shall be conducted with the informed consent of the individual or their lawful legal guardian. PUBLIC COMMENT ON PROPOSED RULEMAKING
Department of Health and Human Services
Administration for Children and Families
45 CFR Parts 211 and 1390 | Docket No. ACF-2026-0661 | RIN 0970-AD48
'Reducing Bureaucracy and Burden for the Repatriation of Mentally Ill Nationals'

I. INTRODUCTION
These comments are submitted in response to the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) published by the Administration for Children and Families (ACF) on September 4, 2026 (91 FR 56826–56828). While streamlining regulatory code and accurately reflecting agency oversight under the Office of Human Services Emergency Preparedness and Response (OHSEPR) are constructive administrative goals, the proposed text of 45 CFR § 1390.1 creates substantial procedural due process vulnerabilities and lacks vital clinical safeguards.

II. SPECIFIC LEGAL AND PROCEDURAL DEFECTS

1. Outdated Legal Terminology and Violation of Due Process (§ 1390.1(a)(2)(i), 91 FR 56827):
Proposed § 1390.1(a)(2)(i) authorizes repatriation eligibility based on a certificate stating an individual has been 'legally adjudged insane in a specified foreign country.' The term 'insane' is medically obsolete and legally imprecise. Furthermore, foreign judicial proceedings may lack basic due process guarantees comparable to Fifth Amendment protections. Accepting foreign adjudications of mental incapacity without requiring a contemporaneous clinical assessment upon re-entry compromises individual liberty and constitutional protections established in Addington v. Texas, 441 U.S. 418 (1979).

2. Unchecked Non-Clinical Authority (§ 1390.1(b), 91 FR 56827):
Proposed § 1390.1(b) allows an authorized Department of State official to execute a mental condition certificate when a qualified mental health professional is unavailable. Granting non-clinicians unguided authority to certify mental conditions—without defining mandatory criteria, exigency limits, or a maximum time frame before a formal clinical evaluation must occur—violates APA standards requiring rational and non-arbitrary administrative procedures.

3. Lack of Timeframe and Due Process Protections for Temporary Care and Hospitalization (§ 1390.1(c)–(d), 91 FR 56827–56828):
Proposed § 1390.1(d) mandates that the agency provide temporary care, treatment, and hospitalization in the 'nearest suitable hospital.' However, the rule omits any statutory time limit for 'temporary' care, explicit rights to legal counsel, or notice of administrative remedies/appeals for individuals detained against their preference.

III. PROPOSED ALTERNATIVE REGULATORY TEXT
To resolve these legal and clinical defects, HHS should revise proposed § 1390.1 to read as follows:

'§ 1390.1 General.
(a) Required certificates. To establish eligibility, the following certificates are required:
  (1) Nationality certificate. A certificate issued by an authorized Department of State official stating that the individual is a United States national.
  (2) Mental condition certificate. Either:
    (i) A certificate obtained or transmitted by an authorized Department of State official indicating that the individual has been adjudicated as lacking mental capacity or requiring involuntary psychiatric care under the laws of a specified foreign country, accompanied by a modern clinical evaluation where available; or
    (ii) A certificate from a qualified mental health professional stating that the individual was in a specified foreign country and requires acute mental health care and treatment.
(b) Appropriate authority or person. For paragraph (a)(2)(ii), an appropriate authority or person is a qualified mental health professional. If emergency circumstances prevent immediate evaluation by a qualified mental health professional, an authorized Department of State official may issue a temporary 72-hour provisional certification detailing the specific reasons why a professional was unavailable. A comprehensive clinical assessment by a qualified U.S. mental health professional must occur within 24 hours of arrival at the port of entry.
(c) Reception and temporary assistance. Upon arrival at the port of entry, the agency shall meet the individual, inform them of their rights in accessible language, arrange an immediate medical examination, and plan needed voluntary temporary care and treatment in consultation with the individual, their chosen advocate, legal guardian, or other designated representatives.
(d) Temporary care, treatment, and protections. The agency shall provide voluntary temporary care, treatment, and assistance necessary for the individual’s health and welfare, including hospitalization, medical care, transportation, and legal advocacy assistance. Hospitalization or involuntary detention shall not exceed 72 hours without judicial oversight or formal commitment proceedings conducted in accordance with applicable state and federal constitutional due process requirements.'

IV. CONCLUSION
ACF must ensure that regulatory streamlining does not diminish substantive constitutional rights. Implementing these modifications will satisfy administrative requirements while safeguarding civil rights.

COMMENTS OF CIVIC ADVOCATES AND SAFETY RESEARCHERS

Docket No. CPSC-2023-0004
16 CFR Part 1263: Safety Standard for Button Cell or Coin Batteries and Consumer Products Containing Such Products

I. INTRODUCTION & EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
On September 3, 2026, the Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) published a Notice of Availability and Request for Comment (91 FR 56604-56605) regarding the revised voluntary standard UL 4200A-2026. Under Section 2(f) of Reese's Law (15 U.S.C. 2056e(f)), CPSC must evaluate whether UL 4200A-2026 improves the safety of consumer products containing button cell or coin batteries. We submit these comments to urge CPSC to perform a rigorous technical comparison between UL 4200A-2023 and UL 4200A-2026 before permitting the revision to take effect.

II. PROCEDURAL AND ACCESS CONCERNS
1. Abbreviated Comment Period: The 14-day comment deadline (ending September 17, 2026) imposes an extreme procedural limitation on consumer groups, independent laboratories, and manufacturers seeking to perform empirical stress testing or statutory evaluations of the revised standard.
2. Incorporation by Reference (IBR) Accessibility: While UL provides read-only viewing, restricting copy/paste/print capabilities severely hampers public comparative analysis. Under 5 U.S.C. 552(a) and administrative fair-use doctrines (see ASTM v. Public.Resource.Org, 896 F.3d 437), critical standards incorporated into federal law must be fully transparent and accessible.

III. SUBSTANTIVE STATUTORY ANALYSIS UNDER REESE'S LAW SECTION 2(f)
Under Reese's Law, the baseline requirement for accepting a voluntary standard revision is an affirmative finding that the revision "improves the safety of the consumer product covered by the standard." 
CPSC staff must verify that UL 4200A-2026:
- Does not carve out exceptions for specific product categories (e.g., remote controls, wearable devices, or light-up novelties) that weaken secure battery enclosure requirements;
- Maintains or increases mechanical abuse testing parameters (drop, impact, torque, and tension tests);
- Retains clear warning label placement and pictogram requirements on both product packaging and battery compartments.

IV. PROPOSED ACTION & REGULATORY WORDING
If CPSC staff identifies any area where UL 4200A-2026 lowers safety thresholds or introduces ambiguity, CPSC must issue a formal rejection within 90 days pursuant to 15 U.S.C. 2056e(f)(2).

Proposed Form of Order / Federal Register Rulemaking Text:
"Pursuant to section 2(f) of Reese's Law (15 U.S.C. 2056e(f)), the Commission has evaluated UL 4200A-2026. [If safety improvements are verified]: The Commission accepts UL 4200A-2026 as the mandatory safety standard for products incorporating button cell or coin batteries, effective 180 days from notification, codified at 16 CFR Part 1263. [If any safety degradation is identified]: The Commission determines that provisions of UL 4200A-2026 [insert specific section numbers] fail to improve safety under Reese's Law, and hereby retains UL 4200A-2023 (16 CFR Part 1263) as the mandatory standard."

ai_data.summary_of_main_idea: The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) proposes a new airworthiness directive (AD) for all Airbus SAS Model A318, A319, A320, and A321 series airplanes following reports of engine fire switches self-releasing, which causes uncommanded in-flight engine shutdowns. Third, the economic assessment underestimates true compliance costs by omitting out-of-service aircraft downtime and potential global supply chain bottlenecks for replacement panels. COMMENTS OF CIVIC ADVOCATES AND AIRLINE MAINTENANCE OPERATORS

Docket No. FAA-2026-8795; Project Identifier MCAI-2025-01636-T; RIN 2120-AA64
Proposed Airworthiness Directive: Airbus SAS Airplanes

I. INTRODUCTION
We appreciate the opportunity to submit public comments on the Federal Aviation Administration's (FAA) Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) regarding Airbus SAS Model A318, A319, A320, and A321 series airplanes (Docket No. FAA-2026-8795). While we support the FAA's mandate to resolve uncommanded engine switch releases and maintain civil aviation safety, the proposed rule contains procedural and technical issues that require modification prior to final publication.

II. SPECIFIC CITATIONS AND RATIONALE

1. Mandated Manufacturer Reporting Burden (Pages 56602–56603, Regulatory Text Paragraph (g) / EASA AD 2025-0274R1)
Rationale: The proposed AD adopts EASA's requirement to report all inspection results to Airbus. The FAA projects this will cost U.S. operators $159,035 (1,871 hours). Under the Paperwork Reduction Act (44 U.S.C. § 3501) and Administrative Procedure Act, mandatory collection of information must demonstrate practical utility for airworthiness. Mandatory reporting of routine negative inspection results adds administrative overhead without accelerating physical panel replacement or directly mitigating the in-flight shutdown hazard.
Proposed Alternative Wording for Paragraph (h):
Add paragraph (h)(5) to read: "(5) Where EASA AD 2025-0274R1 specifies reporting inspection results to the manufacturer, this AD does not require submitting inspection reports if no defects or discrepancies are found during the general visual inspection."

2. Ambiguity in Definition of Serviceable Parts (Page 56603, Paragraph (h)(1))
Rationale: Paragraph (h)(1) removes "in accordance with Airbus instructions" from the definition of a serviceable part, leaving the phrase as "Fire panels, eligible for installation." Stripping the standard manufacturer reference without specifying an explicit FAA-approved standard or part number creates regulatory uncertainty for maintenance providers and FAA Principal Maintenance Inspectors (PMIs).
Proposed Alternative Wording for Paragraph (h)(1):
Revise paragraph (h)(1) to read: "(1) Where EASA AD 2025-0274R1 defines a serviceable part as 'Fire panels, eligible for installation in accordance with Airbus instructions', for this AD replace that text with 'Fire panels that have been inspected in accordance with paragraph (g) of this AD and found free of defects, or replacement fire panels bearing part numbers approved by the FAA or under an FAA-approved Alternative Method of Compliance (AMOC).'"

3. Accounting for Aircraft Downtime and Parts Availability (Page 56602, Cost of Compliance)
Rationale: The economic evaluation restricts labor to 3 work-hours for panel replacement and up to 7 hours for inspection. This excludes financial impacts associated with out-of-service aircraft downtime, schedule disruption, and potential parts shortages during widespread fleet retrofits.
Proposed Action: The FAA should explicitly acknowledge parts availability contingencies in the compliance schedule by adding a provision allowing extended compliance windows if operators experience verified manufacturer supply delays.

III. CONCLUSION
The FAA should adopt these suggested revisions in the Final Rule to eliminate unnecessary paperwork burdens, clarify part eligibility definitions, and maintain public safety while protecting operational stability.

title: Pacific Halibut Fisheries: Catch Sharing Plan; Modify Pacific Halibut Individual Fishing Quota Vessel Use Caps in Individual Fishing Quota Regulatory Areas 4A, 4B, 4C, 4D, and 4E

ai_data.summary_of_main_idea: The National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS) proposes to revise the Pacific Halibut Individual Fishing Quota (IFQ) Program regulations by establishing a permanent vessel harvest limit of 5 percent of the total annual commercial catch limit across IFQ Regulatory Areas 4A, 4B, 4C, 4D, and 4E (Area 4). This rule excludes Community Quota Entity (CQE) derived halibut harvested in Area 4B from counting toward the 5 percent Area 4 limit and adjusts how Area 4 harvests accrue against the 0.5 percent Alaska coastwide vessel cap. The action aims to address declining catch utilization, rising operating costs, and reduced vessel participation in remote western Alaska fishing grounds.
ai_data.challenges:
1. Legal Defects under the Regulatory Flexibility Act (RFA) & APA: NMFS improperly certified under 5 U.S.C. 605(b) that the rule will not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities, bypassing the requirement to prepare an Initial Regulatory Flexibility Analysis (IRFA). This ignores the severe distributional impacts and economic harm inflicted on crew members and small vessel operators caused by rapid fleet consolidation. Furthermore, under the Administrative Procedure Act (5 U.S.C. 706(2)(A)), the rule is vulnerable as arbitrary and capricious because NMFS failed to evaluate reasonable intermediate alternatives (e.g., a 2% or 2.5% cap) and instead jumped from the baseline 0.5% cap directly to a 5% cap—a tenfold increase.

2. Policy & Statutory Deficiencies under the Halibut Act: The 5% cap drastically undermines the core statutory mandates of the Northern Pacific Halibut Act of 1982 (16 U.S.C. 773c) and the foundational objectives of the IFQ Program (50 CFR 679.42). These rules were designed to maintain an owner-operator fleet, prevent hyper-consolidation of quota onto a small fleet of large vessels, and preserve entry-level opportunities for coastal fishing communities.

3. Scientific & Technical Weaknesses: NMFS fails to present empirical biological and spatial modeling regarding localized depletion risks, gear conflicts, and whale depredation dynamics that may intensify when harvest effort is concentrated onto significantly fewer, larger vessels operating in localized Area 4 fishing grounds.

I. INTRODUCTION & SPECIFIC CITATIONS
These comments are submitted in response to the National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS) proposed rule published at 91 FR 56606 (September 3, 2026), specifically addressing proposed regulations at 50 CFR 679.42(h)(1)(iii) and (v) regarding vessel harvest limitations in Regulatory Area 4.

II. RATIONALE & LEGAL DEFECTS
While we acknowledge the operational headwinds faced by participants in Area 4—including reduced processor availability and high fuel costs—the proposed establishing of a 5% vessel use cap (91 FR 56608) represents a tenfold increase over the baseline 0.5% coastwide cap. This drastic increase threatens the foundational owner-operator character of the Alaska halibut fleet.

1. Improper RFA Certification (5 U.S.C. 605(b)): NMFS erred in certifying that this rule will not have a significant economic impact on small entities (91 FR 56609). Permitting 5% of the entire Area 4 commercial quota to be harvested by a single vessel creates substantial economic displacement for small-boat operators, hired skippers, and crew members whose jobs are eliminated as quota consolidates onto fewer large platforms. NMFS must perform a full Initial Regulatory Flexibility Analysis (IRFA).

2. Failure to Consider Intermediate Regulatory Alternatives: Under APA 5 U.S.C. 706(2)(A), NMFS's reliance on a binary choice between returning to 0.5% or jumping to 5.0% is arbitrary and capricious. The agency failed to analyze reasonable compromise alternatives, such as a 2.0% or 2.5% cap, which would provide operational relief without triggering hyper-consolidation.

III. PROPOSED ALTERNATIVE REGULATORY TEXT
We respectfully request that NMFS modify the proposed text at 50 CFR 679.42(h)(1)(iii) as follows:

title: Exemption of Debt Obligations Issued by the European Union under the Securities Exchange Act for Purposes of Trading Futures Contracts on Those Securities

ai_data.summary_of_main_idea: The Securities and Exchange Commission proposes amending 17 CFR 240.3a12-8 (Rule 3a12-8) under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 to designate debt obligations of the European Union (EU) as 'exempted securities' solely for the purpose of trading futures contracts on those securities in the U.S. or by U.S. persons. By classifying EU debt obligations as exempted securities, the rule transfers regulatory oversight of futures on EU debt from joint SEC/CFTC security-futures jurisdiction to the CFTC's exclusive futures framework. The proposal aims to expand U.S. investor access, harmonize regulatory treatment between EU supranational debt and the debt of eleven EU member states currently exempted under the Rule, and facilitate cross-border hedging.
ai_data.challenges: The proposed rule presents several legal, administrative, and market surveillance challenges. First, under Administrative Procedure Act (APA) § 706(2)(A), the SEC's classification of the European Union—a supranational organization—as a 'foreign government' under Exchange Act Section 3(a)(12) stretches statutory text beyond its plain meaning without explicit statutory definition, creating legal risk of ultra vires administrative action. Second, the SEC's proposal arbitrarily excludes sixteen individual EU member states (e.g., Poland, Greece, Portugal) and other euro-area supranationals (e.g., European Stability Mechanism) from similar relief without offering an economically coherent rationale, leaving the rule vulnerable to claims of arbitrary and capricious decision-making. Third, the SEC acknowledges that U.S. regulators lack visibility and compulsory data-sharing arrangements for foreign over-the-counter (OTC) cash bond markets for EU debt, creating cross-market manipulation risks between underlying spot markets and U.S.-accessible futures venues.

ai_data.proposed_comment:
COMMENTS OF CIVIC ADVOCATES AND POLICY ANALYSTS

Re: Exemption of Debt Obligations Issued by the European Union Under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 for Purposes of Trading Futures Contracts on Those Securities (Release No. 34-106225; File No. S7-2026-29; RIN 3235-AN82; 91 FR 56387)

I. INTRODUCTION & EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
We appreciate the opportunity to comment on the Securities and Exchange Commission's ('Commission' or 'SEC') proposed rule to amend 17 CFR 240.3a12-8 ('Rule 3a12-8') to designate debt obligations issued by the European Union ('EU') as 'exempted securities' for the purpose of trading futures contracts (91 FR 56387). While we support regulatory efficiency and improving cross-border risk management, the rule as drafted suffers from legal defects under the Administrative Procedure Act ('APA'), arbitrary exclusions of peer sovereign debt issuers, and cross-market surveillance vulnerabilities.

II. LEGAL AND STATUTORY DEFECTS
1. Administrative Procedure Act and Statutory Bounds (15 U.S.C. § 78c(a)(12)): Section 3(a)(12)(A)(vii) of the Exchange Act authorizes the Commission to exempt securities consistent with the public interest. However, expanding Rule 3a12-8 to cover a supranational entity (the EU) without statutory clarification blurs the distinction between sovereign nations and multilateral organizations. 
2. Arbitrary and Capricious Exclusion of EU Member States (91 FR 56396, Question 10): The SEC designates the EU entity while leaving 16 EU member states (e.g., Greece, Poland, Portugal) subject to the more restrictive security-futures regime. This creates an unjustified regulatory disparity among economically integrated European issuers, violating APA § 706(2)(A).
3. Clarification of Rule 144A Resales (91 FR 56397, Question 16): The definition of 'Designated Foreign Government Security' in 17 CFR 240.3a12-8(a)(1) requires that underlying debt not be registered under the Securities Act. The Commission should explicitly clarify that private placements offered under Rule 144A to Qualified Institutional Buyers (QIBs) do not disqualify underlying EU debt obligations from generating qualifying futures under Rule 3a12-8.

III. CROSS-MARKET SURVEILLANCE & INVESTOR PROTECTION CONCERNS
As noted on 91 FR 56404, U.S. regulators lack compulsory access to European over-the-counter (OTC) trade repositories for underlying cash EU bonds. Permitting broader retail access to EU debt futures without mandatory cross-market trade reporting between European venue operators and the CFTC/SEC increases susceptibility to cross-venue manipulation (e.g., wash sales or marking-the-close in cash markets to affect futures settlement).

IV. PROPOSED TEXTUAL AMENDMENTS
To resolve these legal and procedural deficiencies, we recommend revising proposed 17 CFR 240.3a12-8 as follows:

1. Amend § 240.3a12-8(a)(1) to read:
'(a)(1) The term designated foreign government security shall mean a security not registered under the Securities Act of 1933 (other than securities offered or sold pursuant to an exemption under Rule 144A (§ 230.144A of this chapter)) nor the subject of any American depositary receipt so registered, and representing:
(i) a debt obligation of the European Union;
(ii) a debt obligation of any member state of the European Union; or
(iii) a debt obligation of the government of [list existing non-EU sovereigns].'

2. Amend § 240.3a12-8(a)(3) to read:
'(3) The term debt obligation of the European Union shall mean debt that is issued directly by the European Commission on behalf of the European Union, or guaranteed directly and unconditionally by the European Union.'

V. CONCLUSION
We urge the Commission to refine this proposal by adopting a comprehensive approach for all EU member states and formalizing information-sharing arrangements with foreign regulatory bodies prior to finalizing the rule.

ai_data.proposed_comment:
RE: Docket No. FAA-2026-8794; Project Identifier MCAI-2025-01464-T; Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) – Airworthiness Directives; Airbus Canada Limited Partnership Airplanes

I. INTRODUCTION & SUMMARY
This comment is submitted regarding the FAA’s Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) published at 91 FR 56377 (September 2, 2026). While supporting the underlying safety objective of preventing fuel line abrasion and fire risks on Airbus Canada BD-500-1A10 and BD-500-1A11 aircraft, the proposed rule contains critical procedural and technical deficiencies that must be rectified prior to issuing a Final Rule.

II. PROCEDURAL FLAWS: INCORPORATION BY REFERENCE AND PUBLIC DOCKET ACCESS
Under 5 U.S.C. § 553 and 1 CFR Part 51, rulemaking agencies must provide reasonable access to materials incorporated by reference (IBR). Transport Canada AD CF-2025-47 relies on manufacturer service documents that define the precise execution criteria for inspecting and torquing the motive flow (MF) flexible fuel line assemblies. Withholding these service instructions from the public regulations.gov docket prevents operators and maintenance technicians from meaningful opportunity to comment on the feasibility and burden of the required maintenance actions.

III. TECHNICAL DEFICIENCIES IN DAMAGE CRITERIA (PAGE 56379, PARAGRAPH (h)(3))
Paragraph (h)(3) mandates that if 'any damage (including any permanent deformity) is found on any motive flow flexible fuel line assembly, replace the damaged assembly before further flight.' This blanket directive lacks objective, quantifiable engineering limits. Minor surface cosmetic scuffing on an outer protective shroud does not necessarily compromise the structural integrity of the inner fuel line or create an immediate risk of fuel leakage before scheduled maintenance.

IV. UNREALISTIC ECONOMIC IMPACT ESTIMATION (PAGE 56378)
The FAA estimates on-condition replacement costs at $10,005 per pylon (1 hour labor + $9,920 parts). This underestimates true operational impacts. For scheduled air carriers, a 'before further flight' replacement requirement without allowable deferral limits or dispatch under a Master Minimum Equipment List (MMEL) framework can force un-forecasted AOG events costing upwards of $50,000 to $100,000 per day in passenger disruptions and logistical delays.

V. PROPOSED REGULATORY ALTERNATIVE WORDING
To address these issues, the FAA should amend Paragraph (h)(3) on page 56379 to read as follows:

'(3) Where Transport Canada AD CF-2025-47 specifies to "if necessary, replace the left and right motive flow fuel line assemblies", for this AD, replace that text with: "If damage exceeding the manufacturer's allowable structural wear limits specified in the applicable service instructions (including depth of shroud abrasion or structural hose permanent deformation) is found on any motive flow flexible fuel line assembly, replace the damaged assembly before further flight, or accomplish an approved temporary ferry flight or deferral procedure in accordance with the provisions of 14 CFR 39.23."'

title: Heightened Import Disclosures for Supply Chain Visibility

ai_data.summary_of_main_idea: U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) is issuing an Advance Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (ANPRM) pursuant to Executive Order 14411 to consider regulations that enhance supply chain visibility for merchandise imported into the United States. The contemplated rules would mandate that importers obtain and submit or retain foreign export documentation filed with foreign customs authorities, replace or supplement the Manufacturer Identification Code (MID) with Global Business Identifiers (GBIs), and require supply chain tracing technologies and cybersecurity restrictions within the Customs Trade Partnership Against Terrorism (CTPAT) program. 1. Statutory Authority and Recordkeeping Limits: Mandating that U.S. Importers of Record (IORs) produce foreign export documents submitted by independent overseas entities to foreign governments exceeds CBP's authority under 19 U.S.C. 1484 and 1508. The Tariff Act of 1930 governs records created or maintained in the ordinary course of business by the importer; requiring third-party foreign sovereign filings imposes an impossible compliance burden where IORs lack legal entitlement or contractual privity.

2. Foreign Sovereign Law Conflicts and Data Privacy Blocking Statutes: Requiring foreign export declarations and tax/business identifiers directly conflicts with foreign privacy laws (e.g., EU General Data Protection Regulation) and data export/blocking statutes (e.g., China's Data Security Law and Personal Information Protection Law). Overseas suppliers risk civil and criminal liability under foreign law if they disclose state-regulated export records to U.S. entities.

3. Regulatory Flexibility Act & Paperwork Reduction Act Defects: The ANPRM fails to adequately quantify the cumulative cost burden on Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs), which account for over 70% of CTPAT members. Imposing mandatory GBI onboarding, advanced supply chain tracing software, and multi-tier record retention creates significant barriers to entry without demonstrating a proportional reduction in trade enforcement risk.

PUBLIC COMMENT ON ADVANCE NOTICE OF PROPOSED RULEMAKING
Department of Homeland Security — U.S. Customs and Border Protection
Docket No. USCBP-2026-1058 | RIN 1685-AA47
Heightened Import Disclosures for Supply Chain Visibility (91 FR 56408–56414)

I. INTRODUCTION
These comments are submitted in response to the Advance Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (ANPRM) published by U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) on September 2, 2026, titled "Heightened Import Disclosures for Supply Chain Visibility" (91 FR 56408). While we support CBP’s mission to combat illicit transshipment and trade fraud, the proposed regulatory framework introduces severe legal, operational, and statutory defects that must be resolved prior to drafting any Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM).

II. SPECIFIC COMMENTS AND LEGAL DEFECTS

1. Overreach of Recordkeeping Mandates under 19 U.S.C. 1508 (Section III.A, 91 FR 56410–56412)
CBP requests feedback on whether Importers of Record (IORs) should be mandated to obtain, transmit, and retain foreign export documentation filed with foreign customs administrations (Questions Q1–Q8). Under 19 U.S.C. 1508 and 1509, an importer’s duty to maintain records applies to documents generated in the normal course of business or required for the entry of merchandise. Foreign export declarations are filed by foreign entities (exporting trading companies, manufacturers, or forwarders) directly with foreign sovereign nations. U.S. importers typically lack legal privity or access to these regulatory filings. Requiring U.S. importers to guarantee the authenticity of foreign government filings creates an unworkable standard of care under 19 U.S.C. 1484, exposing compliant importers to improper penalty actions under 19 U.S.C. 1592.

2. Conflicts with Foreign Data Privacy and Sovereignty Laws (Section III.A.1, 91 FR 56411)
Mandating foreign business tax disclosures and raw export data (Questions Q9–Q13, Q41) fails to account for international blocking statutes and strict data sovereignty frameworks, including the EU GDPR, China’s Personal Information Protection Law (PIPL), and Data Security Law. Overseas suppliers are legally prohibited from sharing certain export tax and transaction records with foreign private parties or external customs agencies without state approvals. Imposing these mandatory disclosures as a condition of entry will result in systemic supply chain disruptions.

3. Global Business Identifiers (GBI) and MID Replacement Burden (Section III.B, 91 FR 56412–56413)
Transitioning from the Manufacturer Identification Code (MID) to mandatory Global Business Identifiers (GBIs) such as LEI, D-U-N-S, GLN, or Altana ID (Questions Q24–Q45) creates disproportionate costs for non-U.S. sub-tier manufacturers and suppliers, particularly in developing nations. While GBIs offer granular tracking, mandating multi-tier entity identifiers at entry summary will freeze customs clearance for small-business importers whose suppliers refuse or cannot afford third-party identifier subscriptions.

4. Mandatory Technology and CTPAT Program Alterations (Section III.C, 91 FR 56413–56414)
Transforming CTPAT from a voluntary security coalition under the SAFE Port Act (6 U.S.C. 961 et seq.) into a mandatory digital surveillance mechanism (Questions Q56–Q61) fundamentally undermines the program's statutory foundation. Mandating proprietary AI tracing platforms or blanket restrictions on foreign logistics software without clear standards violates APA notice-and-comment principles.

III. PROPOSED ALTERNATIVE REGULATORY WORDING

To align CBP’s objectives with statutory authority and operational realities, we propose the following regulatory modifications for inclusion in any future NPRM:

1. Amend 19 CFR 163.1 (a)(1)(A) List regarding Foreign Export Records:
"Foreign export documentation (including foreign export declarations and foreign export permits) shall not be required as part of the mandatory entry summary documentation package under 19 CFR Part 141. Foreign export documentation shall be classified as a secondary recordkeeping element under 19 U.S.C. 1508, required only upon written CBP demand during a formal audit or focused assessment under 19 U.S.C. 1509, and subject to an affirmative defense where the importer demonstrates reasonable care and good-faith efforts to request such documentation from the foreign supplier."

2. Safe Harbor Provision for Global Business Identifiers (19 CFR Part 141):
"The submission of Global Business Identifiers (GBIs) at entry or entry summary shall remain voluntary. Importers of Record who elect to submit validated GBIs (D-U-N-S, GLN, or LEI) for foreign manufacturers, sellers, and shippers shall be eligible for reduced risk-scoring in CBP automated targeting systems and streamlined entry processing."

3. Regulatory Flexibility for Small Business Importers:
"Entities qualifying as small businesses under SBA size standards, as well as validated CTPAT Tier 2 and Tier 3 partners, shall be exempt from mandatory multi-tier digital supply chain tracing software requirements."

IV. CONCLUSION
CBP should refine its approach by retaining voluntary incentives within CTPAT and utilizing targeted risk-based record requests rather than imposing broad, extraterritorial disclosure mandates on all U.S. importers.
