title: Bicycle Use in Park Areas

ai_data.summary_of_main_idea: The National Park Service (NPS) proposes to amend 36 CFR 4.30 to remove long-standing procedural requirements for designating roads and trails for traditional bicycle and electric bicycle (e-bike) use within the National Park System. The rule eliminates mandates to prepare Environmental Assessments (EAs) or Environmental Impact Statements (EISs), mandatory 30-day public comment periods, mandatory park planning documents, superintendent written determinations, and regulatory mandates for sustainable trail design. Under the proposed framework, e-bikes are allowed by default on public park roads, and superintendents are granted discretionary authority to authorize trail designations without Federal Register rulemaking unless the location has never been improved by artificial or processed materials or meets high-controversy thresholds under 36 CFR 1.5(b).
ai_data.challenges: The proposed rule suffers from key legal, scientific, and procedural defects: 1. APA and NEPA Legal Vulnerabilities: Eliminating mandatory EAs, public comment periods, and written determinations shifts trail designations primarily to Categorical Exclusions (CEs), violating NEPA's core purpose of ensuring informed decision-making and public participation (42 U.S.C. 4321 et seq.). Bypassing site-specific environmental review for motorized e-bikes undermines the NPS Organic Act's mandate to conserve park resources unimpaired (54 U.S.C. 100101). 2. Scientific Deficiencies Regarding E-Bike Impacts: The rule arbitrarily equates human-powered bicycles with motorized Class 1-3 e-bikes. Empirical scientific literature demonstrates that e-bikes generate higher speeds, increased kinetic energy, accelerated tread displacement/erosion on natural surfaces, and significantly larger wildlife disturbance zones compared to non-motorized trail uses. 3. Arbitrary and Capricious Distinctions (5 U.S.C. 706(2)(A)): Utilizing any past presence of 'artificial or processed materials' (e.g., historical rail beds or old gravel roads) as the sole threshold to bypass rulemaking and environmental review creates an arbitrary standard that fails to evaluate current ecological sensitivity or re-established wildlife corridors. 4. Removal of Sustainable Design and Cost Standards: Abandoning mandatory evaluations of lifecycle maintenance costs, user conflicts, and sustainable trail design guidelines shifts long-term financial burdens to taxpayers while increasing park deferred maintenance backlogs.

PUBLIC COMMENT SUBMISSION

Date: November 2, 2026
Docket ID: NPS-WASO-DTS#NPS0042897
RIN: 1024-AE97
Agency: National Park Service, Interior
Action: Proposed Rule – Bicycle Use in Park Areas (36 CFR Part 4; 91 FR 56095–56101)

I. INTRODUCTION AND STATEMENT OF INTEREST
This comment is submitted regarding the National Park Service's (NPS) proposed rule to revise 36 CFR 4.30 governing bicycle and electric bicycle (e-bike) use across National Park System units. While expanding active recreation opportunities is a worthy goal, the proposed rule impermissibly eliminates essential procedural safeguards, NEPA environmental reviews, mandatory public participation, and scientific evaluation required under the NPS Organic Act (54 U.S.C. 100101) and the Administrative Procedure Act (5 U.S.C. 553, 706).

II. SPECIFIC COMMENTS AND LEGAL DEFECTS

1. Rescission of Mandatory Environmental Assessments (EAs) and Public Comment (91 FR 56096-56097)
The proposed rule eliminates the requirement to conduct an EA or EIS prior to designating trails for bicycle and e-bike use, relying instead on broad Categorical Exclusions (CEs). This is legally flawed under NEPA. Motorized e-bikes operate at higher average speeds and weights than traditional bicycles. Scientific studies confirm that e-bikes introduce unique disturbance vectors for local fauna and increase trail wear. Relying on CEs without mandatory public review ignores cumulative impacts and violates the agency's statutory mandate under 54 U.S.C. 100101 to prioritize resource protection over recreational development when potential impairment exists.

2. Arbitrary Threshold for Rulemaking Based on Historical Material Use (91 FR 56099; Proposed 36 CFR 4.30(b))
The proposed rule establishes that Federal Register rulemaking is required only on locations 'that have never been improved by artificial or processed materials.' This threshold is arbitrary and capricious under 5 U.S.C. 706(2)(A). A trail situated on a historic 19th-century rail bed or abandoned logging path containing legacy gravel may now be ecologically sensitive, supporting threatened species or delicate soil crusts. Under the proposed rule, superintendents could authorize high-speed e-bike networks on such trails via internal notice without public comment or Federal Register publication. Surface composition alone is a legally non-rational proxy for environmental impact.

3. Rescission of Sustainable Trail Design and Lifecycle Cost Planning (91 FR 56097-56098)
Rescinding the requirement for written determinations evaluating soil suitability, lifecycle maintenance costs, user safety, and resource mitigation deprives park superintendents of enforceable baseline criteria. Removing mandatory sustainable trail design guidelines guarantees increased maintenance backlogs and accelerated resource degradation.

III. PROPOSED ALTERNATIVE REGULATORY TEXT

To correct these legal and procedural deficiencies, the NPS should revise proposed 36 CFR 4.30 as follows:

Sec. 4.30 Bicycles and Electric Bicycles.

(a) Park roads and parking areas. Traditional bicycles are allowed on public park roads and parking areas. Electric bicycles may be allowed on public park roads and parking areas subject to superintendent designation and safety evaluation.

(b) Trail designations and other locations. Bicycles and electric bicycles may be designated for use on trails or administrative roads only after:
(1) The superintendent completes a site-specific Environmental Assessment (EA) pursuant to NEPA, providing a minimum 30-day public comment period;
(2) The superintendent issues a written determination demonstrating that bicycle or electric bicycle use will not cause resource impairment, severe soil erosion, unacceptable user conflict, or significant disturbance to wildlife;
(3) Designations on unpaved natural surfaces, sensitive habitats, or multi-use backcountry trails are authorized by special regulation published in the Federal Register.

(c) Sustainable Design. All newly designated or constructed bicycle trails must adhere to established NPS sustainable trail design principles and lifecycle maintenance planning.

IV. CONCLUSION
NPS must retain public oversight, scientific rigor, and mandatory environmental review to fulfill its statutory duty to preserve national parks unimpaired for future generations.

title: Proposal of Special Measure Regarding Banque Misr UAE as a Financial Institution Operating Outside of the United States of Primary Money Laundering Concern

ai_data.summary_of_main_idea: FinCEN is proposing a rule under Section 311 of the USA PATRIOT Act that designates the five United Arab Emirates-based branches of Banque Misr (Banque Misr UAE) as a financial institution of primary money laundering concern due to alleged facilitation of Iranian shadow banking networks. The proposed rule imposes Special Measure Five, which prohibits U.S. financial institutions from opening or maintaining correspondent accounts for Banque Misr UAE and requires special due diligence and notification mechanisms to prevent indirect access through foreign correspondent accounts. The proposed action explicitly excludes Egypt-based parent entity Banque Misr and its non-UAE branches from the prohibition.
ai_data.challenges: The proposed rule suffers from key legal, technical, and economic defects. Legally, FinCEN relies heavily on unclassified summaries of non-public intelligence and broad allegations of $1.8 billion in potential shadow banking transfers without establishing actual institutional knowledge or willful compliance failures by Banque Misr UAE, creating vulnerabilities under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA) for unreasoned decision-making under the precedents set in FBME Bank Ltd. v. Lew. Technically, carving out UAE branches while excluding the parent bank in Egypt creates severe operational confusion for domestic covered financial institutions attempting to filter payment messages (such as SWIFT MT103/202), as parent and branch networks often share institutional BICs, corporate routing, and settlement clearing channels. Economically and procedurally, FinCEN arbitrarily restricts the public comment period to 30 days and summarily dismisses less restrictive alternatives—such as conditioned correspondent access under Special Measure Five or enhanced transactional reporting under Special Measures One through Four—without providing granular cost-benefit data or regulatory impact assessments for correspondent banks.

COMMENTS OF CIVIC AND FINANCIAL POLICY ADVOCATES

Docket No. FINCEN-2026-0232
RIN 1506-AB76
Notice of Proposed Rulemaking: Proposal of Special Measure Regarding Banque Misr UAE as a Financial Institution Operating Outside of the United States of Primary Money Laundering Concern (91 FR 56085)

I. INTRODUCTION AND INTEREST OF COMMENTERS

We submit these public comments regarding the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network's (FinCEN) Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) published at 91 FR 56085 (September 1, 2026). While supporting the Department of the Treasury's mandate to safeguard the U.S. financial system from illicit finance and sanctions evasion networks, we write to point out procedural defects under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), 5 U.S.C. 553, technical ambiguities regarding entity identification, and insufficient analysis of less restrictive alternatives under Section 311 of the USA PATRIOT Act (31 U.S.C. 5318A).

II. SPECIFIC COMMENTS AND LEGAL DEFECTS

1. Reliance on Non-Public Data and Failure to Provide Adequate Notice (91 FR 56087, Section V.A)
In Section V.A (91 FR 56087), FinCEN asserts that Banque Misr UAE processed approximately USD 1.8 billion across 103 potential front companies based on 'non-public information made available to FinCEN.' Under the APA and judicial precedent governing Section 311 actions (see FBME Bank Ltd. v. Lew, 209 F. Supp. 3d 299 (D.D.C. 2016)), FinCEN is legally obligated to provide the public and affected parties with a meaningful opportunity to comment on the evidentiary foundation of its rulemaking. Aggregated summary assertions based on unreleased non-public data deprive stakeholders of the ability to evaluate whether these transactions involved actual institutional complicity or third-party deception.

2. Operational Ambiguity in Entity Carve-Outs (91 FR 56090, Section VII.A.1)
Section 1010.667(a)(1) defines 'Banque Misr UAE' as all five branches in the UAE while explicitly excluding Egypt-based parent Banque Misr and its non-UAE branches. However, covered financial institutions processing automated international wire transfers (via ISO 20022 or SWIFT MT series) frequently encounter shared Bank Identifier Codes (BICs) or intermediate parent routing. Mandating that domestic banks screen out branch-specific transactions without FinCEN issuing dedicated, standardized SWIFT BIC identifiers or clear screening lists will lead to widespread over-blocking, unwarranted account closures, and de-risking of legitimate Egyptian commercial transactions.

3. Arbitrary Rejection of Less Restrictive Alternatives (91 FR 56089-56090, Section VI.E)
Section 311 requires the Secretary to consider whether less restrictive measures (Special Measures 1 through 4, or conditioned access under Special Measure 5) would adequately address identified risks. FinCEN's brief dismissal of conditioned access (such as capping transaction volumes, requiring enhanced transactional reporting, or mandating independent third-party compliance monitoring for the UAE branches) fails to provide a reasoned explanation. A total prohibition is an administrative remedy of last resort that requires empirical demonstration that conditional reporting or targeted sanctions under E.O. 13224 / E.O. 13902 are insufficient.

III. PROPOSED REGULATORY TEXT AMENDMENTS

To cure these operational and procedural deficiencies, we propose the following amendments to the proposed regulatory text in 31 CFR 1010.667:

1. Amend § 1010.667(a)(1) to require specific technical identification:
'(1) Banque Misr UAE. The term Banque Misr UAE means all five branches of Banque Misr located in the United Arab Emirates as listed on the Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons List or a dedicated FinCEN 311 Entity Identifier List, including their specific Bank Identifier Codes (BICs). Egypt-based Banque Misr, and its offices, branches, affiliates, and operations in countries other than the United Arab Emirates are expressly excluded from the definition of Banque Misr UAE.'

2. Amend § 1010.667(b)(3)(i)(A) to clarify notice obligations:
'(A) Notifying those foreign correspondent account holders that the covered financial institution knows or has reasonable cause to believe provide direct clearing services to Banque Misr UAE that such correspondents may not provide Banque Misr UAE with access to the correspondent account maintained at the covered financial institution;'

3. Insert a safe harbor provision under § 1010.667(b)(3)(iv):
'(iv) Safe Harbor. A covered financial institution that maintains standard commercially available OFAC and Section 311 screening software and exercises reasonable due diligence pursuant to paragraph (b)(3) shall be deemed to be in compliance with this section absent actual knowledge or willful blindness regarding a transaction involving Banque Misr UAE.'

IV. CONCLUSION

FinCEN should extend the comment period by 30 days, publish additional non-sensitive operational guidance regarding BIC filtering, and evaluate conditional access mechanisms prior to issuing a final rule.

ai_data.summary_of_main_idea: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) proposes to amend 12 CFR Part 4 by establishing a two-tiered regulatory framework that divides statutory and regulatory noncompliance into 'substantive violations' and 'technical violations.' Under the proposal, the OCC limits the issuance of Matters Requiring Attention (MRAs) strictly to substantive violations while prohibiting examiners from specifying corrective actions, tracking remediation, or setting action plans for technical violations. Arbitrary threshold distinctions—such as requiring harm to be 'predictable' or 'more than minimal'—create enforceability gaps and legal vagueness subject to challenge under 5 U.S.C. 706(2)(A). Dear Comptroller Gould:

We submit these comments in response to the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency’s (OCC) Notice of Proposed Rulemaking regarding 'Violations of Laws or Regulations.' While we appreciate the OCC’s stated goal of prioritizing supervisory resources on high-impact violations, the proposed framework creates significant supervisory blind spots and exceeds administrative discretion under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), 5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A), and statutory mandates under 12 U.S.C. § 1818(b).

I. Detailed Legal and Policy Analysis

1. Impermissible Restriction of Statutory Oversight Duties (12 U.S.C. § 1818(b))
Proposed 12 CFR § 4.92(i)(3) prohibits the OCC from directing an institution to take specific corrective actions or tracking remediation for 'technical violations.' This self-imposed restriction abdicates the OCC's core regulatory mandate under 12 U.S.C. § 1(a) and § 1818(b) to halt legal violations. Preventing examiners from tracking whether a bank remedies an identified violation creates an institutional blind spot, permitting small compliance failures to compound into severe systemic or consumer harms.

2. Arbitrary and Capricious Qualifying Standards in 12 CFR § 4.92(d)
The reliance on qualifying phrases such as 'direct, clear, predictable' and 'more than minimal' in defining substantive violations introduces severe ambiguity. Hindsight restrictions—such as excluding unpredicted deposit outflows caused by legal violations—arbitrarily shield bad management practices from MRA issuance, violating established standards of reasoned decision-making under the APA.

II. Proposed Regulatory Text Revisions

To ensure full compliance with statutory enforcement mandates while preserving examiner efficiency, we recommend amending proposed 12 CFR § 4.92 as follows:

1. Revise 12 CFR § 4.92(d)(2) to read:
'(2) Have had, or present a reasonable risk of causing, a direct or indirect impact on the institution's financial condition, capital, or risk profile;'

2. Amend 12 CFR § 4.92(i)(3) to read:
'(3) For technical violations, the OCC may direct the institution to implement a corrective action plan and may track remediation to verify that the institution has corrected the violation and established controls to prevent reoccurrence.'

Thank you for considering these comments.

The undersigned submit these comments in response to the Federal Aviation Administration's (FAA) Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) published at 91 FR 56083 (September 1, 2026), proposing to modify Class D and Class E airspace over Tweed/New Haven Airport (HVN) in New Haven, CT.

II. PROCEDURAL AND TECHNICAL DEFICIENCIES

1. Lack of Empirical Data in Docket (5 U.S.C. § 553 / APA Defect)
At 91 FR 56084, Column 2, the FAA states that 'current IFR operations [are] sufficiently contained within a smaller surface area,' justifying a lateral reduction of the Class D airspace from a 5.0-mile radius to a 4.7-mile radius. However, the docket contains no radar flight track analysis, Terminal Instrument Procedures (TERPS) evaluation, or mathematical modeling showing how published IFR arrival and departure procedures remain fully protected within 4.7 nautical miles under varying wind and operational conditions. Under the Administrative Procedure Act, agencies must disclose the technical studies and data upon which a proposed rule relies to allow meaningful public comment. State Farm, 463 U.S. at 43.

2. VFR Transition Traffic Conflicts Along Long Island Sound
Tweed/New Haven Airport sits immediately adjacent to active VFR flight corridors along the Connecticut shoreline. Compressing Class D airspace without demonstrating traffic flow management for VFR pilots operating in Class G/E airspace near the new 4.7-mile boundary risks creating compressed congestion points for transient aircraft.

III. PROPOSED ALTERNATIVE AMENDMENTS

To remedy these deficiencies, the FAA should either disclose the complete radar trajectory dataset in the public docket and extend the comment period by 30 days, or amend the proposed legal description for Paragraph 5000 as follows:

'Paragraph 5000 Class D Airspace.
ANE CT D New Haven, CT [Amended]
Tweed/New Haven Airport, CT
(Lat. 41°15'49'' N, long. 72°53'16'' W)

That airspace extending upward from the surface to and including 2,500 feet MSL within a 5.0-mile radius of the Tweed/New Haven Airport. This Class D airspace area is effective during the specific dates and times established in advance by a Notice to Airmen. The effective date and time will thereafter be continuously published in the Chart Supplement.'

IV. CONCLUSION

Unless full TERPS containment data is added to Docket No. FAA-2026-9967, the FAA should maintain the existing 5.0-mile Class D radius while proceeding with the administrative updates to airport coordinates and terminology.

The Commission proposes to amend 47 CFR §§ 54.603(b) and 54.612(a) to require that secondary/backup services 'must reasonably reflect its use as a secondary service and must be the most cost-effective option available.' Under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), agency action is arbitrary and capricious if it fails to consider an important aspect of the problem. Restricting rural health care providers to low-cost, high-latency backup technologies (e.g., geostationary satellite) where low-latency failover (e.g., LEO satellite or redundant fiber) is necessary to sustain real-time Electronic Health Record (EHR) sync violates this principle. We applaud the Commission's decision to move away from overly burdensome Method 3 cost studies (91 FR 55818). title: Maximizing Efficiencies in Universal Service Administration

ai_data.summary_of_main_idea: The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) proposes comprehensive reforms to the administration, operational structure, cost management, and governance of the Universal Service Fund (USF) and its administrator, the Universal Service Administrative Company (USAC). Key proposals include expanding USAC's express audit authority to non-carrier beneficiaries (such as schools, libraries, and rural healthcare providers), codifying the use of statistical sampling extrapolation to calculate financial recoveries across all USF programs, adopting a 'pay-and-dispute' model for fund recoveries during appeals, establishing budget caps for USAC, and restructuring the USAC Board of Directors.
ai_data.challenges: The NPRM presents significant administrative, constitutional, and technical defects under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), 5 U.S.C. § 706. First, applying statistical extrapolation across highly heterogeneous programs like E-Rate and Rural Health Care (RHC) violates fundamental statistical principles, as procurement decisions and local bidding environments are non-uniform and independent; applying extrapolated clawbacks across disparate transactions is arbitrary and capricious. Second, implementing a mandatory 'pay-and-dispute' model before a final agency adjudication deprives small rural providers and non-profit beneficiaries of procedural due process and risks immediate financial distress or insolvency for essential community entities. Third, expanding USAC's discretion without definitive statutory guidelines worsens existing non-delegation doctrine vulnerabilities surrounding the private administration of federal universal service mechanisms.

BEFORE THE
FEDERAL COMMUNICATIONS COMMISSION
WASHINGTON, DC 20554

In the Matter of )
Maximizing Efficiencies in Universal Service Administration ) WC Docket No. 26-173; FCC 26-52

COMMENTS OF CIVIC ADVOCATES AND PROGRAM BENEFICIARIES

I. INTRODUCTION AND EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
We submit these comments in response to the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) published at 91 FR 55826 (August 31, 2026). While we support the Commission’s objective to eliminate waste, fraud, and abuse in the Universal Service Fund (USF), core elements of the proposed rules—specifically the broad authorization of statistical extrapolation for clawbacks in 47 CFR § 54.707(d) and the adoption of a pre-appeal 'pay-and-dispute' model—impose severe, unlawful, and disproportionate burdens on non-carrier beneficiaries and small telecommunications providers.

II. STATISTICAL EXTRAPOLATION ACROSS NON-HOMOGENEOUS USF PROGRAMS IS ARBITRARY AND CAPRICIOUS (91 FR 55829)
Proposed 47 CFR § 54.707(d) would permit USAC to calculate monetary recoveries by extrapolating findings from a sample across an auditee’s full disbursement population. In programs such as E-Rate and Rural Health Care (RHC), individual disbursements stem from distinct, highly localized competitive bidding processes, customized service agreements, and unique administrative actions. Extrapolating a discrete administrative error in a single procurement across an applicant’s entire funding history assumes statistical homogeneity that does not exist. Under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), 5 U.S.C. § 706, adopting a statistical method that fails to account for non-independent, heterogeneous variables is arbitrary, capricious, and unsupported by sound statistical science.

III. THE 'PAY-AND-DISPUTE' MODEL DEPRIVES BENEFICIARIES OF DUE PROCESS (91 FR 55829-55830)
Requiring USF recipients to pay substantial recovery demands following an initial Bureau decision—prior to full Commission review or judicial exhaustion—creates irreparable financial harm for rural hospitals, schools, and small competitive carriers. These entities operate on tight annual budgets and cannot absorb multi-million dollar clawbacks while appealing erroneous administrative rulings. A pay-and-dispute model compromises financial stability without providing compensatory interest mechanisms that adequately remedy wrongfully withheld federal support.

IV. PROPOSED ALTERNATIVE REGULATORY TEXT
To resolve these legal and procedural deficiencies, we propose amending the text of 47 CFR § 54.707 as follows:

§ 54.707 Audit controls.
(a) The Administrator shall have the authority to audit contributors, carriers, and beneficiaries (including participating schools, libraries, and health care providers) reporting data to the Administrator. The Administrator shall establish clear, standardized procedures to verify discounts, offsets, and support amounts...
(d) The Administrator may calculate a recovery based on extrapolation of a statistically representative sample of disbursements ONLY within the High Cost program where funding mechanisms are uniform and standardized. Extrapolation shall not be utilized in the E-Rate, Rural Health Care, or Lifeline programs unless the Administrator demonstrates that the sample frame consists of homogeneous, statistically independent transactions. Auditees shall be provided 90 days to present rebuttal evidence before any recovery calculation is finalized.
(e) Recovery demands resulting from audit findings shall be stayed automatically pending the resolution of a timely filed Petition for Reconsideration or Application for Review before the Commission.

Respectfully submitted,

title: Federal Sector Equal Employment Opportunity

ai_data.summary_of_main_idea: The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) proposes a major overhaul of 29 CFR Part 1614 to restructure the federal sector EEO complaint process. The rule eliminates mandatory pre-complaint counseling in favor of direct 60-day complaint filing, replaces automatic entitlement to Administrative Judge (AJ) hearings prior to Final Agency Decisions (FADs) with discretionary AJ referrals on appeal, and eliminates administrative class complaint adjudications. Additionally, it introduces heightened plausibility pleading standards, restricts attorney fee rate matrices, revises same-decision evidentiary standards, and incorporates reporting and transparency mandates under the Elijah E. Cummings Federal Employee Antidiscrimination Act of 2020.
ai_data.challenges: The proposed rule suffers from significant administrative law defects, procedural unfairness, and unvetted economic assumptions. First, eliminating pre-FAD AJ hearing rights (§ 1614.110, § 1614.406) forces federal workers to rely solely on internal investigations conducted by the very agency accused of discrimination, creating an inherent conflict of interest and depriving employees of neutral fact-finding prior to final agency action. Second, importing a heightened 'plausibility' pleading standard (§ 1614.106(c)) into an administrative intake process creates an insurmountable procedural barrier for pro se complainants who lack access to pre-filing discovery. Third, barring administrative class action adjudications (§ 1614.204) severely undermines enforcement against systemic and institutional discrimination across federal agencies, shifting an onerous burden to federal district courts. Fourth, prohibiting non-statutory monetary sanctions against agencies (§ 1614.501(f)) removes vital deterrence against agency bad-faith delays, spoliation, and procedural defaults during investigations. Finally, the EEOC's cost-benefit analysis under Executive Order 12866 significantly underestimates the financial impact on federal employees seeking judicial relief after defective agency FADs.

COMMENTS OF CIVIC AND FEDERAL EMPLOYEE ADVOCATES ON THE EQUAL EMPLOYMENT OPPORTUNITY COMMISSION'S PROPOSED RULE REGARDING FEDERAL SECTOR EQUAL EMPLOYMENT OPPORTUNITY (29 CFR PART 1614, RIN 3046-AB46, DOCKET NO. EEOC-2026-0001)

I. INTRODUCTION AND INTEREST OF COMMENTERS
The undersigned civic organizations, civil rights advocates, and federal employee representatives submit these public comments in response to the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission’s (EEOC) Proposed Rule published at 91 FR 55690 (August 28, 2026). While we support streamlining procedural delays and fully implementing the Elijah E. Cummings Federal Employee Antidiscrimination Act of 2020, we strongly oppose the proposed elimination of pre-decision Administrative Judge (AJ) hearing rights (§ 1614.406), the prohibition of administrative class complaint adjudications (§ 1614.204), and the imposition of court-style plausibility pleading standards on administrative filers (§ 1614.106(c)).

II. SPECIFIC OBJECTIONS AND LEGAL RATIONALE

1. Depriving Aggrieved Employees of Independent Pre-FAD Fact-Finding (91 FR 55691–55693, 55714, 55720)
Proposed §§ 1614.110 and 1614.406 strip federal employees of the right to request an independent hearing before an EEOC AJ prior to the employing agency issuing a Final Agency Decision (FAD). Forcing employees to undergo an internal agency investigation and receive a FAD written by the defending agency’s own EEO/General Counsel staff creates an unresolvable structural conflict of interest. Agency EEO offices frequently lack operational independence. Reserving AJ hearings to a discretionary post-appeal referral model under § 1614.406(b) transforms the EEOC into a distant appellate body and eliminates neutral cross-examination at the critical fact-finding phase.

2. Elimination of Administrative Class Complaints Deprives Workers of Systemic Relief (91 FR 55693, 55715–55716)
Proposed § 1614.204 bars administrative class action complaints, requiring class claims to be brought solely as putative assertions for exhaustion prior to federal court litigation. Administrative class actions are a critical tool for exposing agency-wide discriminatory policies (e.g., biased promotion testing, systemic reasonable accommodation denials). Eliminating administrative class adjudication severely penalizes low-wage federal workers who cannot afford immediate federal district court litigation.

3. Plausibility Pleading Standard Imposes Unfair Burden on Pro Se Aggrieved Aggrieved Persons (91 FR 55695, 55712)
Proposed § 1614.106(c) requires complaints to contain 'sufficient factual allegations, accepted as true, to state a claim for relief that is plausible on its face.' Importing the judicial Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly / Ashcroft v. Iqbal standard into an administrative intake stage—where complainants have had zero discovery and often lack legal counsel—violates the remedial purpose of Title VII and the Rehabilitation Act.

4. Prohibition of Monetary Sanctions Weakens Agency Accountability (91 FR 55719, 55724)
Proposed §§ 1614.404(d) and 1614.501(f) prohibit monetary sanctions against federal agencies. Removing financial penalties for egregious agency non-compliance, spoliation of evidence, or severe delays eliminates any meaningful legal deterrence against agency misconduct during administrative processing.

III. PROPOSED ALTERNATIVE REGULATORY WORDING

To remedy these defects, we propose the following specific amendments to the proposed rule text:

1. Revise Section 1614.110(b) (Page 55714) to preserve hearing election rights:
'§ 1614.110(b) Election of hearing or immediate final agency decision. After completion of the investigation under § 1614.108, the agency shall provide the complainant with a copy of the investigative file and notice that the complainant has the right to request a hearing and decision from an administrative judge or to request an immediate final decision from the agency within 30 days of receipt of the investigative file.'

2. Revise Section 1614.406(a) (Page 55720) to maintain automatic hearing availability:
'§ 1614.406 Administrative judge proceedings. (a) Right to a hearing. Upon timely request by a complainant following receipt of the investigative file under § 1614.110, an administrative judge shall be assigned to conduct discovery, hold an evidentiary hearing, and issue a binding decision on the merits of the complaint, which the agency shall implement or appeal pursuant to § 1614.401.'

3. Revise Section 1614.106(c) (Page 55712) to restore notice pleading standards:
'§ 1614.106(c) Contents of complaint. A complaint must contain a signed statement from the person claiming to be aggrieved or that person's attorney, identifying the complainant, the agency, and basic factual information sufficient to provide fair notice of the challenged action, protected basis, and approximate timeframe. Technical legal pleading standards shall not apply.'

IV. CONCLUSION
We urge the Commission to withdraw the proposed restrictions on AJ hearings, class complaint processing, and pleading standards, and to re-issue a revised rule focused solely on Cummings Act compliance and digital modernization.

ai_data.proposed_comment:
COMMENTS OF CIVIC AND FINANCIAL POLICY ADVOCATES

Re: Disclosure of Information (RIN 3064-AG30; 91 FR 55501; 91 FR 39726)

I. INTRODUCTION AND SUPPORT FOR EXTENSION

We commend the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) for granting an extension of the public comment period for RIN 3064-AG30 to October 5, 2026 (91 FR 55501). The proposed revisions to 12 CFR Parts 303, 306, 309, 327, and 337 represent a substantial restructuring of how Confidential Supervisory Information (CSI) is protected, shared, and disclosed under the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) and legal service of process.

II. SUBSTANTIVE CONCERNS AND LEGAL ANALYSIS

1. Harmonization of CSI Definitions Across Banking Agencies
Under proposed 12 CFR Part 309, insured depository institutions (IDIs) may share CSI with affiliates and service providers without prior FDIC authorization. While intended to reduce administrative burdens, this provision creates inconsistency with parallel OCC (12 CFR Part 4) and Federal Reserve (12 CFR Part 261) regulations. Discrepancies in the scope of permissible recipients across bank regulatory regimes violate basic principles of regulatory consistency and impose undue compliance burdens.

2. Lack of Objective Standards for Discretionary Disclosures
The proposed rules expand FDIC discretion to disclose CSI to third parties. Under 5 U.S.C. 706(2)(A), agency actions must not be arbitrary, capricious, or an abuse of discretion. Allowing broad discretionary release without established criteria, notice-and-opportunity-to-object mechanisms for the affected institution, or formal administrative appeal mechanisms subjects financial institutions to irreparable commercial and reputational harm.

3. Safeguards for Third-Party and Affiliate Access
While allowing sharing with affiliates and certain contractors for legitimate business purposes is practical, the proposed regulatory text lacks mandatory technical safeguards (e.g., encryption, audit logging, and explicit confidentiality agreements) enforceable by the FDIC.

III. PROPOSED AMENDMENTS TO REGULATORY TEXT

To address these defects, we propose the following specific modifications to 12 CFR 309.6:

Proposed 12 CFR 309.6(c)(2) (Affiliate and Service Provider Sharing):
"(i) Permissible Sharing. An insured depository institution may disclose confidential supervisory information to its affiliates, legal counsel, independent auditors, and technology service providers solely for legitimate supervisory or corporate governance purposes, provided that:
(A) The recipient executes a binding written confidentiality agreement adhering to standards approved by the FDIC;
(B) The recipient maintains robust data security controls consistent with Interagency Guidelines Establishing Standards for Safeguarding Customer Information; and
(C) The FDIC is provided prior written notification of any unauthorized access to or disclosure of such confidential supervisory information within 24 hours of discovery."

Proposed 12 CFR 309.6(e) (FDIC Discretionary Disclosure Standard):
"Prior to any discretionary disclosure of confidential supervisory information to non-regulatory third parties, the FDIC shall provide written notice to the affected institution at least 15 business days prior to disclosure, providing an opportunity for the institution to object or seek protective administrative review, unless emergency conditions warrant immediate release."

IV. CONCLUSION

We urge the FDIC to adopt these recommendations to ensure legal clarity, interagency harmonization, and robust data privacy protections.

title: Special Conditions: Skyryse, Robinson Helicopter Company Model R66 Helicopter; Control Margin Awareness

ai_data.summary_of_main_idea: The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) proposes special conditions for the Robinson R66 helicopter modified with Skyryse's SkyOS digital fly-by-wire (FBW) flight control system. Because the FBW system replaces traditional mechanical flight controls, eliminating direct mechanical feedback of cyclic and pedal positions, the proposed rule requires the flight control system to make pilots 'suitably aware' when approaching control authority limits at the main and tail rotors.
ai_data.challenges: The primary defect in the proposed rule is the subjective and legally vague standard of requiring flight crews to be 'suitably aware,' defined merely as an 'appropriate balance between nuisance and necessary operation.' Under the Administrative Procedure Act (5 U.S.C. § 706), this standard is impermissibly arbitrary and unconstitutionally vague because it lacks objective, measurable metrics for compliance. Scientifically and technically, the rule fails to specify multi-modal cueing requirements—specifically tactile/haptic feedback through active inceptors. Human factors research demonstrates that in high-workload or Degraded Visual Environments (DVE), visual or acoustic alerts alone are insufficient to prevent loss of control (LOC) when control margins are exhausted.

references.title: Motor Vehicle Mfrs. Ass'n v. State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co., 463 U.S. 29 (1983) (Establishing that agency rules lacking clear, reasoned explanation or objective standards are arbitrary and capricious under the APA).

ai_data.proposed_comment:
PUBLIC COMMENT ON PROPOSED SPECIAL CONDITIONS

Docket No. FAA-2026-1585; Notice No. XX-XX-XX-SC
Special Conditions: Skyryse, Robinson Helicopter Company Model R66 Helicopter; Control Margin Awareness

I. INTRODUCTION
These comments are submitted in response to the FAA's Notice of Proposed Special Conditions for the Robinson Helicopter Company Model R66, modified by Skyryse to incorporate the SkyOS fly-by-wire (FBW) flight control system (89 FR 55501-55503). While modernizing rotorcraft flight controls with FBW technology offers significant potential safety benefits, the regulatory standards proposed on Page 55503 are legally deficient under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA) and technically incomplete regarding human factors engineering.

II. LEGAL DEFECT: UNCONSTITUTIONAL VAGUENESS AND APA ARBITRARINESS
On Page 55503, column 3, the proposed special condition states:
"The system design must ensure that the flight crew is made suitably aware whenever the means of primary flight control approaches the limits of control authority. For the context of this special condition, the term 'suitable' indicates an appropriate balance between nuisance and necessary operation."

Defining regulatory compliance using subjective phrases such as "suitably aware" and "appropriate balance" fails the requirement under 5 U.S.C. § 706 for clear, objective administrative standards. An applicant cannot determine what specific design thresholds (e.g., force feedback gradients, visual cue thresholds, soft-stop displacement percentages) satisfy this requirement. This lack of clear guidance creates an unlevel playing field and exposes the agency to legal challenges for arbitrary and capricious enforcement.

III. TECHNICAL DEFECT: INSUFFICIENT HUMAN FACTORS CUEING SPECIFICATIONS
Rotorcraft operations frequently occur in high-workload phases of flight (e.g., low-altitude hover, confined-area landings, degraded visual environments). Decades of rotorcraft human factors research show that pilots head-up/eyes-out cannot rely on visual or secondary auditory warnings to gauge proximity to control limits. Without active tactile/haptic feedback (such as variable force gradient build-up or soft detent stops on the flight control inceptor), pilots operating FBW systems face heightened risk of spatial disorientation or unexpected control saturation leading to loss of control.

IV. PROPOSED ALTERNATIVE TEXT
To resolve these legal and technical deficiencies, the FAA should revise the Proposed Special Conditions on Page 55503 to read as follows:

"In addition to the existing § 27.143 requirements, the following special condition applies:

(a) The flight control system design must provide distinct, unambiguous, and timely control margin awareness to the flight crew before and upon reaching 85% and 95% of available control authority at the main rotor and tail rotor/anti-torque systems.

(b) Awareness must be provided through a tactile cueing mechanism integrated into the pilot flight control inceptors (such as active force feedback gradients, stick shakers, or tactile soft stops) complemented by secondary visual and/or auditory indications on the primary flight display.

(c) The tactile and visual cueing parameters must remain clearly distinguishable across all approved environmental and operational envelopes, including high-workload and Degraded Visual Environments (DVE), without creating excessive nuisance alerts that degrade pilot performance."

title: Passports: Expanding Online Passport Renewal Overseas

ai_data.summary_of_main_idea: The Department of State proposes to amend 22 CFR Part 51 to expand the Online Passport Renewal (OPR) system to eligible U.S. citizens residing abroad in designated foreign countries. Additionally, the proposed rule eliminates the fixed requirement that an applicant's prior passport must have one year or less of remaining validity, opting instead to allow the Department to determine validity requirements and country availability dynamically on its public website. The rule aims to reduce administrative burdens and processing costs for both overseas applicants and consular posts.
ai_data.challenges:
The proposed rule suffers from key legal, procedural, and technical flaws under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA):

1. APA Procedural Violations (5 U.S.C. 553): By leaving core eligibility criteria—such as which foreign countries qualify and the specific remaining validity thresholds—to uncodified web postings at travel.state.gov/renewonline, the Department impermissibly sidesteps notice-and-comment rulemaking. Sub-regulatory web modifications bypass public scrutiny and create binding standards without statutory authority.
2. Arbitrary and Capricious Decision-Making (5 U.S.C. 706(2)(A)): The agency fails to articulate clear, objective legal or technical criteria governing how foreign posts will be selected or phased into the program, leading to potential unequal treatment of Americans abroad without a reasoned explanation.
3. Flawed Economic Assumptions in RIA: The preliminary Regulatory Impact Analysis relies on broad wage averages ($21.36/hr from OECD data) and speculative travel time savings without accounting for regional economic variations or foreign internet accessibility constraints, potentially skewing the cost-benefit analysis.
4. Cybersecurity and Fraud Risks: The rule does not establish binding technical or identity-verification standards for online submissions initiated across untrusted foreign networks, heightening risks of digital identity theft and unauthorized access.

COMMENTS OF CIVIC ADVOCATES AND PUBLIC POLICY ANALYSTS

RE: Department of State Proposed Rule: Passports: Expanding Online Passport Renewal Overseas (22 CFR Part 51; RIN 1400-AF97; Docket No. DOS-2026-0925; 91 FR 55505)

I. INTRODUCTION AND EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
We submit these comments in response to the Department of State's Proposed Rule published at 91 FR 55505 (August 28, 2026). While we support modernizing passport services and expanding Online Passport Renewal (OPR) to U.S. citizens residing abroad, the rule as drafted contains critical procedural and regulatory defects under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), 5 U.S.C. § 553.

II. LEGAL DEFECTS: UNLAWFUL DELEGATION OF ELIGIBILITY STANDARDS TO WEB GUIDANCE
Under proposed 22 CFR § 51.21(b)(2)(i), the Department states that an online applicant's prior passport must remain valid for 'a period prescribed on the Department's website at travel.state.gov/renewonline.' Similarly, paragraph (b)(2) limits eligibility to foreign countries 'listed on its website.'

This structure violates fundamental administrative law principles:
1. Impermissible Rulemaking via Guidance: Delegating substantive eligibility conditions (qualifying locations and validity thresholds) to an informal website allows the agency to alter legal rights and burdens without public notice and comment (Appalachian Power Co. v. EPA, 208 F.3d 1015). 
2. Lack of Objective Standards: The rule provides no governing criteria explaining how or when a country will be listed or removed, rendering the rollout vulnerable to challenges as arbitrary and capricious under 5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A).

III. RECOMMENDATIONS AND PROPOSED AMENDMENTS
To cure these defects, the Department must establish objective, codified criteria in the regulatory text while reserving administrative flexibility. We propose amending the regulatory language at 22 CFR § 51.21(b)(2) as follows:

Proposed Regulatory Wording Amendments:

§ 51.21(b)(2) A person in the United States, or in a foreign country where the Department has authorized online passport applications based on technical infrastructure and risk assessment standards published pursuant to paragraph (e) of this section, who previously has been issued a passport valid for 10 years in his or her own name may apply for a new passport by submitting an online application via the Department's official website if:
(i) The applicant's most recently issued passport was issued when the applicant was 16 years of age or older, and was issued not more than 15 years prior to the date of application;
(ii) The application complies with secure digital verification protocols established by the Department; and
(iii) The most recently issued passport of the same type is available for verification via the online process.

[Add Paragraph (e)]:
(e) Criteria for Overseas Online Renewal Authorization. The Department shall publish in the Federal Register and maintain on its website the objective operational, security, and diplomatic criteria used to determine post and country eligibility for online passport renewal.

IV. CONCLUSION
By codifying clear eligibility criteria and preserving formal notice mechanisms, the Department can achieve its efficiency goals while maintaining administrative integrity and protecting citizen rights worldwide.

title: Airworthiness Directives: Embraer S.A. Airplanes

1. Administrative Process and Regulatory Delay (APA § 706): The FAA delayed nearly five years (from ANAC's 2021 directive to this 2026 NPRM) to propose mandatory actions for an unsafe condition categorized as potential loss of aircraft controllability. 2. Technical Defect in Remedy: The proposed AD specifies replacing the failing seal with a part bearing the exact same Part Number (P/N 550-04725-901) without requiring revised surface preparation, superior adhesive specifications, or structural redesign. 3. Incomplete Economic Analysis: The FAA's cost evaluation ($1,561 per aircraft; $85,855 total U.S. fleet) omits downtime costs, scheduled maintenance disruption, and out-of-service revenue losses incurred by fractional and charter operators.

title: Swap Execution Facility Order Book Requirement for Permitted Transactions

ai_data.summary_of_main_idea: The Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) proposes to amend 17 CFR 37.3(a)(2) to eliminate the requirement that Swap Execution Facilities (SEFs) offer an electronic order book for 'Permitted Transactions'—swaps that are not subject to the mandatory trade execution requirement under Section 2(h)(8) of the Commodity Exchange Act. The proposed rule seeks to codify CFTC Staff No-Action Letter 25-24, reasoning that mandatory order books for illiquid or episodically traded swaps impose heavy operational and financial costs on SEFs while generating negligible trading volume and minimal pre-trade price transparency.
ai_data.challenges: The proposal suffers from three major defects. First, legally and procedurally under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), the CFTC relies on isolated representations from select SEF operators rather than conducting a broad empirical evaluation of market-wide pre-trade transparency, thereby failing to demonstrate how a blanket removal aligns with its statutory mandate under CEA Section 5h(e) to promote pre-trade transparency. Second, economically, eliminating order books entirely without establishing a conditional or volume-based threshold mechanism risks locking in dealer-centric market fragmentation (e.g., RFQ-to-3 or voice execution), foreclosing opportunities for buy-side liquidity provision and wider quote competition as markets evolve. Third, the rule fails to consider hybrid transparency alternatives, such as mandatory indicative pricing streams or low-cost central limit order displays, which would preserve pre-trade price discovery without imposing full matching-engine overhead.

ai_data.proposed_comment:
COMMENTS OF CIVIC ADVOCATES AND MARKET STRUCTURE ANALYSTS

To: Christopher Kirkpatrick, Secretary
Commodity Futures Trading Commission
Three Lafayette Centre, 1155 21st Street NW, Washington, DC 20581

Re: Swap Execution Facility Order Book Requirement for Permitted Transactions (RIN 3038-AF79; 91 FR 55030, August 26, 2026)

I. INTRODUCTION AND EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
We appreciate the opportunity to comment on the Commodity Futures Trading Commission's ('CFTC' or 'Commission') Notice of Proposed Rulemaking ('NPRM') regarding amendments to 17 CFR Part 37, 'Swap Execution Facility Order Book Requirement for Permitted Transactions' (91 FR 55030). 

While we recognize the operational costs highlighted by SEF operators on pages 55032–55033 of the NPRM, we strongly object to the complete, unconditioned elimination of the Order Book Requirement for all Permitted Transactions. CEA Section 5h(e) explicitly establishes that a primary statutory goal of SEFs is to promote pre-trade price transparency and trading on SEFs. A blanket removal of the minimum order book functionality for all non-mandated swaps—regardless of liquidity, trading volume, or product evolution—undermines these statutory directives and risks enshrining opaque, multi-dealer request-for-quote (RFQ) and voice workflows as permanent market fixtures.

II. SPECIFIC COMMENTS AND LEGAL DEFICIENCIES

1. APA Procedural and Empirical Deficiencies (91 FR 55032)
In Section II.A.1, the Commission bases its rationale primarily on NAL No. 25-24 and self-reported data from select registrants (e.g., LSEG SEF and Bloomberg SEF). Relying on qualitative assertions of operational burden without establishing a standardized, empirical evaluation across all registered SEFs creates an inadequate administrative record under 5 U.S.C. 706. The low usage of order books historically is partly a symptom of dealer preference for RFQ workflows rather than an inherent failure of order book mechanics.

2. Failure to Adopt a Volume-Based or Tiered Threshold (Response to Request for Comment #2, 91 FR 55033)
In Request for Comment #2 (p. 55033), the Commission asks whether it should use 'another method, such as trading volume in a certain swap, to require the use of an Order Book for some Permitted Transactions.' We strongly advocate for a volume-based threshold. Permitted Transactions are not a homogenous class; certain liquid benchmark swaps that have not yet been formally made subject to a trade execution requirement under Section 2(h)(8) possess sufficient activity to support order book price discovery. A dynamic threshold ensures that as a Permitted Transaction matures in volume and liquidity, market participants benefit from pre-trade order book transparency automatically.

III. PROPOSED ALTERNATIVE REGULATORY TEXT

To balance operational burdens against the statutory mandate to promote pre-trade transparency, we propose modifying 17 CFR 37.3(a)(2) to incorporate a conditional liquidity assessment standard rather than a total exemption:

Proposed Revision to § 37.3(a)(2):

'§ 37.3 Requirements and procedures for registration.
(a) * * *
(2) Minimum trading functionality. 
(i) Required Transactions. A swap execution facility shall, at a minimum, offer an Order Book as defined in paragraph (a)(3) of this section for Required Transactions as defined in § 37.9(a)(1).
(ii) Permitted Transactions. A swap execution facility shall offer an Order Book for Permitted Transactions, as defined in § 37.9(c)(1), that meet or exceed quarterly trading volume and liquidity thresholds established by the Commission. For all other Permitted Transactions, a swap execution facility may satisfy minimum trading functionality by offering an Order Book or an alternative trading functionality that displays executable or indicative quotes to all market participants on the facility.'

IV. CONCLUSION
The Commission should refine its proposal to ensure that market structure reform actively encourages competitive, pre-trade price transparency, rather than permanently deregulating execution methods for non-cleared or non-mandated swaps.

title: Pro Rata Share of Subpart F Income, Tested Income, or Tested Loss

ai_data.summary_of_main_idea: This proposed regulation from the Internal Revenue Service and Department of the Treasury implements statutory amendments from the One, Big, Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) regarding how United States shareholders calculate their pro rata share of Subpart F income, tested income, and tested loss from Controlled Foreign Corporations (CFCs). It eliminates former rules requiring ownership on the 'last relevant day' and replaces them with a daily proration regime across periods of ownership during the CFC's taxable year. Additionally, the rule establishes mandatory taxable year closing upon a CFC status change event and provides a 50% ownership variance elective year-closing mechanism, while phasing out extraordinary reduction rules under §1.245A-5.
ai_data.challenges:
1. Administrative Procedure Act (APA) Arbitrary & Capricious Weakness: The rigid mandatory application of daily proration under proposed § 1.951-1(e)(2) without an interim closing of books or an 'extraordinary items' exception fails to account for major discrete income events (such as substantial asset dispositions) occurring before or after ownership transfers. Failing to provide standard accounting exceptions misallocates tax burdens contrary to economic reality and administrative precedents (e.g., Treas. Reg. § 1.706-4 and § 1.1502-76(b)).

2. Overly Restrictive Elective Year-Closing Threshold: Proposed § 1.951-1(d)(2) restricts elective year-closing exclusively to transactions resulting in a greater than 50 percentage point shift among non-related shareholders. For transfers between 10% and 50%, selling U.S. shareholders lose operational control yet remain fully exposed to post-closing actions of buyers that inflate Subpart F or GILTI inclusion amounts without contractual recourse or remedy.

3. Excessively Onerous Substantiation Requirements: Proposed § 1.951-4(h) rejects public comments on Notice 2025-75 and mandates onerous, subjective third-party documentation to prove a dividend increased taxable income for transition rule purposes. The refusal to provide a administrative safe harbor or per se rule creates severe compliance friction for historical, closed transactions.

October 20, 2026

CC:PA:01:PR (REG-115646-25)
Room 5503
Internal Revenue Service
P.O. Box 7604, Ben Franklin Station
Washington, DC 20044

RE: Comments on Proposed Regulations under Sections 951, 951A, and 6038 (REG-115646-25; RIN 1545-BR77): Pro Rata Share of Subpart F Income, Tested Income, or Tested Loss

Dear Officers and Drafting Counsel:

We submit these comments in response to the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking published in the Federal Register (91 FR 55037-55062) on August 26, 2026. While we support Treasury and the IRS's efforts to implement the statutory revisions under the One, Big, Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA), key aspects of the proposed regulations impose significant economic distortions and administrative burdens that fail the standards of reasoned decision-making under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA).

1. Need for an Extraordinary Items Exception in Daily Proration (§ 1.951-1(e)(2))
As drafted, proposed § 1.951-1(e)(2) mandates a pure daily proration approach for allocating a CFC's Subpart F income, tested income, and tested loss when ownership shifts during the year. This blanket method creates significant economic distortions if a CFC recognizes a large extraordinary gain (such as a discrete asset sale under Section 337 or Section 1001) either prior to or following a stock transfer. A taxpayer selling stock early in the year could be retroactively allocated a pro rata share of Subpart F income generated by an extraordinary transaction conducted months later by an unrelated buyer.

Recommendation: Treasury and the IRS should adopt an 'extraordinary items' exception modeled on Treas. Reg. § 1.706-4 and § 1.1502-76(b). Under this exception, extraordinary discrete gains or losses would be specifically allocated to the period in which they occurred rather than prorated daily across the entire taxable year.

2. Lowering the Threshold for Elective Closing of Taxable Year (§ 1.951-1(d)(2))
Proposed § 1.951-1(d)(2) limits the elective closing of a CFC's taxable year to cases where there is a 'significant ownership variance' exceeding 50 percentage points among non-related shareholders. This threshold is overly restrictive. A shareholder disposing of a 20% or 30% stake frequently surrenders operational oversight and lacks the audit rights or contractual power to prevent buyers from altering business operations or tax choices before year-end.

Recommendation: Lower the threshold for an elective year-closing under proposed § 1.951-1(d)(2)(ii)(A) from 50 percentage points to 20 percentage points, or permit a joint election whenever a U.S. shareholder disposes of its entire stock interest in a CFC.

3. Adoption of a Safe Harbor for Transition Rule Substantiation (§ 1.951-4(h))
Proposed § 1.951-4(h) mandates that taxpayers submit a detailed statement proving that a dividend increased a U.S. person's taxable income without establishing clear safe harbors for taxpayers who lack third-party access.

Recommendation: Adopt a per se safe harbor stating that dividends received by domestic corporations subject to standard federal corporate income tax (where no deduction under Section 245A or foreign tax credit offsets apply) automatically satisfy the substantiation requirement.

PROPOSED REGULATORY TEXT CHANGES:

Modify proposed § 1.951-1(d)(2)(ii)(A) as follows:
"(A) In general. A significant ownership variance occurs if, taking into account all specified transfers that occur pursuant to the same plan during the same taxable year of a controlled foreign corporation... the percentage of the outstanding stock of the controlled foreign corporation owned by one or more section 958(a) U.S. shareholders decreases, in the aggregate, by [REPLACE: more than 50 percentage points] [WITH: 20 percentage points or more, or results in a complete disposition of a section 958(a) U.S. shareholder's interest]."

Modify proposed § 1.951-1(e)(2)(i)(A) as follows:
"(A) Daily proration. Subject to paragraph (e)(2)(i)(B) of this section and paragraph (e)(2)(i)(C) (Extraordinary Items Exception), if the controlled foreign corporation has only one class of stock outstanding..."

Respectfully submitted,

COMMENTS OF CIVIC ADVOCATES AND MARITIME INTERESTS

Docket No. USCG-2026-0035; RIN 1625-AA01
Anchorage Regulation; San Juan Bay, San Juan, PR
91 FR 55062 (August 26, 2026)

I. INTRODUCTION AND STATEMENT OF INTEREST
These comments are submitted in response to the Coast Guard's Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) regarding revisions to Anchorage D in San Juan Harbor, Puerto Rico (91 FR 55062–55064). While we support the agency's primary goal of ensuring maritime safety and avoiding collisions between commercial vessels and anchored craft in the San Antonio Channel, the rule as drafted imposes arbitrary restrictions on recreational mariners and lacks required procedural and environmental documentation.

II. PROCEDURAL AND LEGAL DEFICIENCIES

1. Inadequate Arbitrary and Capricious Justification under the APA (5 U.S.C. 553)

COMMENTS OF CIVIC ADVOCATES AND POLICY ANALYSTS ON THE PROPOSED RULE:
List of Approved Spent Fuel Storage Casks: TN Americas, LLC Standardized NUHOMS Horizontal Modular Storage System, Renewed Amendment No. 19
Docket ID: NRC-2026-2806 | RIN: 3150-AL72 | 10 CFR Part 72

I. INTRODUCTION & EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
We submit these public comments regarding the Nuclear Regulatory Commission's (NRC) proposed rule to approve Renewed Amendment No. 19 to Certificate of Compliance (CoC) No. 1004 for the TN Americas, LLC Standardized NUHOMS Horizontal Modular Storage System (88 FR 55028, August 26, 2026). While design optimizations that streamline manufacturing are understandable, the proposed implementation of a staggered plate design in the 61BTH basket introduces structural, thermal, and regulatory questions that require comprehensive public disclosure and technical justification prior to final approval.

II. SPECIFIC TECHNICAL AND LEGAL DEFECTS

1. Inadequate Structural and Thermal Margin Justification (88 FR 55028, Section I / Safety Evaluation Report ML26103A252):
The NRC proposes approving the 61BTH staggered plate basket based on technical similarities to the 24PTH Type 3 basket (CoC 1004, Amend 18) and EOS 37PTH/89BTH baskets (CoC 1042). However, changing the geometry of structural plates directly affects thermal dissipation capacity and load distribution during drop or seismic events. The rule relies heavily on design analogies rather than providing fully unredacted finite element dynamic impact modeling and transient heat transfer analyses for high-burnup fuel loads. Under 10 CFR 72.236(l), dry storage designs must evaluate structural integrity under normal, off-normal, and accident conditions; cross-referencing separate CoC approvals without providing integrated, public stress-strain evaluations for the modified 61BTH basket prevents meaningful public review under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), 5 U.S.C. § 553.

2. Reliance on Outdated Environmental Assessments (88 FR 55030, Section VI):
The NRC cites environmental assessments dated 1989 (ML051230231) and 2010 (ML100710441) to satisfy its NEPA obligations. The physical properties of high-burnup fuel, combined with the extended storage periods envisioned under the CoC 1004 renewal, create thermal stress and cladding degradation risks that were not analyzed in 1989 or 2010. Reliance on legacy environmental documents to justify structural basket weight reductions for renewed CoCs fails to satisfy NEPA's mandate for a 'hard look' at cumulative environmental impacts.

III. PROPOSED ALTERNATIVE WORDING AND REGULATORY ACTION

To ensure complete safety and regulatory compliance, the NRC should withdraw the direct final rule and issue a revised proposed rule incorporating the following text within the 10 CFR 72.214 entry for CoC No. 1004, Renewed Amendment No. 19:

Proposed Technical Specification Requirement Addition:
"For the 61BTH improved basket design using staggered plates, general licensees shall verify that site-specific seismic acceleration limits and peak cladding temperature margins do not exceed the baseline parameters established in Revision 0 of the Safety Evaluation Report. Prior to first use of the 61BTH staggered plate configuration for spent fuel exceeding 45,000 MWd/MTU burnup, licensees must conduct a finite element structural dynamic analysis confirming basket plate integrity under maximum credible drop and seismic scenarios, and submit the analysis to the NRC for public docketing under Docket ID NRC-2026-2806."

IV. CONCLUSION
The NRC must ensure that economic and manufacturing convenience does not compromise structural redundancy or environmental review standards. We urge the Commission to address these comments as significant adverse comments under the procedure described at 88 FR 55029, withdraw the direct final rule, and publish a detailed supplemental evaluation for public review.

title: Membership Adjustment of the Mushroom Council

ai_data.summary_of_main_idea: The USDA Agricultural Marketing Service (AMS) proposes to amend the Mushroom Promotion, Research, and Consumer Information Order (7 CFR Part 1209) by realigning the geographic regions and member seats on the Mushroom Council. Specifically, the rule reallocates one Council seat from Region 1 (Eastern/Other States) to Region 3 (Western States) based on 4-year average production and shipment data. The objective is to adjust Council representation to reflect regional shifts in domestic mushroom production volume.
ai_data.challenges:
The proposed rule exhibits several legal, procedural, and empirical weaknesses under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA) and the Regulatory Flexibility Act (RFA):

1. Reliance on Unvalidated Proxy Data: Because USDA National Agricultural Statistics Service (NASS) discontinued individual state-level reporting for California in 2025, AMS estimated production ratios for Regions 1 and 3 using static 2022 Census of Agriculture square-footage figures. Applying 2022 square-footage proportions to 2021-2024 NASS production data assumes constant yield per square foot across all regions and time periods. This methodology is scientifically flawed, fails to reflect regional efficiency gains, and introduces arbitrary estimates into formal rulemaking.

2. Severe Governance Disproportion for Importers: Importers contribute roughly 198 million pounds annually (~22-30% of total U.S. mushroom volume), yet remain capped at 1 member out of 9 (11% representation). While statutory limits exist, AMS relies on a rigid reallocation framework without providing economic analysis on the disparate assessment-to-representation ratio imposed on importers.

3. Procedural Shortcomings and Inadequate Comment Period: A truncated 30-day comment window limits the ability of small producers in Region 1—who stand to lose 33% of their voting power—to conduct independent data collection to verify or challenge AMS's square-footage allocation estimates.

These comments are submitted regarding the Agricultural Marketing Service's (AMS) proposed rule to reallocate seats on the Mushroom Council from Region 1 to Region 3. To compensate, AMS calculated a fixed ratio (45% for Region 1 and 55% for Region 3) using growing area square footage from the 2022 Census of Agriculture, and applied this 2022 static ratio across all 2021–2024 production figures.

This proxy methodology is fundamentally flawed:
1. Yield Variability: Crop yield per square foot differs significantly between advanced commercial growing operations in California/West and legacy operations in the East. Assuming uniform productivity across all square footage introduces systemic bias.
2. Temporal Mismatch: A static 2022 area metric cannot accurately capture dynamic shifts in production efficiency or farm closures occurring in 2023 and 2024.
3. Lack of Empirical Validation: AMS failed to cross-validate these proxy calculations against actual assessment collection records held by the Mushroom Council.

III. SMALL BUSINESS AND RFA IMPACTS (91 FR 54816)
Under the Initial Regulatory Flexibility Act Analysis, AMS notes that 96% of mushroom producers (1,213 of 1,258) are small entities. AMS should delay finalization of this reallocation until actual, verified producer assessment shipment volumes from the Mushroom Council—rather than NASS proxy estimates based on 2022 square footage—are published for public audit. Alternatively, AMS should adopt a phased reallocation or establish a temporary advisory seat for Region 1.

title: Special Conditions: Pratt and Whitney Canada, PW220A; New Engine Rating: Idle-Cruise Regime

ai_data.summary_of_main_idea: The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) proposes special conditions for the Pratt & Whitney Canada (P&WC) PW220A turboshaft engine to establish airworthiness safety standards for an unusual 'Idle-Cruise Regime' (ICR) power rating structure. Under ICR, twin-engine transport helicopters can operate one engine at low stand-by idle while the active engine provides 100% of required cruise power to significantly improve fuel efficiency and extend flight range. The proposed special conditions create new definitions, operating limitations, control system requirements, and modified testing criteria for icing, rain ingestion, endurance, and transient power response under 14 CFR Part 33.
ai_data.challenges:
The primary challenges and regulatory defects in the proposed special conditions concern safety margins during sudden engine-out emergencies, environmental icing risk, thermal fatigue, and Administrative Procedure Act (APA) procedural sufficiency:

1. Safety and Acceleration Response Latency (§ 33.73): Allowing up to 5 seconds for an engine to transition from ICR stand-by power to 95% takeoff power creates a critical performance lag. In the event of a sudden flameout or failure of the active engine, a 5-second recovery delay risks significant rotor droop, control loss, or rapid loss of altitude before the stand-by engine can supply sufficient power.
2. Environmental Icing and Relight Risk (§ 33.68 & § 33.78): Because an engine operating at ICR stand-by produces substantially less waste heat, ice and water accumulation on intake blades, guide vanes, and combustor probes during extended low-power cruise in icing or heavy rain conditions could cause engine flameout or delayed relight during sudden acceleration.
3. Thermal Shock and Low-Cycle Fatigue (§ 33.87): Rapidly cycling between low stand-by idle and maximum continuous or 2-minute emergency power subjects hot-section turbine components to severe thermal gradients and mechanical strain. The proposed endurance test cycles may fail to capture long-term low-cycle fatigue (LCF) and thermal mechanical fatigue (TMF) blade degradation over the engine's lifecycle.
4. Procedural & Substantiation Deficiencies under the APA: The FAA has not provided empirical test data or rotorcraft flight dynamics modeling to justify why a 5-second acceleration response time ensures an equivalent level of safety for transport category twin-engine helicopters operating under 14 CFR Part 29.

COMMENTS OF CIVIC ADVOCATES AND SAFETY RESEARCHERS ON PROPOSED SPECIAL CONDITIONS

Docket No. FAA-2026-3073; Notice No. 33-25-03-SC
Special Conditions: Pratt and Whitney Canada, PW220A; New Engine Rating: Idle-Cruise Regime

I. INTRODUCTION AND EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
We submit these comments in response to the Federal Aviation Administration's (FAA) Notice of Proposed Special Conditions for the Pratt & Whitney Canada (P&WC) Model PW220A engine. While we support fuel-efficiency innovations in rotorcraft propulsion, the proposed Idle-Cruise Regime (ICR) creates novel failure modes that demand stricter safety parameters to protect civil aviation safety under 14 CFR Part 33 and Part 29.

II. SPECIFIC TECHNICAL CONCERNS AND RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Transient Acceleration Time Limits (§ 33.73 - Power or Thrust Response)
- Issue: The FAA proposes allowing a 5-second response time from rated ICR stand-by power to 95% rated takeoff power. In a twin-engine rotorcraft, if the active engine suffers an abrupt uncommanded shutdown during cruise, a 5-second delay before the stand-by engine reaches power will result in dangerous main rotor RPM decay (rotor droop).
- Recommendation: The acceleration time from ICR stand-by to 95% rated takeoff power must be shortened to no more than 3.0 seconds under all ambient temperatures and bleed air load conditions. Alternatively, the FAA must require an integrated automated rotorcraft flight control system override that prevents transient rotor droop beyond allowable safety limits.

2. Extended Icing Exposure and Ingestion Safety (§ 33.68 & § 33.78)
- Issue: Low engine thermal output during extended ICR stand-by flight in icing conditions increases the risk of ice accretion in the induction system and combustor flameout during rapid power expansion.
- Recommendation: Section 33.68 testing should require a minimum continuous 30-minute exposure at rated ICR stand-by power in continuous maximum icing conditions prior to rapid acceleration, ensuring no ice shed induces engine stall or flameout.

3. Endurance and Thermal Mechanical Fatigue Verification (§ 33.87)
- Issue: The proposed endurance cycles do not adequately account for the cumulative thermal mechanical fatigue (TMF) resulting from repeated rapid step-changes between cold stand-by idle and hot 2-minute ICR power.
- Recommendation: Add a mandatory supplemental low-cycle thermal shock test requiring 500 direct rapid acceleration/deceleration cycles between ICR stand-by and ICR 2-minute power to evaluate turbine blade erosion and creep failure modes.

III. PROPOSED ALTERNATIVE REGULATORY TEXT

We propose the following amendments to the proposed special condition text:

Section 33.73 Power or Thrust Response:
"The design and construction of the engine must enable an increase from the rated ICR stand-by power lever position to 95 percent rated takeoff power in not over 3.0 seconds. The 3.0-second power response must occur from a stabilized static condition using maximum allowable bleed air and accessories loads necessary to run the engine and rotorcraft services."

Section 33.68 Induction System Icing:
"Compliance with § 33.68 must be demonstrated at 'rated ICR stand-by power rotor speeds' for a continuous duration of not less than 30 minutes in standard icing conditions prior to demonstrating rapid engine acceleration without engine surge, stall, or flameout."

IV. CONCLUSION
The FAA should revise these special conditions to incorporate these essential safeguards prior to final issuance.

title: Fee for Certain H–1B Petitions

ai_data.summary_of_main_idea: The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) proposes establishing an additional, standalone fee of $103,265 on all H-1B cap-subject petitions, including those eligible for the advanced degree exemption. ai_data.challenges:
The proposed rule suffers from major legal, economic, and procedural defects:
1. Statutory Overreach under INA § 286(m) and (n): Section 286(m) limits fee assessments to recovering the full costs of 'providing adjudication and naturalization services.' Attempting to fund foreign refugee travel/medicals (DOS/PRM), removal proceedings (DOJ/EOIR), border biometric technology (CBP), and multi-agency labor enforcement (DOL) transforms a targeted user fee into an unauthorized tax lacking statutory authority.
2. Arbitrary and Capricious Cost-Shifting (APA 5 U.S.C. § 706): DHS explicitly acknowledges that it has never before transferred 100% of multi-agency operational deficits onto a single benefit category based on an unbacked 'ability to pay' principle. Disregarding the traditional Activity-Based Costing (ABC) framework and OMB Circular A-25 without a rational nexus violates administrative law standards.
3. Regulatory Flexibility Act (RFA) & Economic Flaws: DHS admits that 76% of small business H-1B petitioners will suffer a severe economic impact exceeding 1% of revenue. Despite this, DHS summarily rejected small-business exemptions or tiered fee structures without empirical economic modeling, relying instead on a single non-peer-reviewed working paper (Borjas 2026) to claim H-1B demand is inelastic.

PUBLIC COMMENT SUBMISSION

Date: September 20, 2026
To: U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, Department of Homeland Security
Docket No.: USCIS-2026-0298
