Re: Notice of Proposed Rulemaking – Fee for Certain H-1B Petitions (91 FR 54817-54839)

I. INTRODUCTION & STATEMENT OF INTEREST
The undersigned organization submits this public comment in response to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) titled "Fee for Certain H-1B Petitions," published at 91 FR 54817 (August 25, 2026). The proposed rule would establish an unprecedented $103,265 supplemental fee on all H-1B cap-subject petitions, creating an unsustainable burden on employers, higher education institutions, and small businesses.

II. STATUTORY DEFECTS: DHS EXCEEDS ITS AUTHORITY UNDER INA § 286(m) & (n)
As stated at 91 FR 54819–54820, DHS relies on Sections 286(m) and (n) of the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA), 8 U.S.C. § 1356(m) and (n), to justify recovering $8.8 billion across six federal agencies. However, Section 286(m) explicitly mandates that fee levels must ensure recovery of the full costs of "providing adjudication and naturalization services." 

Funding DOJ Executive Office for Immigration Review (EOIR) court proceedings ($2.95 billion, 91 FR 54830), DOS Bureau of Population, Refugees, and Migration (PRM) overseas refugee travel ($66 million, 91 FR 54830), and CBP border technology ($76.2 million, 91 FR 54829) exceeds the statutory scope of "adjudication services." Under Supreme Court precedent in National Cable Television Ass'n v. United States, 415 U.S. 336 (1974), an administrative user fee that funds broad public benefits rather than specific services rendered to the payor constitutes an unconstitutional tax. DHS lacks statutory authority to levy an enterprise-wide immigration tax on H-1B employers.

III. ARBITRARY AND CAPRICIOUS COST SHIFTING UNDER THE APA
DHS concedes in the preamble (91 FR 54821) that it "has never directly transferred the costs of one program to another based on a determination that requestors under one program can afford higher fees more than other general or specific requestors." Suddenly abandoning established Activity-Based Costing (ABC) principles—which match fee levels with actual processing burdens—in favor of a subjective "ability-to-pay" standard violates 5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A).

Furthermore, DHS relies on an unvetted working paper (Borjas 2026, 91 FR 54835) to assert that H-1B petition demand will remain at 85,000 despite a 2,000%+ fee increase. DHS failed to model the economic displacement of domestic innovation, talent migration to foreign jurisdictions, and downstream employer bankruptcy, rendering the rule's economic analysis fundamentally flawed.

IV. VIOLATION OF THE REGULATORY FLEXIBILITY ACT (RFA)
In the Initial Regulatory Flexibility Analysis (IRFA) at 91 FR 54837, DHS admits that the proposed fee will have a "significant economic impact on 11,051 small entities (76 percent of small entities that filed cap-subject petitions)." Despite this severe finding, DHS summarily rejected small entity exemptions or fee reductions based on unsupported assertions regarding "perverse incentives." This failure to consider viable regulatory alternatives violates 5 U.S.C. § 603.

V. PROPOSED REGULATORY ALTERNATIVE Wording
To remedy these legal and procedural defects, DHS must withdraw the proposed 8 CFR § 106.2(a)(3)(xii) in its entirety. If DHS seeks to adjust H-1B filing fees, it must do so strictly based on USCIS's actual adjudication costs under established Activity-Based Costing methodologies.

Proposed Regulatory Revision:
Paragraph 8 CFR § 106.2(a)(3)(xii) should be amended/removed as follows:

Option A (Withdrawal):
"8 CFR 106.2(a)(3)(xii) [Removed and Reserved]"

Option B (Capped Adjudication Cost Alternative):
"8 CFR 106.2(a)(3)(xii): In addition to the fee prescribed in paragraph (a)(3)(i) of this section, an additional adjudication cost recovery fee for H-1B cap-subject petitions may be required in an amount not to exceed $1,200, representing solely the direct and indirect costs incurred by USCIS in adjudicating Form I-129 H-1B cap-subject petitions under section 286(m) of the Act."

Respectfully submitted,

PUBLIC COMMENT ON NOTICE OF INTENT TO PREPARE AN ENVIRONMENTAL IMPACT STATEMENT: TRAVEL MANAGEMENT REGULATIONS (36 CFR PARTS 212 AND 261)
Docket ID: FS-2026-0100 | FR Doc No: 2026-17211

I. INTRODUCTION
These comments are submitted in response to the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) Forest Service Notice of Intent (NOI) to prepare an Environmental Impact Statement (EIS) and revise its Travel Management Regulations at 36 CFR Parts 212 and 261, published at 91 FR 54686–54691 (August 24, 2026).

II. SPECIFIC CITATIONS AND LEGAL & PROCEDURAL DEFECTS

1. Arbitrary Removal of Minimization Criteria (91 FR 54688–54689)
The USDA proposes to remove the mandatory 'minimization criteria' currently set forth in 36 CFR §§ 212.55 and 212.80. Under established case law (e.g., Center for Biological Diversity v. BLM), agencies designating motorized routes must demonstrate how they minimized damage to soil, watershed, vegetation, and wildlife habitats. Removing these criteria violates the Agency's statutory obligation under the Forest Service Organic Act of 1897 (16 U.S.C. § 551) to preserve national forests from destruction and degradation.

2. Legitimization of Unauthorized Routes via Aerial Imagery (91 FR 54687)
The proposal allows 'commonly available public data sets, including aerial imagery' to serve as evidence of existing routes. This framework invites the automatic adoption of thousands of miles of illegal, user-created 'ghost trails,' causing severe fragmentation of core wildlife habitats and increased sediment loading into priority watersheds.

3. Inadequate Public Participation Window (91 FR 54687, 54691)
Providing only a 30-day comment period for a nationwide overhaul of travel management policy without holding regional scoping meetings violates the spirit and letter of Council on Environmental Quality (CEQ) NEPA regulations (40 CFR § 1501.9) regarding robust public involvement on major federal actions.

III. PROPOSED ALTERNATIVE REGULATORY WORDING

To ensure statutory compliance with the Organic Act and NFMA, the USDA should adopt Alternative Regulatory Wording in the forthcoming proposed rule as follows:

1. Retain the Closed-Unless-Designated-Open Standard (36 CFR § 212.51):
'Motor vehicle use on National Forest System lands is prohibited off designated roads, trails, and areas, as identified on authoritative Motor Vehicle Use Maps (MVUMs). No route, trail, or airfield shall be presumed open to motorized use unless specifically designated through site-specific environmental analysis.'

2. Mandatory Inclusion of Minimization Criteria (36 CFR § 212.55):
'In designating National Forest System roads, trails, and areas for public motor vehicle use, the responsible official shall apply site-specific data and minimize: (a) damage to soil, watershed, vegetation, and other forest resources; (b) harassment of wildlife and significant disruption of wildlife habitats; and (c) conflicts between motor vehicle use and existing or proposed recreational uses.'

3. Proof of System Routes:
'Aerial imagery or public GIS datasets alone shall not constitute evidence of legal jurisdiction, rights-of-way, or authorization for motorized use.'

IV. CONCLUSION
The Forest Service must maintain science-based travel management that protects natural resources and public safety while accommodating sustainable recreation.

title: Airworthiness Directives: Airbus Helicopters

ai_data.summary_of_main_idea: The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) proposes to supersede Airworthiness Directive (AD) 2025-17-03 for all Airbus Helicopters Model AS332L, AS332L1, AS332L2, and EC225LP helicopters. The proposed rule retains prior requirements to inspect and replace emergency sea anchors while adding a mandatory additional inspection based on European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) AD 2025-0278R1. The rule aims to prevent corrosion-induced failure of the emergency sea anchor pin, which could lead to in-flight release of the anchor, main rotor damage, and catastrophic loss of helicopter control.
ai_data.challenges:
1. APA Procedural Defects & Arbitrary Prohibition of Special Flight Permits: Section (j) strictly prohibits Special Flight Permits under 14 CFR 21.197 and 21.199 without providing empirical justification or risk-mitigated options (e.g., single-pilot ferry flights without passengers or un-ballasted sea anchor configurations). For offshore operators in remote maritime environments, grounding aircraft immediately without ferry allowances creates an unreasoned economic and operational burden under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), 5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A).
2. Technical & Scientific Deficiencies: The proposed AD incorporates EASA AD 2025-0278R1 by reference, which relies primarily on visual inspection for pin corrosion. Visual inspections are insufficient to detect subsurface stress-corrosion cracking (SCC) or micro-pitting caused by salt-spray exposure in heavy maritime operating conditions. Without requiring Non-Destructive Testing (NDT) such as Eddy Current or Ultrasonic Inspection, the rule risks failing to detect latent structural integrity loss prior to pin fracture.
3. Economic Downtime Underestimation: The FAA's economic evaluation accounts only for 2 labor hours ($170) per inspection and $4,833 for part replacement. It completely ignores supply-chain lead times for maritime replacement parts and the substantial revenue loss for offshore support operators during un-serviced downtime in remote offshore stations.

COMMENTS OF CIVIC ADVOCATES AND HELICOPTER OPERATORS

Docket No. FAA-2026-8786; Project Identifier MCAI-2025-01803-R
Airworthiness Directives: Airbus Helicopters (14 CFR Part 39)

I. INTRODUCTION AND INTEREST OF COMMENTERS
The undersigned organizations and aviation safety analysts submit these comments regarding the FAA's Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) published at 91 FR 54683 (August 24, 2026). While supporting the agency's imperative to eliminate catastrophic in-flight sea anchor release hazards on Airbus Model AS332 and EC225LP helicopters, we write to address significant technical and procedural flaws in the proposed text.

II. SPECIFIC COMMENTS AND RATIONALE

1. Blanket Prohibition of Special Flight Permits (Page 54686, Section (j))
Rationale: Paragraph (j) explicitly states that 'Special flight permits as described in 14 CFR 21.197 and 21.199, are not allowed.' In maritime and offshore energy support operations, aircraft often undergo routine inspections at remote offshore platforms or unequipped airfields. Restricting ferry permits entirely prevents operators from flying un-passengered, low-risk ferry flights to certified repair stations. The FAA has failed to show why a restricted ferry flight—where the emergency sea anchor is mechanically secured, deactivated, or removed prior to flight—presents an unmanageable safety risk under 14 CFR 21.197. Under the APA, failing to consider less restrictive, safe operational alternatives constitutes arbitrary and capricious decision-making.

2. Reliance on Basic Inspection Methods without Non-Destructive Testing (NDT) Guidelines (Page 54685, Section (g))
Rationale: EASA AD 2025-0278R1 specifies visual inspection for corrosion. Marine sea anchor pins exposed to continuous ocean spray are uniquely vulnerable to intergranular stress corrosion cracking that is undetectable to the naked eye until structural failure occurs. The FAA should mandate high-frequency Eddy Current Inspection (ET) or Ultrasonic Testing (UT) whenever surface micro-pitting is observed.

III. PROPOSED ALTERNATIVE REGULATORY TEXT

We propose revising the draft regulatory text as follows:

1. Amend Paragraph (j) Special Flight Permit (Page 54686):
'Special flight permits (14 CFR 21.197 and 21.199) may be issued provided that: (1) The flight is a non-revenue ferry flight to a maintenance facility; (2) No passengers are carried; and (3) The emergency sea anchor is either pinned with a secondary mechanical safety lock or deactivated in accordance with FAA-approved maintenance procedures prior to flight.'

2. Amend Paragraph (h) Exceptions to EASA AD 2025-0278R1 (Page 54685):
Add subparagraph (h)(5): '(5) Where the service information referenced in EASA AD 2025-0278R1 specifies visual inspection of the emergency sea anchor pin, any evidence of surface pitting or surface discoloration requires an Eddy Current Inspection (ET) to ensure no sub-surface stress corrosion cracking is present prior to returning the pin to service.'

IV. CONCLUSION
The FAA should adopt these technical and procedural modifications in the Final Rule to balance high aviation safety standards with operational viability.

title: Environmental Impact Statements; Availability, etc.: Travel Management; National Forest System Lands

ai_data.summary_of_main_idea: The U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) Forest Service is initiating rulemaking and an Environmental Impact Statement (EIS) to revise its Travel Management Regulations at 36 CFR Parts 212 and 261 following Executive Order 14408. The proposed rule establishes a uniform national policy featuring a default presumption that existing roads, trails, airfields, and access points on National Forest System lands are open to public use unless explicitly closed or restricted based on documented site-specific criteria. Additionally, the proposal removes national 'minimization criteria,' eliminates the requirement for a 'minimum road system,' simplifies procedural requirements for route designation revisions, and categorically exempts Class 1 electric bicycles on non-motorized bicycle trails.
ai_data.challenges:
1. Legal Defects under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA) & NFMA: Rescinding the long-standing national 'minimization criteria' (36 CFR 212.55(b)) without demonstrating that resource protection will be maintained constitutes arbitrary and capricious rulemaking under APA § 706(2)(A). Shifting to a default 'open unless closed' presumption conflicts with the Forest Service's statutory duties under the National Forest Management Act (NFMA, 16 U.S.C. 1604) and the Multiple-Use Sustained-Yield Act (MUSYA, 16 U.S.C. 528) to protect soil, watershed, and wildlife values from resource degradation.

2. Scientific and Technical Weaknesses: The proposal relies on aerial imagery and public data to establish existing physical routes while removing standardized environmental screening criteria. Decades of peer-reviewed conservation science show that unmanaged motorized access leads to severe soil erosion, stream sedimentation, direct wildlife displacement, and habitat fragmentation. Replacing mandatory minimization criteria with discretionary local closures shifts the burden of proof onto under-resourced field staff.

3. Economic Defects: The Forest Service currently faces a multi-billion-dollar deferred maintenance backlog on existing forest roads and trails. Establishing an open presumption and requiring annual reviews of all closed routes will severely inflate administrative and maintenance overhead without providing dedicated funding, exacerbating land management deficits and public safety risks.

Docket No. FS-2026-0100 | FR Doc. 2026-17211

I. INTRODUCTION
These comments are submitted in response to the USDA Forest Service Notice of Intent (NOI) to prepare an Environmental Impact Statement (EIS) and revise the Travel Management Regulations at 36 CFR Parts 212 and 261, published at 91 FR 54686–54691 (Aug. 24, 2026).

II. SPECIFIC CITATIONS AND LEGAL RATIONALE

1. Arbitrary Removal of Minimization Criteria (91 FR 54688–54689):
The Department proposes to exercise independent statutory discretion to remove national minimization criteria previously codified at 36 CFR 212.55(b). Under Motor Vehicle Mfrs. Ass'n v. State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co., 463 U.S. 29 (1983), an agency changing course must provide a reasoned explanation for disregarding prior factual findings. The TMR minimization criteria were designed to safeguard natural resources, water quality, and wildlife from severe damage caused by motorized vehicles. Eliminating these objective safeguards without presenting empirical evidence that environmental harm will not increase violates APA § 706(2)(A).

2. Reversal of Access Presumption and NFMA Inconsistency (91 FR 54687, 54689):
The NOI outlines a national framework establishing a presumption that all existing physical routes, airfields, and access points are 'open to appropriate public use' unless closed by local decree. This approach fundamentally subverts the principle of closed-unless-designated-open established in the 2005 TMR to curb user-created resource damage. Furthermore, decoupling travel management from Land Management Plans (91 FR 54688) creates a risk of non-compliance with NFMA statutory standards (16 U.S.C. § 1604(i)).

3. Procedural Shortcomings for Minor Revisions (91 FR 54688):
Exempting 'minor designation revisions' from standard public involvement and environmental screening under NEPA deprives local stakeholders of meaningful participation, in violation of 40 CFR 1500.2.

III. PROPOSED ALTERNATIVE REGULATORY TEXT

To ensure statutory compliance while enabling efficient local management, the USDA should adopt the following alternative text in the forthcoming proposed rule:

Section 212.55 (Designation Criteria): 'In designating National Forest System roads, National Forest System trails, and areas on National Forest System lands for public motor vehicle use, the responsible official SHALL apply the minimization criteria. Specifically, designations must be located to minimize: (1) damage to soil, watershed, vegetation, and other forest resources; (2) harassment of wildlife and significant disruption of wildlife habitats; (3) conflicts between motor vehicle use and existing or proposed recreational uses; and (4) conflicts among different classes of motor vehicle uses. Existing designations remain in effect until modified through site-specific NEPA analysis. No route shall be presumed open prior to completing environmental review and formally establishing legal jurisdiction and maintenance capacity.'

IV. CONCLUSION
The Forest Service must retain mandatory minimization criteria and reject an open-by-default presumption in the draft EIS.

title: Regulation Crypto Assets

ai_data.summary_of_main_idea: The Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) is proposing 'Regulation Crypto Assets' (17 CFR Part 228) to establish a tailored registration exemption and offering framework for covered investment contracts involving crypto assets. The rule creates a $5 million 'Startup Exemption' (with a 4-year duration limit) and a two-tiered 'Fundraising Exemption' permitting offerings up to $20 million (Tier 1) or $75 million (Tier 2) per 12-month period, backed by principles-based disclosure requirements. ai_data.challenges:
The proposed rule suffers from several key procedural, economic, and legal defects under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA):

1. Arbitrary Cap & Time Horizon on Startup Exemption (Rule 200, 91 FR 54532): The $5 million 4-year aggregate cap fails to reflect the realistic capital expenditure and timeline required to build secure, production-grade distributed ledger infrastructure. Forcing early-stage projects into full financial statement audits or abrupt sunsetting after four years creates an artificial cliff that harms network growth and capital formation.

2. GAAP Accounting Impossibility for Tier 2 Offerings (Rule 300 / Form 1-CRYPTO Part F/S, 91 FR 54546): Mandating standard U.S. GAAP audits without finalized FASB accounting standards governing token allocations, staking rewards, treasury distributions, and wrapped assets creates compliance impossibility and subjects startup issuers to prohibitive audit costs ($450,000+).

3. Arbitrary Retail Investment Limits in Tier 1 Offerings (Rule 300(c)(2)(i)(C), 91 FR 54541): Imposing a 10% income/net worth limitation on non-accredited investors across Tier 1 offerings directly conflicts with the technical necessity of cultivating widespread 'network effects' and programmatic token usage, depressing token velocity and user adoption.

4. Vague Safe Harbor Trigger Standards (Rule 400, 91 FR 54554): The standard for completing 'essential managerial efforts' remains overly subjective. The rule lacks bright-line guidance clarifying that routine post-launch software maintenance, protocol grant funding, and bug bounties do not constitute ongoing managerial efforts.

I. The $5 Million Aggregate Cap and 4-Year Sunset under Rule 200(b) Are Arbitrary and Unworkable (91 FR 54532).

Proposed Rule 200(b)(4) caps covered transactions under the Startup Exemption at $5,000,000 across a 4-year period. In modern distributed software engineering, $5 million is entirely insufficient to cover protocol security audits, formal verification, incentive allocations, and legal compliance. Furthermore, setting a hard 4-year sunset (Rule 200(b)(1)) ignores the realities of open-source development, where progressive decentralization often requires 5 to 7 years. Capping capital raising at $5 million forces early-stage developers into premature Tier 2 filings or offshore jurisdictions.

Proposed Revision to Rule 200(b)(1) & (4):
- Amend Rule 200(b)(1)(i) to read: '(i) Five years after the date of such filing, subject to a one-time two-year extension upon filing an updated Form NOR;'
- Amend Rule 200(b)(4) to read: 'The sum of the aggregate offering price in the covered transaction plus the gross proceeds from all covered transactions before the start of and during the current covered transaction must not exceed $10,000,000.'

II. The Application of Retail Investment Limits in Tier 1 Offerings Restricts Network Effects (91 FR 54541).

Proposed Rule 300(c)(2)(i)(C) limits non-accredited investor purchases in Tier 1 offerings to 10% of annual income or net worth. Unlike traditional equity securities, crypto assets derive security and utility from widespread distribution ('network effects'). Restricting individual retail user participation in low-cap Tier 1 offerings ($20 million or less) creates artificial friction for platform utility users without offering commensurate investor protection benefits.

Proposed Revision to Rule 300(c)(2)(i)(C):
- Amend Rule 300(c)(2)(i)(C) to add: 'Provided, however, that the investment limitations set forth in this paragraph (c)(2)(i)(C) shall not apply to Tier 1 offerings where the subject crypto asset is immediately usable for utility or governance functions within an operational or testnet associated crypto network or application.'

III. Clarification of Non-Managerial Post-Launch Activities under Rule 400 (91 FR 54554).

Proposed Rule 400(a) conditions the Investment Contract Safe Harbor on the complete cessation of 'essential managerial efforts.' To eliminate chilling uncertainty, the text of Rule 400 must explicitly clarify that open-source grant funding, protocol bug bounties, routine maintenance, and non-binding governance participation do not constitute essential managerial efforts.

Proposed Addition to Rule 400(a):
- Insert Instruction 1 to Rule 400(a): 'Instruction 1: For purposes of paragraph (a), an issuer's ongoing provision of open-source software updates, bug bounties, technical maintenance, ecosystem grant distributions, or non-binding governance recommendations shall not, standing alone, be deemed to constitute essential managerial efforts.'

Conclusion

By adjusting offering caps, exempting utility-focused Tier 1 transactions from retail caps, and clarifying post-launch maintenance under the safe harbor, the Commission can establish a truly fit-for-purpose regulatory framework that balances robust investor protection with American technological leadership.

Respectfully submitted,

/s/ Civic Advocates & Administrative Law Coalition

title: Listing of Compute Derivatives Contracts - Request for Comment

The initiative seeks to evaluate how these nascent instruments can comply with statutory requirements under the Commodity Exchange Act (CEA), specifically Core Principle 3 (ensuring contracts are not readily susceptible to manipulation) and Core Principle 4 (market surveillance). ai_data.challenges: The listing of compute derivatives presents severe legal, economic, and technical defects under the Commodity Exchange Act (CEA) and the Administrative Procedure Act (APA). First, compute lacks physical standardization and fungibility across hardware generations (e.g., NVIDIA B200 vs. H100), latency configurations, and cloud provider ecosystem dependencies, violating baseline criteria set forth in 17 CFR Part 38 Appendix C. Second, the cash market for compute is highly concentrated and fragmented, characterized by opaque, privately negotiated bilateral transactions rather than liquid, transparent spot markets. Reference price indices derived from provider-posted rates or thin trading venues are inherently vulnerable to price manipulation, self-dealing, and wash trading by dominant hyperscalers (CEA Section 5(d)(3), 7 U.S.C. 7(d)(3)). Third, permitting DCMs to list compute contracts via self-certification under 17 CFR 40.2 without establishing binding benchmark standards constitutes arbitrary and capricious agency action under the APA (5 U.S.C. 706(2)(A)).

Re: Request for Comment on the Listing of Compute Derivatives Contracts (RIN 3038-AF77; 91 FR 54259–54264)

I. Introduction
We submit these comments in response to the Commodity Futures Trading Commission's ("CFTC" or "Commission") Request for Comment ("RFC") regarding the listing of derivatives contracts referencing artificial intelligence processing capacity ("compute derivatives"). While recognizing the rapid macroeconomic expansion of AI infrastructure as noted on page 54260, we urge the Commission to enforce strict statutory compliance with the Commodity Exchange Act ("CEA") before approving or permitting the listing of any compute futures or swaps.

II. Substantive Legal and Economic Weaknesses

1. Incompatibility with DCM Core Principle 3 (7 U.S.C. 7(d)(3) & 17 CFR Part 38, Appendix C)
As acknowledged on pages 54262–54263 of the RFC, compute is currently an unstandardized, non-fungible, and non-storable service flow rather than a standardized physical commodity. Price formation occurs almost entirely through opaque, long-term bilateral transactions that are withheld from public view. Settlement price indices constructed from posted provider rates or low-volume spot venues fail to satisfy Appendix C to Part 38, which mandates that a cash-settled contract must rely on a cash price series that is liquid, reliable, and resistant to manipulation. Dominant compute providers possess the capability and financial incentive to distort underlying cash benchmark rates during observation windows to benefit off-exchange or on-exchange derivative positions.

2. Surveillance Infeasibility under DCM Core Principle 4 (7 U.S.C. 7(d)(4))
As highlighted in Question 2(d) on page 54263, DCMs currently lack information-sharing arrangements with private compute capacity providers and cloud execution venues. Without direct, verifiable access to primary transaction logs, independent audits, and order-book data, DCMs cannot fulfill their statutory obligation to monitor and prevent price distortion, corners, or squeezes.

3. Impermissibility of Rule 40.2 Self-Certification
Permitting DCMs to list cash-settled compute derivatives through self-certification pursuant to 17 CFR 40.2 creates grave market vulnerability. Given the structural risk of index manipulation, any attempt to bypass rigorous pre-approval under 17 CFR 40.3 would constitute arbitrary and capricious regulation under Section 706 of the Administrative Procedure Act.

III. Proposed Alternative Wording and Regulatory Framework

To ensure compliance with CEA Core Principles and protect market participants, the Commission should amend its Part 38 guidance by adopting the following binding provision:

"Proposed Rule Amendment (17 CFR § 38.202 - Mandatory Commission Review for Compute and Emerging Digital Infrastructure Derivatives):
(a) Prior Approval Required. Notwithstanding 17 CFR 40.2, no designated contract market or swap execution facility may list for trading any contract referencing the price, yield, or capacity of compute, artificial intelligence processing units, or cloud hardware, unless the Commission has formally approved such contract pursuant to 17 CFR 40.3.
(b) Benchmark Integrity Standard. Approval under paragraph (a) shall require the listing facility to demonstrate that:
  (1) At least 80% of the underlying index volume is derived from arm's-length, executed transactions subject to independent, third-party audit;
  (2) Sole reliance on posted, unexecuted, or provider-administered rates is expressly prohibited;
  (3) Binding information-sharing agreements exist between the DCM and venues accounting for a majority of the cash market underlying the index."

Respectfully submitted,
[Civic Advocates & Public Interest Coalition]

PUBLIC COMMENT ON PROPOSED RULEMAKING
Department of Homeland Security
8 CFR Part 103 [CIS No. 2798-25; DHS Docket No. USCIS-2026-0331; RIN 1615-AD21]
Genealogy Program Regulations To Clarify the Impact of Federal Records Requirements

I. INTRODUCTION AND STATEMENT OF INTEREST
The undersigned submit this formal public comment regarding DHS's Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) amending 8 CFR Part 103. While we recognize the statutory obligation of USCIS to transfer permanent records to the National Archives and Records Administration (NARA) pursuant to 44 U.S.C. 3102 and 36 CFR part 1220, the rule as written creates significant legal defects and procedural unfairness for public researchers, professional genealogists, and historians.

II. SPECIFIC CITATIONS AND LEGAL DEFECTS

1. Proposed 8 CFR 103.38(c) & 103.40(a) – Absence of Refund or Direct Referral Mechanisms
As proposed, 8 CFR 103.38(c) states that USCIS will not provide requesters with historical records transferred to NARA. However, the preamble (91 FR 54254) notes that when an individual submits Form G-1041 (Index Search Request) or Form G-1041A (Records Request) for records already at NARA, USCIS will simply 'inform the requestor that such records may be requested directly from NARA.' 
This process is arbitrary and capricious under 5 U.S.C. 706(2)(A). Requesters pay $30 (online) or $80 (paper) per request. Under the proposed rule, USCIS retains the fee despite performing no meaningful retrieval, while forcing the user to pay a secondary fee to NARA. USCIS must implement an automated verification system prior to payment or establish an inter-agency referral system that forwards requests and fees directly to NARA without requiring duplicative submissions.

2. Initial Regulatory Flexibility Analysis (IRFA) Deficiencies (91 FR 54256-54257)
DHS states that it 'does not currently have sufficient data to definitively assess the impact on small entities.' Disregarding the economic impact on thousands of self-employed professional genealogists and historical research small businesses violates the Regulatory Flexibility Act (5 U.S.C. 603). USCIS has collected Form G-1041 filings for nearly two decades and cannot rely on self-induced data blindspots to bypass its RFA statutory duties.

III. PROPOSED ALTERNATIVE REGULATORY TEXT
To resolve these procedural and legal deficiencies, we urge DHS to adopt the following amended text prior to finalizing the rule:

Amend 8 CFR 103.38 by revising paragraph (c) to read as follows:

'§ 103.38 Genealogy Program.
***
(c) Effect of Transfer of Historical Records to National Archives and Records Administration. 
(1) Under the genealogical research request process, USCIS will not provide requestors with historical records, as defined under 8 CFR 103.39, that have been transferred to the legal custody of the National Archives and Records Administration in accordance with the records schedule that governs the disposition of the records.
(2) Mandatory Search Refunds and Referral. If a requester submits Form G-1041 or Form G-1041A for a record series that USCIS has transferred to the legal custody of NARA, USCIS shall either: (i) automatically transfer the request and applicable filing fee to NARA for processing; or (ii) issue a full refund of the fee collected within 30 days of determining that legal custody rests with NARA, accompanied by specific instructions on how to request the file from NARA.'

title: Pesticide Tolerance; Exemptions, Petitions, Revocations, etc.: Petitions Filed for Residues of Pesticide Chemicals in or on Various Commodities—June 2026

ai_data.summary_of_main_idea: The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) is issuing a notice of receipt for several pesticide petitions submitted under Section 408 of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FFDCA), requesting the establishment or modification of maximum residue tolerances for active ingredients across multiple food and feed commodities. The petitions propose new residue thresholds for thiabendazole (cotton gin byproducts), fenpropathrin (various crop groups including leafy greens, tree nuts, and legumes), iptriazopyrid (rice, aquatic organisms, and animal tissue/milk products), and aviglycine HCl (almonds). The notice solicits public comment on these requested tolerances, analytical measurement methods, and potential commodity variations before the Agency conducts its full risk evaluations.
ai_data.challenges:
1. Administrative Procedure Act (APA) & FFDCA Procedural Deficiencies: The Agency solicits public comments on petitions prior to publishing its own preliminary risk assessments or verifying data completeness. Requiring public comment before providing EPA's independent evaluation of dietary risk, ecotoxicity, and bioaccumulation deprives the public of a meaningful opportunity to comment under APA 5 U.S.C. 553.
2. Bioaccumulation and Ecotoxicological Risks for Aquatic Species (Iptriazopyrid): Petition PP 5F9219 seeks tolerances for novel herbicide iptriazopyrid residues in fish, shellfish, and crustaceans at 0.04 ppm, alongside elevated poultry liver tolerances (0.60 ppm). The notice lacks empirical bioaccumulation kinetics or degradation pathways in aquatic environments, risking unchecked trophic transfer in marine and freshwater ecosystems.
3. Cumulative Exposure Violations under Food Quality Protection Act (FQPA) (Fenpropathrin): Petition PP 5E9210 significantly expands fenpropathrin (a synthetic pyrethroid) tolerances across wide crop subgroups (e.g., brassica, leafy greens at 15 ppm). Fenpropathrin shares a common mechanism of toxicity with other broad-spectrum pyrethroids. Establishing expanded tolerances without a updated cumulative risk assessment that factors in combined daily dietary exposure violates FFDCA § 408(b)(2)(C).
4. Enforcement Method Confidentiality & Validation Deficiencies: Petitions reference proprietary analytical methods (e.g., GRM040.01A, generic LC-MS/MS) without providing public access to method validation reports or standard operating procedures required for public health enforcement monitoring by state and federal regulatory agencies.

I. INTRODUCTION
These comments are submitted regarding the Environmental Protection Agency's (EPA) Notice of Filing for pesticide petitions proposing tolerance limits under FFDCA Section 408, published at 91 FR 53832–53834. While we recognize the statutory requirement under 21 U.S.C. 346a(d)(3) to publish petition notices, the Agency must ensure that tolerance approvals adhere to strict safety margins established by the Food Quality Protection Act (FQPA) and Administrative Procedure Act (APA) notice-and-comment standards.

II. LEGAL & SCIENTIFIC DEFICIENCIES

1. Inadequate Data Disclosure Under APA § 553 (89 FR 53833, Unit I.C)
EPA explicitly notes on page 53833 that it 'has not fully evaluated the sufficiency of the submitted data at this time or whether the data supports granting the pesticide petitions.' Requesting public comment on petitions without releasing the Agency's preliminary human health risk assessments (HHRAs) or ecological risk assessments (ERAs) denies stakeholders a meaningful opportunity to critique the technical foundations of these requests.

2. Failure to Account for Cumulative Pyrethroid Risk (PP 5E9210, Docket ID EPA-HQ-OPP-2026-3599)
The petition submitted by the IR-4 Project requests widespread tolerance expansions for fenpropathrin, including high tolerances such as 15 ppm in brassica leafy greens subgroup 4-16B and 5 ppm in cherry subgroup 12-12A. Fenpropathrin is a neurotoxic synthetic pyrethroid. Under 21 U.S.C. 346a(b)(2)(C), EPA must evaluate cumulative exposure from all pesticides sharing a common mechanism of toxicity. EPA cannot grant these modified tolerances without updating the comprehensive pyrethroid cumulative risk model to ensure aggregate dietary exposure does not exceed the acceptable daily intake (ADI).

3. Unsubstantiated Residue Tolerances for Aquatic Ecosystems and Animal Products (PP 5F9219, Docket ID EPA-HQ-OPP-2026-1784)
Nissan Chemical Corporation seeks tolerances for a new chemical entity, iptriazopyrid, across rice, animal fat/tissue, and specifically 'fish, shellfish, crustacean' at 0.04 ppm. Rice paddy effluents discharge directly into surrounding watersheds. Establishing a tolerance in aquatic organisms without providing public access to bioconcentration factor (BCF) data or depuration kinetics creates an unquantified risk of trophic biomagnification in coastal and estuarine food webs.

To ensure regulatory compliance and public health protection, EPA should adopt the following procedural and substantive rules prior to final tolerance determinations:

I. INTRODUCTION & PROCEDURAL DEFECTS
We submit these comments regarding the Environmental Protection Agency's (EPA) Notice of Filing of Pesticide Petitions for Residues of Pesticide Chemicals in or on Various Commodities (August 20, 2026, 91 FR 53832). Under Section 408(d)(3) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FFDCA), 21 U.S.C. § 346a(d)(3), EPA is required to provide public notice and opportunity for comment on pesticide petitions. However, as published in Unit I.C (91 FR 53833), the Agency admits that it 'has not fully evaluated the sufficiency of the submitted data at this time or whether the data supports granting the pesticide petitions.' 

By withholding raw hazard, exposure, and toxicological data from the public docket, EPA denies commenters a meaningful opportunity to participate, in violation of Administrative Procedure Act (APA) notice-and-comment requirements, 5 U.S.C. § 553. 

II. SPECIFIC SUBSTANTIVE CONCERNS

1. Cumulative Risk Analysis for Synthetic Pyrethroids (PP 5E9210 / Docket EPA-HQ-OPP-2026-3599):
The request by IR-4 Project to establish broad crop group tolerances for fenpropathrin across multiple crop subgroups (e.g., barley subgroup 15-22B, leafy greens 4-16B, tree nuts 14-12) must not be approved without a comprehensive cumulative risk assessment. Fenpropathrin shares a common mechanism of toxicity (voltage-gated sodium channel modulation) with other Type I and Type II pyrethroids. EPA must apply an additional 10-fold safety factor under FFDCA § 408(b)(2)(C) to protect infants and young children from cumulative neurodevelopmental impacts.

2. Ecotoxicity and Bioaccumulation of Iptriazopyrid (PP 5F9219 / Docket EPA-HQ-OPP-2026-1784):
Nissan Chemical Corporation requests tolerances for iptriazopyrid in rice grain (0.90 ppm) and straw (2.0 ppm), as well as livestock and aquatic organisms (fish, shellfish, crustacean at 0.04 ppm). Establishing tolerances in aquatic species indicates significant environmental persistence and potential for water column runoff from flooded rice fields into aquatic food webs. EPA must evaluate biomagnification risks in non-target aquatic organisms prior to approving these residue tolerances.

III. PROPOSED ALTERNATIVE REGULATORY TEXT

We request that EPA modify its final action by incorporating the following mandatory prerequisites into 40 CFR Part 180:

'Prior to establishing or modifying any tolerance listed in this Notice of Filing:
(a) The Administrator shall publish a full quantitative cumulative exposure assessment for all synthetic pyrethroids sharing a common mechanism of toxicity with fenpropathrin, incorporating an explicit 10x FFDCA safety factor for infants and young children.
(b) For iptriazopyrid (PP 5F9219), the Administrator shall complete a bioconcentration factor (BCF) and aquatic runoff exposure model demonstrating that residues in wild-caught and aquaculture fish/shellfish species will not exceed human health benchmark safety margins during peak agricultural discharge periods.
(c) The Agency shall reopen a 30-day public comment period upon disclosing complete toxicity, metabolism, and analytical validation studies in the public docket.'

I. INTRODUCTION
This comment is submitted in response to the Federal Aviation Administration's (FAA) Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM), Docket No. FAA-2026-8785, regarding Airworthiness Directives for Dassault Aviation Model FALCON 7X airplanes. The FAA estimates 1 work-hour per airplane ($85 labor) to perform the SPECU replacement. Real-world labor totals between 3.5 to 5.0 work-hours per unit, excluding potential operational downtime. The economic assessment should be adjusted to reflect $297.50–$425.00 in labor costs per aircraft, raising total U.S. fleet labor impact substantially.

2. Supply Chain Availability and Interim Operational Mitigations (FR Page 53787, Paragraph (g))
Because the proposed AD expands the applicability to additional SPECUs, part availability challenges are highly probable across the 160 U.S.-registered aircraft. Paragraph (g) currently mandates compliance solely per EASA AD 2026-0016 without specifying interim dispatch conditions or alternative temporary operational limitations (e.g., deactivation/pulling circuit breakers for non-essential standby systems during specific ground states) should replacement hardware be backordered.

1. Modify Section 'Costs of Compliance' Table on Page 53786:
Re-calculate labor estimates to reflect 4 work-hours per product ($340 labor cost), updating the total cost per product to $22,937 and total operator cost to $3,669,920.

2. Insert New Paragraph (h)(5) under Section (h) 'Exceptions to EASA AD 2026-0016':
'(5) Where EASA AD 2026-0016 mandates replacement within a specified compliance time, if an affected SPECU is unavailable due to documented manufacturer supply chain backorders, operators may request an Alternative Method of Compliance (AMOC) under paragraph (j)(1) of this AD allowing interim operational procedures or flight limitations approved by the Manager, International Validation Branch, FAA.'

title: GENIUS Act Regulations on Payment Stablecoin Issuance, Offer, and Sale

ai_data.summary_of_main_idea: The proposed rule by the Department of the Treasury establishes regulations implementing Section 3 of the Guiding and Establishing National Innovation for U.S. Stablecoins (GENIUS) Act (12 U.S.C. 5902), regulating the issuance, offer, and sale of payment stablecoins in the United States. It restricts stablecoin issuance to permitted domestic issuers or qualified foreign issuers under Section 18(a), while subjecting digital asset service providers (DASPs) to strict compliance, due diligence, and technological mandates when offering stablecoins to U.S. persons. Additionally, it defines key statutory terms, delineates extraterritorial jurisdiction, sets DASP due diligence standards for foreign legal compliance, and outlines participation activities subject to statutory civil and criminal penalties.
ai_data.challenges:
The proposed rule suffers from key legal, procedural, and economic defects:
1. Statutory Overreach & APA Flaws (Collapse of Issuer and DASP Categories): By defining any person that engages in the business of issuing payment stablecoins for profit as a 'digital asset service provider' under proposed § 1523.1(c) (91 FR 53371), Treasury conflates distinct statutory definitions in Sections 2(7) and 2(23) of the GENIUS Act. This creates double regulatory exposure and exceeds Treasury's statutory authority, violating the Administrative Procedure Act (APA) under Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo.
2. Due Process & Vagueness in 'Participation' Liabilities: Proposed § 1523.2(d) (91 FR 53378) extends severe criminal penalties under 12 U.S.C. 5902(f) to third parties (e.g., liquidity providers, white-label branders, initial listing exchanges) without establishing a clear scienter/mens rea standard or bright-line safe harbors, rendering the provision void for vagueness and arbitrary under State Farm.
3. Unworkable DASP Verification Standards: Proposed § 1523.3(c) (91 FR 53382) requires DASPs to conduct onerous due diligence and verify code-level 'seize, freeze, and burn' capabilities of foreign issuers. This places an unfeasible audit burden on non-issuer intermediaries and threatens liquidity on domestic exchanges.
4. Deficient Economic & RFA Analysis: Treasury fails to adequately quantify compliance costs for open-source protocol developers, liquidity pools, and non-custodial intermediaries, relying on flawed assumptions regarding compliance overlaps and market concentration risks.

ai_data.proposed_comment:
COMMENTS OF CIVIC AND FINANCIAL INNOVATION ADVOCATES

To: Department of the Treasury
Re: Notice of Proposed Rulemaking on GENIUS Act Regulations on Payment Stablecoin Issuance, Offer, and Sale
Docket No.: TREAS-DO-2026-0496 | RIN 1505-AC95 | 12 CFR Part 1523 (91 FR 53368–53391)

I. INTRODUCTION AND STATEMENT OF INTEREST
We submit these public comments in response to the Department of the Treasury's Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) regarding 12 CFR Part 1523 implementing Section 3 of the Guiding and Establishing National Innovation for U.S. Stablecoins (GENIUS) Act (12 U.S.C. 5902). While we support clear rules of the road for stablecoins, key aspects of the proposed rule exceed statutory authority under the GENIUS Act, create severe due process concerns, and impose unworkable compliance burdens on market participants.

II. LEGAL DEFECTS AND PROPOSED AMENDMENTS

1. Impermissible Expansion of 'Digital Asset Service Provider' to Include Issuers (§ 1523.1(c), 91 FR 53371)
Rationale: Proposed § 1523.1(c) states that 'a person that, for compensation or profit, engages in the business in the United States of issuing payment stablecoins is a digital asset service provider.' This interpretation conflates two distinct statutory roles created by Congress in Sections 2(7) and 2(23) of the Act. Forcing issuers into the DASP framework creates redundant regulatory obligations and subjects issuers to conflicting offer/sale restrictions intended solely for secondary intermediaries. Under Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, 144 S. Ct. 2244 (2024), courts will not defer to Treasury's overbroad reading of clear statutory definitions.
Proposed Wording for § 1523.1(c):
"Digital asset service provider has the meaning set forth in section 2(7) of the Act (12 U.S.C. 5901(7)). For the avoidance of doubt, an entity acting strictly in its capacity as a permitted payment stablecoin issuer or registered foreign payment stablecoin issuer under section 18(a) of the Act shall not be deemed a digital asset service provider solely by virtue of issuing or redeeming payment stablecoins in accordance with its statutory authority."

2. Due Process Deficiencies and Scienter Standard in Participation Penalties (§ 1523.2(d), 91 FR 53378, 53390)
Rationale: Proposed § 1523.2(d) enumerates examples of secondary activities—such as white-label branding, software coordination, or market making—that constitute criminal 'participation' under Section 3(f) of the Act (12 U.S.C. 5902(f)). As drafted, this section lacks an explicit mens rea requirement, threatening market makers and software providers with strict criminal liability for routine liquidity activities. To satisfy Due Process and avoid impermissible vagueness, Treasury must clarify that criminal participation requires actual knowledge and intentional facilitation of an unlawful issuance.
Proposed Wording for § 1523.2(d):
"(d) A person knowingly participates in a violation of paragraph (a) for purposes of the penalty in section 3(f) of the Act (12 U.S.C. 5902(f)) only if the person has actual knowledge that the payment stablecoin issuance violates paragraph (a) and intentionally acts to facilitate such unlawful issuance by:
(1) Directly incurring a primary or secondary legal obligation to convert, redeem, or repurchase the unlawful payment stablecoin;
(2) Purposefully coordinating with the issuer to directly execute the unlawful minting or distribution; or
(3) Acting as a primary underwriter or designated market maker directly for the issuer in the initial distribution of the unlawfully issued payment stablecoin with actual knowledge of its unapproved status."

3. Adoption of a Bright-Line Regulation S Offshore Framework for DASPs (§ 1523.3(e), 91 FR 53384, 53390)
Rationale: The proposed due diligence standard in § 1523.3(c) and (e) creates an impossible verification burden for DASPs regarding foreign issuer code capabilities and future legal compliance. Treasury specifically requested comment on whether to adopt a Regulation S-style framework (Questions 45, 65). Adopting an offshore-transaction standard provides clarity, aligns with existing SEC compliance infrastructure, and prevents regulatory flowback issues without stifling domestic commerce.
Proposed Wording for § 1523.3(e):
"(e) Safe Harbor for Offshore Transactions. A digital asset service provider shall be deemed not to offer, sell, or make available a payment stablecoin to a person located in the United States if:
(1) The offer or sale is executed in an offshore transaction where the buyer is reasonably believed to be outside the United States at the time the order is placed;
(2) The digital asset service provider maintains IP-geofencing, identity verification, or contractual prohibitions reasonably designed to prevent access by U.S. residents; and
(3) The digital asset service provider does not engage in directed selling efforts or targeted marketing campaigns directed to individuals located in the United States."

III. CONCLUSION
Treasury should revise the proposed rule to respect statutory boundaries, provide explicit mens rea protections for secondary market actors, and implement a pragmatic Regulation S safe harbor.

title: Airworthiness Directives: The Boeing Company Airplanes

ai_data.summary_of_main_idea: The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) proposes to adopt a new airworthiness directive (AD) for Boeing Model 737-300, -400, and -500 series airplanes following reports of nuisance stick shaker activations caused by frozen angle of airflow (AOA) sensor vanes. The proposed rule mandates installing new external case heaters on left and right AOA sensors, conducting repetitive functional tests, and executing extensive concurrent actions such as replacing insulation blankets with flame-retardant material and rewiring air data probe heat systems. The agency aims to prevent stall warning system failures that could compromise continued safe flight and landing.
ai_data.challenges:
The proposed rule suffers from key legal, economic, and technical vulnerabilities:

1. Regulatory Flexibility Act (RFA) Defect: The FAA improperly certified under 5 U.S.C. 605(b) that the rule would not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities. While the core modification costs $2,125 per aircraft, required 'concurrent actions' add up to 888 work-hours and $109,883 per aircraft—amounting to over $14.6 million for the 133 affected U.S. airplanes. Because 737 Classic aircraft are predominantly flown by small regional cargo operators, this heavy economic burden severely impacts small businesses without adequate RFA analysis.

2. Administrative Procedure Act (APA) Procedural Flaws regarding Material Incorporated by Reference (IBR): The rule conditions compliance on proprietary Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin 737-30A1081 RB, Revision 1, which is locked behind commercial paywalls (myboeingfleet.com) or restricted viewing. Requiring public compliance with non-public technical specifications violates 5 U.S.C. 552(a) and deprives stakeholders of a meaningful opportunity to comment under APA section 533.

3. Overbroad Scope of Concurrent Requirements: Mandating 888 hours of major structural overhaul (replacing fuselage insulation blankets and modifying circuit breaker panels) under the guise of an AOA sensor heater fix lacks demonstrated risk-proportionality and causal necessity under 14 CFR Part 39, overreaching the immediate safety imperative.

ai_data.proposed_comment:
COMMENTS OF CIVIC ADVOCATES AND MARITIME STAKEHOLDERS

Docket No. USCG-2024-0667 | RIN 1625-AA01
33 CFR Part 110: Anchorages; Bolivar Roads Channel, Galveston, TX
Published at 91 FR 53395 (August 18, 2026)

I. INTRODUCTION AND STATEMENT OF INTEREST
We respectfully submit these comments in response to the Coast Guard’s Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) published at 91 FR 53395 (August 18, 2026), regarding the proposed 48-hour time limit for Bolivar Anchorage Area (A) East under 33 CFR 110.197(b)(2). While we support the Coast Guard's objective of enhancing port safety and managing navigation congestion, the proposed rule as written contains critical procedural defects under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA) and poses unstudied operational and economic risks to commercial maritime operations.

II. SPECIFIC COMMENTS AND LEGAL DEFECTS

1. Lack of Empirical Supporting Evidence in the Public Docket (91 FR 53395, Section II)
The preamble states that the Coast Guard determined the necessity of a 48-hour restriction '[a]fter discussion with the local maritime community during a Harbor Safety Committee meeting.' However, the Coast Guard has placed no empirical traffic studies, queuing data, or safety audit records into Docket No. USCG-2024-0667. Under the Administrative Procedure Act, 5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A), agency action is arbitrary and capricious if it relies on factors Congress did not intend, entirely fails to consider an important aspect of the problem, or offers an explanation that runs counter to the evidence. Informal committee dialogue alone does not constitute a robust factual basis for federal regulatory action.

2. Improper Regulatory Flexibility Certification (91 FR 53395-53396, Section IV.A)
The Coast Guard certifies under 5 U.S.C. § 605(b) that this rule will not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities because it 'merely institutes a 48-hour time limitation in an already existing anchorage area.' This conclusion fails to consider the real-world operational realities of lightering, bunkering, and terminal delays in the Galveston/Houston ship channel. Forcing small vessel operators, tug/barge fleets, and ocean carriers to heave anchor after 48 hours to seek permissions or move offshore incurs hundreds of thousands of dollars annually in pilotage fees, fuel burn, and demurrage costs. A formal Regulatory Flexibility Analysis under 5 U.S.C. § 603 is required.

3. Operational Need for Lightering and Weather Exceptions (33 CFR 110.197(b)(2))
While the rule provides an exception for 'stress of weather,' it fails to explicitly accommodate ongoing commercial operations, such as ship-to-ship transfers (lightering), bunkering, or documented delays in berth availability at local facilities. Requiring vessels mid-transfer or awaiting berth clearances to submit individualized permission requests to the Captain of the Port (COPT) creates unnecessary administrative overhead for both the Coast Guard VTS and mariners.

III. PROPOSED ALTERNATIVE REGULATORY TEXT

To resolve these legal and operational deficiencies, we propose amending the regulatory text at 33 CFR 110.197(b)(2) to explicitly incorporate operational extensions for ongoing cargo operations, bunkering, and terminal congestion delays:

Proposed Revision to 33 CFR § 110.197(b)(2):

"(2) Except when stress of weather makes sailing impractical or hazardous, or when engaged in active lightering, bunkering, or awaiting documented terminal berth availability, vessels shall not anchor in anchorage areas (A), (A) East, (B), or (C) for more than 48 hours unless expressly authorized by the Captain of the Port Houston-Galveston. Permission to anchor for longer periods may be requested through Coast Guard Vessel Traffic Service Houston/Galveston on VHF-FM channels 12 (156.60 MHz) or 13 (156.65 MHz) or via electronic notification. An extension of up to 48 additional hours shall be routinely granted for vessels demonstrating active lightering or pending terminal readiness."

IV. CONCLUSION
We urge the Coast Guard to perform a complete economic impact analysis and revise 33 CFR 110.197(b)(2) with flexible operational language prior to issuing a Final Rule.

I. INTRODUCTION
The undersigned submit these comments in response to the Federal Aviation Administration's (FAA) Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) published at 91 FR 53393 on August 18, 2026, proposing to establish Class E airspace extending upward from 700 feet above the surface at Trading Bay Production Airport, Trading Bay, AK.

II. PROCEDURAL AND TECHNICAL DEFECTS UNDER THE ADMINISTRATIVE PROCEDURE ACT
The proposed rule fails to satisfy the basic notice requirements of Section 553 of the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), 5 U.S.C. § 553, due to fatal factual, mathematical, and nomenclature errors:

1. Critical Longitude Discrepancy: On page 53394, the FAA states that the Class E airspace boundary split line is 'centered approximately 250 feet west of the airport reference point' at long. 151°50'13" W. However, the official Airport Reference Point (ARP) listed in the proposed regulatory text (page 53395) is Lat. 60°49'00" N, Long. 151°47'59" W. At 60.8° North latitude, a difference of 2 minutes and 14 seconds of longitude (151°47'59" W vs. 151°50'13" W) equals approximately 1.09 nautical miles (over 6,600 feet)—not 250 feet as asserted in the narrative. This severe mathematical discrepancy renders the geographic boundary legal description fundamentally flawed and legally ambiguous.
2. Conflicting Facility Naming: Page 53394 refers to the facility as 'Trader Bay Production Airport' in 'The Proposal' narrative, whereas the title, summary, and legal designation use 'Trading Bay Production Airport'. 

Because the public cannot determine the true legal boundaries of the proposed airspace from this flawed notice, the FAA must issue a corrected Supplemental Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (SNPRM).

III. UNADRESSED IMPACTS ON VFR GENERAL AVIATION AND AIR TAXI OPERATIONS
The Cook Inlet coastal corridor is a vital low-altitude transit route for Visual Flight Rules (VFR) general aviation pilots, commercial air charter services, and local fishery support flights. Establishing Class E airspace down to 700 feet AGL imposes 14 CFR § 91.155 VFR weather minimums (3 miles visibility, 500 ft below / 1,000 ft above clouds), depriving pilots of the Class G daylight weather minimums (1 mile visibility, clear of clouds). In Alaska’s frequent ceiling and visibility constrained climate, this action creates a critical low-altitude bottleneck, forcing unequipped VFR aircraft into hazardous terrain or offshore maritime routes.

IV. DEFICIENT REGULATORY FLEXIBILITY ACT ANALYSIS
The FAA's certification under 5 U.S.C. § 605(b) that this rule will result in 'de minimis costs' is unreasoned and arbitrary. The agency failed to analyze the cumulative economic burden imposed on local Part 135 charter operators, small commercial entities, and rural air taxis who will experience flight delays, cancellations, or fuel penalties due to lost Class G VFR passage.

V. PROPOSED ALTERNATIVE TEXT
Should the FAA proceed, it must reissue an amended NPRM correcting the boundary calculations and capping the Class E designation to protect a VFR transit corridor:

Proposed Amendment to 14 CFR § 71.1:

'AAL CA E5 Trading Bay, AK [Amended]
Trading Bay Production Airport, AK
(Lat. 60°49'00" N, long. 151°47'59" W)

That airspace extending upward from 700 feet above the surface within a 3.9-mile radius west and a 7-mile radius east of long. 151°48'03" W (centered 250 feet west of the airport reference point), excluding that airspace below 1,200 feet AGL along the immediate coastal VFR transit corridor standard route.'

VI. CONCLUSION
The FAA must withdraw the NPRM, correct the technical geographic descriptions, conduct a real-world study of VFR traffic flow along the Cook Inlet, and issue an amended proposal for public review.

This comment is submitted regarding the Federal Aviation Administration's (FAA) Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) published at 91 FR 53200 (August 17, 2026). While supporting the core safety objective of preventing engine in-flight shutdowns (IFSD) caused by oil pressure anomalies in Rolls-Royce Trent XWB engines, we submit that the proposed rule exhibits significant economic underestimation, procedural deficiencies under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), and operational vagueness.

II. PROCEDURAL AND APA DEFICIENCIES REGARDING INCORPORATION BY REFERENCE
On page 53201, the FAA proposes to incorporate European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) AD 2024-0070 by reference. However, the foundational technical service materials developed by Rolls-Royce specifying the physical steps and part numbers are not fully accessible in the public Federal eRulemaking docket at regulations.gov. Under 5 U.S.C. 553, the APA mandates that agencies provide a meaningful opportunity to comment on the complete rationale and supporting technical data of a proposed rule. Relying on proprietary manufacturer documents behind paywalls or restricted access limits public scrutiny and procedural due process.

III. UNDERESTIMATION OF ECONOMIC IMPACT AND LABOR HOURS
In the Costs of Compliance section (pp. 53201–53202), the FAA estimates labor at 3.5 work-hours ($297.50 per engine) and parts at $6,375, totaling $6,672.50 per engine. This estimate is unsupportable for heavy widebody engine maintenance. Modifying the front bearing housing oil feed tube assembly routinely requires major cowling access, engine disassembly, or engine removal depending on the aircraft maintenance status. The FAA fails to evaluate aircraft downtime costs, which can exceed $50,000 to $100,000 per day for long-haul widebody aircraft (e.g., Airbus A350). The FAA must perform a realistic economic evaluation under the Regulatory Flexibility Act and Executive Order 12866.

IV. PROPOSED REVISIONS TO REGULATORY TEXT
To resolve these defects, we propose amending Paragraph (g) and Paragraph (h) of the proposed regulatory text on page 53202 as follows:

Paragraph (g) Proposed Text Revision:
'(g) Required Actions: Except as specified in paragraphs (h) and (i) of this AD, perform all required actions within the compliance times specified in EASA AD 2024-0070. Alignment with Scheduled Maintenance: Operators may accomplish the modification required by this AD during the next scheduled engine shop visit or within 24 calendar months after the effective date of this AD, whichever occurs first, provided that differential oil pressure monitoring protocols are maintained in accordance with FAA-approved maintenance procedures.'

Paragraph (h)(4) Proposed Addition:
'(h)(4) Where the service material referenced in EASA AD 2024-0070 specifies immediate unscheduled removal, this AD permits continued operation provided real-time oil pressure telemetry shows continuous compliance above amber limits.'

V. CONCLUSION
The FAA should publish the underlying service bulletins to the public docket, extend the comment period, and update its cost-benefit analysis before issuing a Final Rule.

The petitions seek new or expanded residue tolerances for active ingredients including indoxacarb, glufosinate-P-ammonium, topramezone, and florylpicoxamid across extensive agricultural crops and livestock products. ai_data.challenges:
The notice presents several legal, scientific, and procedural vulnerabilities under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA) and the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FFDCA):

1. APA Procedural and Transparency Deficiencies (5 U.S.C. § 553): EPA has invited public comment on petitions without disclosing the complete petitioner risk assessments, toxicological endpoints, or exposure modeling in the public docket. Soliciting comment on mere tolerance levels without providing underlying safety data deprives the public of a meaningful opportunity to comment.

2. FFDCA Safety Standard and Aggregate Risk (21 U.S.C. § 346a(b)(2)): FFDCA mandates that a tolerance be established only if there is a 'reasonable certainty that no harm will result from aggregate exposure' (including dietary, drinking water, and non-occupational exposures). Several petitions (e.g., glufosinate-P-ammonium and florylpicoxamid) propose dozens of concurrent new tolerances across major food groups without demonstrating cumulative toxicity assessments or accounting for co-exposures with isomeric forms or related compounds.

3. Food Quality Protection Act (FQPA) Children's Safety Factor: The petitions request tolerances on major staple foods heavily consumed by infants and children (e.g., apples, blueberries, milk, potatoes, juice commodities). FFDCA Section 408(b)(2)(C) requires an explicit 10x safety factor to protect infants and children unless reliable data demonstrate a lower factor is safe. Granting broad tolerances without publishing pre-evaluation neurotoxicity and developmental data risks violating statutory protections for vulnerable sub-populations.

Docket ID: EPA-HQ-OPP-2026-0332
Federal Register Vol. 91, No. 157, pp. 53221–53223 (August 17, 2026)

I. INTRODUCTION

These comments are submitted regarding the Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA) notice of receipt of pesticide petitions proposing to establish or amend tolerances under Section 408 of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FFDCA), 21 U.S.C. § 346a. The petitions under review—specifically PP 5F9204 (Indoxacarb), PP 5F9167 (Glufosinate-P-ammonium), PP 5F9194 (Topramezone), and PP 6F9235 (Florylpicoxamid)—request extensive new tolerances across a wide array of raw agricultural commodities, processed foods, and animal feed products.

While EPA is required by 21 U.S.C. § 346a(d)(3) to publish notice of these filings, the present notice fails to afford the public a meaningful opportunity to comment under Section 553 of the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), 5 U.S.C. § 553. Furthermore, EPA must ensure strict adherence to the safety standards mandated by the Food Quality Protection Act (FQPA) amendments to the FFDCA before any of these petitions are approved.

II. SPECIFIC LEGAL AND TECHNICAL DEFICIENCIES

1. Procedural Inadequacy of the Public Comment Opportunity (APA § 553)
As noted in Unit I.C of the Notice (91 FR 53221–53222), EPA acknowledges that it 'has not fully evaluated the sufficiency of the submitted data at this time or whether the data supports granting the pesticide petitions.' While petitioner summaries are referenced, the underlying raw scientific dossiers, toxicological studies, and dietary exposure models supporting requested tolerances (such as the proposed 30 ppm for florylpicoxamid on hop/leaves or 15 ppm for glufosinate-P-ammonium on cotton seed) have not been made accessible to the public. To ensure procedural due process, EPA must docket the complete hazard and exposure assessments prior to issuing any proposed tolerance regulations.

2. Impermissible Risk Assessment for Glufosinate-P-Ammonium (PP 5F9167)
Albaugh North America Limited requests tolerances for glufosinate-P-ammonium across over 50 crop and livestock commodities. Glufosinate compounds carry well-documented neurotoxic concerns due to glutamine synthetase inhibition. The Agency must perform an explicit aggregate exposure assessment combining dietary intake, municipal drinking water exposure, and residential turf/garden exposure before granting these tolerances. Furthermore, the Agency must evaluate cumulative exposure alongside racemic glufosinate-ammonium compounds to avoid underestimating toxicological load.

3. Mandatory Application of the 10x FQPA Safety Factor (21 U.S.C. § 346a(b)(2)(C))
Several requested tolerances encompass dietary staples heavily consumed by infants, toddlers, and pregnant women (e.g., apples, blueberries, sweet corn, potatoes, and milk). Under FFDCA Section 408(b)(2)(C), EPA must retain an additional tenfold (10x) safety factor to account for potential pre- and post-natal toxicity and completeness of the data unless reliable empirical data prove that a lower factor will be safe for infants and children. EPA must not waive or reduce this 10x margin without publishing an explicit, peer-reviewed scientific justification in the docket.

III. PROPOSED ALTERNATIVE REGULATORY TEXT / ACTIONS

To correct these deficiencies, EPA should adopt the following regulatory actions in any eventual proposed rule or order responding to these petitions:

1. Order Docket Extension & Disclosure: 'EPA shall publish a supplemental docket notice containing the complete toxicological endpoints, dietary exposure assessments, and aggregate risk models for Petitions 5F9204, 5F9167, 5F9194, and 6F9235, reopening the public comment period for 30 days following such publication.'

2. Mandatory Safety Retention Provision in 40 CFR Part 180: 'In establishing tolerances pursuant to Petition 5F9167 (Glufosinate-P-ammonium) and Petition 6F9235 (Florylpicoxamid), the Agency shall maintain an explicit 10-fold FQPA safety margin for pediatric sub-populations across all food commodity categories where acute or chronic neurotoxicity endpoints remain uncharacterized.'

IV. CONCLUSION

EPA must uphold its statutory mandate under 21 U.S.C. § 346a to ensure with 'reasonable certainty that no harm' will result from aggregate exposures. EPA should not grant the petitioned tolerances without first making full toxicological evaluations available for public review and maintaining statutory child-safety protections.

Re: EPA Docket No. EPA-HQ-OPP-2026-0332; FRL-13201-05-OCSPP
Notice of Filing of Pesticide Petitions for Residues of Pesticide Chemicals in or on Various Commodities (May 2026); 91 FR 53221–53223 (Aug. 17, 2026).

I. INTRODUCTION & EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
We submit these public comments regarding EPA’s notice of receipt of pesticide petitions proposing new and modified residue tolerances under Section 408 of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FFDCA), 21 U.S.C. § 346a. While public notice is required under 21 U.S.C. § 346a(d)(3), the Agency’s failure to publish preliminary risk assessments or complete data sufficiency evaluations concurrently with this notice restricts the public's ability to evaluate whether granting these petitions meets the statutory safety standard: 'a reasonable certainty that no harm will result from aggregate exposure to the pesticide chemical residue.' 21 U.S.C. § 346a(b)(2)(A)(ii).

II. SPECIFIC LEGAL AND TECHNICAL DEFICIENCIES

1. Inadequate Information Disclosure under APA 5 U.S.C. § 553 and FFDCA § 408(d)(3)
At 91 FR 53221–53222 (Unit I.C), EPA states that it 'has not fully evaluated the sufficiency of the submitted data at this time or whether the data supports granting the pesticide petitions.' Merely listing proposed parts-per-million (ppm) targets without releasing EPA’s draft hazard characterization, aggregate exposure assessments, or crop field trial data deprives commenters of the technical basis necessary to offer meaningful public input, violating core APA notice-and-comment principles.

2. Lack of Aggregate and Cumulative Exposure Analysis for Glufosinate-P-ammonium (PP 5F9167)
Albaugh North America Limited requests tolerances across over 40 distinct commodities, including major dietary staples (corn, soybean, potatoes, citrus, milk, and meat products). FFDCA § 408(b)(2)(C) mandates that EPA consider available information regarding the special susceptibility of infants and children and aggregate exposure from non-occupational sources. Granting extensive tolerances for glufosinate-P-ammonium—an active isomer with known biological activity—without presenting cumulative toxicity studies alongside other glufosinate formulations undermines the safety finding required by law.

3. Unsubstantiated Animal Feed Transfer Factors for Indoxacarb (PP 5F904) and Florylpicoxamid (PP 6F9235)
Control Solutions, Inc. proposes amending indoxacarb tolerances in milk (0.50 ppm) and cattle fat (1.9 ppm). Corteva Agriscience proposes extensive florylpicoxamid feed tolerances (e.g., wheat forage at 2.0 ppm, barley hay at 2.0 ppm). EPA must ensure that bioaccumulation in dairy and beef livestock is fully accounted for using robust dietary burden calculations under 40 CFR Part 180 before establishing these residue ceilings.

III. PROPOSED ALTERNATIVE REGULATORY TEXT

We request that EPA adopt the following procedural and regulatory directives in any future action on these petitions:

1. Mandatory Pre-Decision Docket Update:
'Prior to issuing a final rule under 21 U.S.C. 346a(d)(4)(A) establishing or amending tolerances for Indoxacarb (PP 5F9204), Glufosinate-P-ammonium (PP 5F9167), Topramezone (PP 5F9194), or Florylpicoxamid (PP 6F9235), the Agency shall publish a full Human Health Risk Assessment and Ecological Risk Assessment in the public docket and reopen the public comment period for a minimum of 30 days.'

2. Addition of Safety Factor Stipulation:
'In establishing any final tolerance under 40 CFR Part 180 for Glufosinate-P-ammonium or Indoxacarb, the Administrator shall apply an additional tenfold (10X) margin of safety for infants and children pursuant to FFDCA section 408(b)(2)(C), unless complete, peer-reviewed neurotoxicity and developmental toxicity datasets conclusively demonstrate that a reduced margin will fully protect public health.'

IV. CONCLUSION
EPA must withhold granting these tolerance petitions until comprehensive toxicity evaluations, aggregate dietary risk assessments, and verified animal transfer studies are published in the docket for public review.
